html:
Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys large, high-quality gemstones, including green Colombian emeralds, Burmese rubies and Ceylon blue sapphires. Certificates are welcome but not required. Bring the complete ring and existing records for evaluation.

In this guide

  • Our focus: large, high-quality gemstones
  • Start with what you know about the ring
  • Discuss the gemstone and the setting separately
  • Organize the paperwork without buying unnecessary reports
  • A purchase offer answers a different question from an appraisal
  • Arrange a gemstone-ring evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Our focus: large, high-quality gemstones

Our gemstone buying is limited to large, high-quality stones. Green Colombian emeralds, Burmese rubies from Myanmar and Ceylon blue sapphires from Sri Lanka are examples of our focus. Certificates are welcome but not required. Describe what you have so we can discuss an appropriate evaluation.

This is separate from our diamond buying: we buy natural, cut and polished diamonds of any size or shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds.

Start with what you know about the ring

Write down the name used on the original receipt, any markings inside the band, and repairs you know about. Describe an unknown stone as unknown. A blue stone is not enough evidence to call a ring a sapphire, and a family description does not establish a geographic origin.

Bring the ring intact. The setting may limit what can be measured or examined, but removing the stone at home can damage both parts. Ask what can be assessed while it is mounted and whether further examination would meaningfully change the purchase decision.

Discuss the gemstone and the setting separately

Stone size alone does not explain quality. For example, GIA's sapphire guide discusses color, clarity, cut and carat weight. Different gemstone varieties need their own assessment; a diamond grading scale cannot simply be applied to every colored stone.

Ask which identification or treatment information is known, which comes from a report, and which remains uncertain. Then ask how the metal, accent diamonds, maker's marks and condition of the ring affect the total offer. Our sapphire and diamond jewelry guide covers pieces with more than one type of stone.

Organize the paperwork without buying unnecessary reports

Keep the laboratory report with the matching ring. A purchase receipt, insurance schedule and repair invoice can each add context, but they serve different purposes. If you cannot match a document confidently, bring it and explain the uncertainty.

  • Bring existing reports and the original sales description, if available.
  • Note a chipped stone, loose setting, resizing or replacement stone.
  • Keep any original box and detached parts with the ring.
  • Photograph the item for your own inventory before the visit.

Ask whether an additional laboratory report is useful before paying for one. Its cost and turnaround should make sense for the actual piece and your reason for selling.

A purchase offer answers a different question from an appraisal

A purchase offer states what a buyer is prepared to pay under the stated terms. A formal appraisal identifies its purpose and valuation basis. GIA's appraisal guidance explains that GIA grades and identifies gems but does not assign their monetary value.

For an insurance or estate assignment, discuss the required document with the professional requesting it. For a sale, compare purchase amounts for the same ring, with the same stones and accessories included. An insurance replacement figure is not a promised resale amount.

Arrange a gemstone-ring evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Contact us before your visit to describe the ring and discuss timing. Payment choices are cash, bank wire and business check; confirm arrangements for your transaction.

Can I bring a ring without a gemstone report?

Yes. Bring what you have and identify any missing information. The actual ring needs examination; a photograph or a seller's description cannot settle every identification question.

Should I clean or repair the ring first?

Discuss its condition before spending money on repairs or using a cleaning treatment. Keep the stone and setting together, and point out any loose or damaged parts when presenting the ring.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

If you need to sell a luxury watch on a deadline, call before visiting. Confirm that the buyer can review your model, ask what authentication or condition checks are needed, and agree on payment arrangements before accepting an offer.

In this guide

  • Explain your deadline when arranging the visit
  • Gather the watch and its history
  • Understand what may need closer examination
  • Confirm the offer and payment together
  • Plan the trip with enough time for questions

Explain your deadline when arranging the visit

Tell the buyer the watch brand, model or reference if known, whether it runs, and whether you have its box and papers. Explain when you need the transaction completed. This helps distinguish an initial evaluation appointment from a confirmed purchase and payment schedule.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys luxury watches in Downtown Los Angeles. Contact the store to discuss your watch and preferred payment method. A timing estimate should reflect your particular watch; a general website promise cannot account for every inspection or banking circumstance.

Gather the watch and its history

Bring the watch, original box, warranty card or papers, available service invoices and any spare bracelet links. Keep the documents together and explain anything that does not appear to match. Missing papers are a point to discuss, rather than a reason to invent the watch's history.

  • Note whether the watch runs, stops or has a known fault.
  • Disclose replacement parts and aftermarket diamonds or other modifications.
  • Bring records of servicing and repairs when available.
  • Keep identifying numbers private when sharing photographs publicly.

Rolex's care and servicing information explains its own maintenance service. A service receipt can document work performed; it does not establish a current purchase offer. Ask before paying for service solely to prepare a sale.

Understand what may need closer examination

A watch's reference, materials, condition and components must agree with its description. Two watches bearing the same model name can differ in configuration and history. A buyer may need more information about a replaced dial, damaged movement or altered bracelet before making an offer.

For a Rolex, distinguish an independent buyer's evaluation from the manufacturer's program. Rolex Certified Pre-Owned has its own certification and participating-retailer process. A watch should not be described as part of that program simply because someone has inspected it. Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is not represented here as a participating retailer.

Our Rolex selling guide explains the preparation process in more detail. For an older watch, bring its history to the discussion before authorizing polishing or replacement parts.

Confirm the offer and payment together

Ask which accessories are included in the purchase amount and whether any further checks remain. If an offer is conditional, clarify the condition and when a final decision will be made. Do not compare an advertised retail listing with a firm purchase offer as though they were the same amount.

Payment choices at Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds are cash, bank wire and business check. Tell us your preference in advance, particularly for a high-value watch or collection. Confirm the final amount, payment timing and receipt arrangements before handing over ownership.

Plan the trip with enough time for questions

The store is at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Call 310-663-1340 to arrange your evaluation. Bring a list if you are presenting several watches so each watch, its paperwork and its offer can be kept together.

Can every luxury-watch sale be completed the same day?

Completion depends on the actual watch, the required evaluation and agreed payment arrangements. Confirm those details with the store for your visit instead of relying on a general time estimate.

What if my watch needs repair?

Describe the fault when you contact us and bring available repair records. Ask whether the watch can be evaluated in its current condition before paying for work that may not be recovered in a sale.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling a luxury watch in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

Bring gold coins with their packaging and documentation for evaluation in Downtown LA. Large quantities of gold and silver coins are welcome.

In this guide

  • Preparing gold coins for a Downtown LA evaluation
  • Gold content and collectible characteristics
  • Keep coins and their documentation together
  • Selling silver coins in quantity
  • How to compare coin purchase offers
  • Arranging a larger transaction

Preparing gold coins for a Downtown LA evaluation

Start with the actual coins and any packaging, labels, or documentation you already have. Keep matching materials together so the buyer can review each item. A description over the phone can help plan a visit, but it does not establish a final offer.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold coins and welcomes substantial quantities. We also buy silver coins in quantity at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014.

Gold content and collectible characteristics

A coin evaluation should identify the individual piece and consider its metal content and condition. Some coins may also require a discussion of collectible characteristics. Do not assume that every coin has the same composition or that its face value establishes its purchase value.

Ask how the offer accounts for the specific coins in your collection. The U.S. Mint’s bullion coin information is a useful reference for its own gold and silver bullion programs.

Keep coins and their documentation together

Bring any grading holders, certificates, original packaging, or purchase records you already have. Avoid removing coins from sealed holders or cleaning them merely to make them look brighter before the evaluation.

If you have a list of the collection, bring it as an organizational aid. Note which coins have matching paperwork and which need identification. You do not need to assign a value to every coin before calling us.

Selling silver coins in quantity

Let us know if your collection includes silver coins as well as gold. Describe the approximate quantity and how the items are organized so we can discuss time for the evaluation.

Keep gold and silver items in separate groups where practical. If you are unsure what a coin is, say so; an uncertain identification is a reason to review the item, not to guess at its metal content.

How to compare coin purchase offers

Compare offers for the same coins and clarify what each total includes. Ask whether the buyer considered only the metal or also identified collectible characteristics. A published gold-price reference is useful background, but it does not establish a complete offer for an unidentified collection.

Read our guide to comparing gold coin offers in Los Angeles before deciding. Review the final amount and payment arrangements before agreeing to sell.

Arranging a larger transaction

Large quantities and high-value transactions are welcome. Call 310-663-1340 to discuss the types of coins, the approximate amount of material, and the time you would like to visit.

Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check. Discuss your preferred payment method when arranging a substantial purchase. You can also bring scrap gold, Cuban chains, and other gold jewelry for evaluation during the visit.

Do I need original packaging to sell a gold coin?

Bring any packaging and records you have, but contact us even if they are missing. The actual coins need to be evaluated before a purchase offer is made.

Do you buy a single coin as well as a collection?

Yes. Individual gold coins and larger quantities are welcome. Call ahead for a substantial gold or silver coin collection.

Where is the coin-buying location?

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, in the Downtown Los Angeles Jewelry District. Contact us for your visit.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys large natural diamonds in Downtown Los Angeles—any size, any shape, loose or set in jewelry. We buy natural diamonds only. We do not buy uncut, rough or laboratory-grown diamonds. Visit us at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014.

In this guide

  • Natural diamonds of any size and shape
  • Loose diamonds, rings and substantial diamond jewelry
  • What goes into a large-diamond offer
  • Bring your grading report if you have one
  • Natural diamonds only
  • Sell your diamond in Downtown Los Angeles

Natural diamonds of any size and shape

Have a substantial center stone, a large loose diamond or a diamond collection to sell? Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds welcomes natural polished diamonds of any carat weight and any shape. Large diamonds are a focus of our buying service, and smaller natural stones are welcome too.

We buy round, oval, emerald-cut, cushion, radiant, princess, pear, marquise, Asscher, heart and other diamond shapes. Each diamond is evaluated individually; an unusual shape does not rule it out.

Loose diamonds, rings and substantial diamond jewelry

Bring loose natural diamonds or complete jewelry: engagement rings, solitaire rings, eternity bands, tennis bracelets, necklaces, pendants and earrings. Keep the piece intact and bring matching stones, removed links or accessories you already have.

For an eternity band or another multi-stone piece, total carat weight describes all the diamonds together. It does not mean that one stone has that weight. A large single diamond and a band containing many smaller stones need different assessments, even when their combined weights are similar.

Our diamond-buying service covers the wider range of natural diamond jewelry. The diamond necklace guide helps you prepare a complete necklace or pendant.

What goes into a large-diamond offer

Carat weight matters, but it is one part of the evaluation. Shape, proportions, color, clarity, condition and any treatment information help describe the actual diamond. GIA explains the 4Cs and why diamonds of similar weight can have different characteristics.

Bring the whole ring or jewelry piece so its mounting and other stones can be considered too. Let us know about any chips, repairs or changes you are aware of. Discuss any proposed removal or additional examination before agreeing to it.

Compare gold buyers using the same items, tested purity, weight units, final purchase amount, and payment terms. Ask how diamonds and collectible pieces are considered.

In this guide

  • Compare the offer for the items you actually own
  • Ask for the weight, purity, and offer basis
  • Give jewelry and coins the appropriate evaluation
  • Choose a selling process you can evaluate
  • Arrange large quantities and payment in advance
  • Questions before your first visit

Compare the offer for the items you actually own

Choosing a gold buyer in Downtown Los Angeles starts with a clear evaluation. Ask what was tested, what was weighed, and how those findings affect the final amount. A large advertised price means little if it applies to a different purity, excludes some of your items, or changes after deductions.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold jewelry, scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Bring one piece or discuss a substantial collection. Our gold-buying service explains the items we evaluate.

Ask for the weight, purity, and offer basis

A useful comparison identifies the same pieces in each offer. For a mixed lot, ask whether 10K, 14K, 18K, and other purities are recorded separately. Confirm the weight unit and how diamonds, springs, or other components affect the metal weight used.

Karat describes the proportion of gold in an alloy: 14K means 14 parts out of 24. Gold plating and gold-filled construction describe different materials. The FTC guide to jewelry markings explains these distinctions. A visible stamp is a starting point for an examination, rather than a substitute for testing the item.

  • Items included: Are both quotes for the complete lot or only selected pieces?
  • Measured weight: Are the units and treatment of non-gold components clear?
  • Tested purity: Is the buyer explaining different karats and any uncertain components?
  • Net payment: What is the final amount after any stated charges, and how will it be paid?

For the calculation behind an estimate, see how gold is valued. There is no universal payout percentage that establishes a fair offer for every item.

Give jewelry and coins the appropriate evaluation

A broken unbranded chain, a diamond-set Cuban bracelet, and a collectible gold coin need different discussions. Ask whether an item is being considered for its metal, its stones, or resale as a complete piece. Avoid dismantling jewelry or removing diamonds before that discussion.

Bring existing diamond reports, maker documentation, and coin inventory notes with the matching items. Those records help identify what you have; they do not guarantee a premium. Keep potentially collectible coins in their holders and mention any known history.

The World Gold Council's purity and fineness guide is useful when interpreting karat and fineness markings. Our coin-buyer guide covers questions specific to coin collections.

Choose a selling process you can evaluate

An in-person visit lets you ask questions while the buyer examines your property. A mail-in service involves shipping, receipt, an evaluation period, and written acceptance or return terms. Before using either option, establish what happens if you decline an offer and when your property or payment will be returned.

An outright sale also differs from a pawn loan: a loan has repayment terms and the item serves as security. Compare the transaction you actually want. The business category alone does not establish which buyer will make the better offer.

Arrange large quantities and payment in advance

For heavy Cuban chains, substantial scrap lots, or quantities of gold and silver coins, call 310-663-1340 before your visit. Describe the types of items and approximate quantity so the visit and evaluation can be coordinated. Keep separate collections labeled and make your own item list.

Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check. Discuss the method and timing before accepting an offer, especially for a high-value transaction. A bank wire or check may have bank processing or availability times; clarify those details rather than assuming every payment method works identically.

Questions before your first visit

Is a purchase offer the same as an insurance appraisal?

No. A purchase offer states what a buyer is willing to pay. An insurance appraisal serves a different purpose and may use a different value basis. Say what you need before arranging an evaluation.

What if I only want to sell some of the items?

Identify those pieces before accepting. Ask for a revised amount for the selected items, because a quote for a full collection may not apply unchanged to a smaller group.

What should I confirm before traveling to Hill Street?

Confirm your visit time, the items you want evaluated, any requested identification or documents, and your preferred payment method. Our contact page provides the Downtown Los Angeles location and appointment options.

We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

Compare gold coin offers for the same identified coins, quantity and condition. Ask how the buyer used fine-gold content and any collectible characteristics, then compare the net amount and payment terms rather than an advertised percentage alone.

In this guide

  • Identify what each offer actually covers
  • Use fine-gold content, not total weight alone
  • Ask whether collectible characteristics were considered
  • Compare a dated reference with a real offer
  • Arrange a large gold or silver coin sale

Identify what each offer actually covers

Make a list of the coins being offered for sale. Record the country, denomination, year and any visible mint mark when you can read them confidently. Include the number of coins and whether each is in a grading holder or original packaging. Mark uncertain identifications for review.

A quote for an entire collection cannot be compared directly with a quote for its most desirable pieces. If you may sell only part of the collection, ask for that group to be identified separately. Our coin preparation checklist helps you organize the visit.

Use fine-gold content, not total weight alone

A gold coin can contain an alloy while still holding a stated amount of fine gold. The U.S. Mint's bullion specifications explain that the one-ounce American Gold Eagle contains one troy ounce of gold plus alloy metals. The American Buffalo is a different coin, made from .9999 fine gold. Do not multiply an Eagle's stated one-ounce gold content by its purity again.

For an unfamiliar coin, establish the issue and its specifications before calculating. Face value, gross scale weight and fine-metal content describe different things. A replica or plated piece must not be assigned the composition of the genuine coin it resembles.

Ask whether collectible characteristics were considered

A metal-content estimate is a starting point for discussing bullion. A coin's condition, particular issue, grading information and potential collector interest may need additional review. Age alone does not prove rarity or a premium.

Keep holders, labels and records together. Do not clean a coin or break it out of a holder merely to make the collection easier to weigh. Ask the buyer to explain whether the offer treats a piece as bullion or recognizes additional collectible characteristics.

Compare a dated reference with a real offer

The World Gold Council publishes gold-price reference data. Note the currency, unit and time of a reference before using it. A market price for gold is not a guaranteed bid for an individual coin or unidentified collection.

  • Are both offers for the same coins and quantity?
  • Was fine-gold content established for each relevant issue?
  • Is any premium included, and what supports it?
  • Are charges, conditions and the final payment amount clear?
  • How long does the quoted offer remain available?

No single percentage proves which coin buyer will provide the strongest offer. Compare actual amounts made on the same basis and clarify changes when a quote is updated.

Arrange a large gold or silver coin sale

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold coins and silver coins in Downtown Los Angeles, including large quantities. Call 310-663-1340 with an approximate inventory to arrange enough time to review the collection.

Payment choices are cash, bank wire and business check. Discuss the method and timing before accepting. Visit 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, or contact us to plan your evaluation.

Does original packaging guarantee a higher offer?

No. Bring it because it can help document the issue and keep items organized, but its effect depends on the specific coin and purchase evaluation.

Can I compare an offer before every coin is identified?

You can discuss an estimate, but note which identifications remain uncertain. Compare final purchase amounts only after the buyers have clearly described the coins included.

We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

Bring fine jewelry as a complete piece, with matching reports, maker information, accessories and repair records when available. An evaluation should consider the actual materials, stones, condition and design before you agree on the items and purchase amount.

In this guide

  • Keep the complete design together
  • Bring documents that help identify the item
  • Consider metal and stones without losing sight of the piece
  • Disclose condition and prior repairs
  • Compare the offer with the relevant information
  • Arrange an evaluation in the Jewelry District

Keep the complete design together

A necklace with a detachable pendant, matching earrings or a bracelet with removed links may need its components considered together. Bring the parts you have and describe anything missing. Keep pieces you intend to retain separate from those you may sell.

GIA's estate-jewelry guidance highlights examination of a previously owned piece. Age, a familiar-looking design or a brand name in a family story is not enough to establish maker or collectible significance.

Bring documents that help identify the item

Useful records can include receipts, matching grading reports, maker paperwork and repair history. An original box can be helpful context, but packaging by itself does not authenticate the jewelry inside it.

For signed pieces, see our Cartier selling guide or Tiffany jewelry guide. If documents are missing, describe what you know and ask what further evaluation is appropriate.

Consider metal and stones without losing sight of the piece

Gold purity and net alloy weight inform a material estimate. Diamonds also need their own characteristics assessed: GIA's quality factors explain why carat weight alone is insufficient.

The complete piece may have resale potential that differs from a sum based on scrap materials. Ask which basis the proposal uses and avoid counting the same materials twice. Our gold valuation guide explains the distinction.

Disclose condition and prior repairs

Point out loose stones, chips, thin areas, altered clasps or replaced parts that you know about. A damaged piece can still contain valuable material, but repair or recutting is not automatically feasible or financially worthwhile.

Avoid unnecessary polishing, stone removal or restoration before discussing an offer. Those steps can change the object and may not recover their cost in a sale.

Compare the offer with the relevant information

An insurance replacement amount is not a current buyer's commitment. GIA distinguishes grading reports from monetary appraisals; bring existing records while keeping their purpose clear.

Confirm the exact items and accessories included, the final amount, any remaining checks or charges, and payment arrangements. If you change the selection, ask for a revised total. Our inherited-collection guide covers decisions about keeping some pieces.

Arrange an evaluation in the Jewelry District

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. We buy gold jewelry, diamonds, estate pieces and other valuables, including heavy Cuban chains with or without diamonds. Single items and substantial collections are welcome.

Call 310-663-1340 or arrange your visit. Discuss cash, bank wire or business-check payment before accepting a purchase offer.

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling estate jewelry in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Compare final offers for the same diamond and setting, with the stone’s identified origin, report information and actual condition considered. Ask which items are included and what checks or charges remain. A retail listing or insurance appraisal is not an equivalent purchase offer.

In this guide

  • Identify what each offer covers
  • Match the stone and its reported characteristics
  • Keep natural and laboratory-grown identification clear
  • Allow for the actual condition and examination
  • Compare purchase amounts with purchase amounts
  • Arrange your diamond evaluation in Downtown LA

Identify what each offer covers

Write down whether the proposal includes a loose diamond, the complete ring, side stones, mounting or other matching jewelry. An offer for a center stone alone cannot be directly compared with an amount for an entire necklace or ring.

Keep reports and accessories matched to the appropriate pieces. If you decide to retain the setting or sell only part of a collection, ask for a revised proposal before assuming how the original total divides.

Match the stone and its reported characteristics

GIA explains carat, color, clarity and cut. Those characteristics should be read together, alongside shape, measurements and other report information. Two diamonds of the same weight do not automatically have the same value.

Bring a report if you already have one. Discuss whether additional identification or grading work would be useful before paying for it. A missing report is a question to resolve, not proof that the stone is false or worthless.

Keep natural and laboratory-grown identification clear

GIA describes the essentially similar properties and different growth histories of natural and laboratory-grown diamonds. Their markets are different, and ordinary appearance cannot reliably determine origin.

Tell the buyer what the documentation states. Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural, cut and polished diamonds only, in any size and shape; we do not buy laboratory-grown or uncut diamonds. Do not substitute a quote for one origin when evaluating a diamond of another origin.

Allow for the actual condition and examination

A report describes the stone examined at that time. Current chips, damage, repairs to the mounting or uncertainty about matching the document can affect the evaluation. Mounted stones may have limits on what can be observed without further work.

Discuss any proposed removal or alteration before agreeing. Our loose-diamond evaluation guide explains useful preparation questions.

Compare purchase amounts with purchase amounts

A retail listing is an asking price for a different transaction. An insurance appraisal may concern replacement, while a grading report does not assign money value, as GIA explains. None of those figures is a guaranteed resale amount.

  • Is the amount final or subject to further checks?
  • Does it include the setting, side stones and accessories?
  • Are any fees or other conditions outstanding?
  • How long is the proposal available?
  • What are the payment method and timing?

An unusually different offer deserves an explanation of its assumptions. A business category or an advertised percentage cannot settle the comparison by itself.

Contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 310-663-1340 to discuss the actual items and arrange a visit to 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Bring matching reports and known condition details.

Choose a diamond appraiser by the purpose of the assignment and the qualifications relevant to your item. Confirm who will use the report, what it must contain, the valuation date, fees and limitations. A buyer’s offer and an insurance appraisal serve different purposes.

In this guide

  • Define the purpose before booking
  • Ask about the person's relevant qualifications
  • Agree on the report and examination
  • Confirm fees, timing and buying interests
  • Use grading reports for their stated information
  • If your purpose is selling a natural diamond

Define the purpose before booking

Begin with what you need to decide or document. You may want a proposal to buy a diamond, a valuation for an insurer, or a report requested by another professional. Those requests should not all be described simply as “an appraisal.”

If a third party needs the report, ask that recipient for its requirements before commissioning work. Tell the appraiser the intended use and valuation date. Do not assume that a report made for an earlier purpose will be accepted for a different one.

Ask about the person's relevant qualifications

GIA's appraisal guidance distinguishes gemological knowledge from appraisal training. Ask the individual to explain both their stone-identification background and the valuation qualifications relevant to the assignment.

Request the exact credential and issuing organization so you can verify the claim. Ask about experience with your type of jewelry, such as an antique mounting, a colored diamond or a large collection. An impressive general title is less useful than an answer about the actual work.

GIA states that its reports and educational awards are not GIA certification of a business or gemstone. A reference to GIA education should identify the credential accurately rather than suggest GIA endorsement of the appraisal.

Agree on the report and examination

Ask for a description or sample of the report format. Confirm which items will be examined, which documents you should bring and how each item will be identified in the resulting report. For a collection, agree whether values will be itemized.

  • What is the stated purpose and valuation date?
  • Which item descriptions and photographs will be supplied?
  • Will stone weights or grades be measured, taken from records or estimated?
  • What examination limits will be disclosed?
  • Does further laboratory work require a separate agreement?

Keep assumptions visible. A mounted stone may prevent some observations, and a prior report must be matched to the actual diamond. Ask how any uncertainty affects the assignment.

Confirm fees, timing and buying interests

Request the fee basis, expected delivery and any additional charges before work begins. Describe the number and complexity of the pieces so the appraiser can answer for your actual collection. A general article cannot supply a reliable quote for every assignment.

Ask whether the appraiser also proposes to buy the item or has another interest in the transaction. If you need an independent valuation, explain that requirement explicitly. Keep any separate purchase proposal clearly labeled.

Use grading reports for their stated information

GIA's sample diamond reports show stone-quality information. They do not replace a monetary appraisal or guarantee what a buyer will pay. Bring existing records without treating their different figures and descriptions as interchangeable.

If your purpose is selling a natural diamond

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural polished diamonds of any size and shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. Our diamond-buying service concerns evaluating an item for purchase.

Call 310-663-1340 or arrange a visit to 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Explain any separate formal-report requirement before assuming a purchase evaluation meets it.

Must I buy an appraisal before requesting an offer?

Not automatically. Explain your purpose and documents first, then decide whether a separate valuation would help with the decision you need to make.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

A gold-bracelet offer depends on tested purity, net metal weight, construction, condition, and any diamonds. Bring Cuban links, bangles, and broken pieces for evaluation.

In this guide

  • Selling Cuban bracelets, bangles, and broken gold
  • Why Cuban-link construction matters
  • Evaluate diamond-set bracelets as complete pieces
  • Broken, vintage, and signed bracelets need different attention
  • Compare the final amount for the same bracelets
  • Bring one bracelet or a substantial collection

Selling Cuban bracelets, bangles, and broken gold

A heavy bracelet can contain substantial gold, but its size alone does not establish its value. A useful evaluation considers its tested purity, metal weight, construction, condition, and any diamonds. Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys Cuban bracelets with or without diamonds, plain gold bangles, and scrap gold in Downtown Los Angeles.

Bring the complete bracelet, including detached links or a broken clasp. If you have matching chains or other unwanted pieces, they can be discussed together through our gold and jewelry buying service.

Why Cuban-link construction matters

Two bracelets of similar width can have different weights. Hollow links contain less metal than comparable solid links, while clasps and repairs may introduce components that need separate examination. Ask which parts are included in the gold calculation rather than treating the entire scale reading as pure gold.

For example, 14K describes an alloy containing 14 parts gold out of 24; it does not mean every gram of the bracelet is pure gold. A gold-plated or gold-filled item has a different construction from karat-gold jewelry. The FTC's explanation of gold markings and plating helps distinguish these terms.

Keep any purchase receipt that identifies the material, and point out known repairs. If you are also selling a matching chain, our 14K and Cuban-chain guide explains the same weight and construction questions in more detail.

Evaluate diamond-set bracelets as complete pieces

A diamond-set Cuban bracelet needs more than a gold-weight calculation. Ask how the stones are identified and whether their contribution is included in the offer. Total diamond weight across many small stones does not describe the size or quality of any individual diamond.

Diamond quality involves carat weight, color, clarity, and cut, as explained in GIA's diamond quality guide. Bring any existing reports, while recognizing that a report may cover a particular stone rather than every stone in a bracelet.

Do not remove stones yourself. Request an evaluation of the complete bracelet first, then clarify the terms of any proposed disassembly. Our diamond-buying service provides a starting point for discussing significant stones.

Broken, vintage, and signed bracelets need different attention

A broken clasp does not remove the gold already present in a bracelet. For a piece evaluated primarily for metal, tested purity and recoverable gold weight remain central. Damage can nevertheless affect the value of jewelry that might otherwise be resold intact.

Keep maker marks, original boxes, and useful history with a signed or antique bracelet. Do not assume an inherited piece should be sold only as scrap. Ask whether the design, condition, or maker gives the complete item a resale opportunity before authorizing repairs, polishing, or dismantling.

For a mixture of damaged jewelry, single earrings, and detached links, use our scrap-gold preparation guide. Keep separate pieces organized so you can follow the evaluation.

Compare the final amount for the same bracelets

Ask each buyer to identify the pieces, tested karats, weight units, treatment of stones, and net payment. A per-gram quote is only comparable when the material and calculation basis match. An attractive preliminary estimate is not the same as an offer following examination.

There is no single percentage of spot price that proves an offer is fair for every bracelet. A complete jewelry offer can reflect a different resale opportunity from a metal-only purchase. Request an explanation and compare the amount you would receive for the same items.

Bring one bracelet or a substantial collection

Visit Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. We buy heavy Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, scrap gold, gold coins, and silver coins. Large quantities and high-value transactions are welcome.

For a substantial lot, arrange your visit and discuss payment beforehand. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check. Confirm the final amount and payment timing before accepting the purchase.

Should I repair a broken bracelet before selling?

Have it evaluated first. A repair may not add enough to the purchase offer to justify its cost, and a vintage or signed piece may need specialist attention. Bring detached components with the bracelet.

Can I sell a bracelet if I do not know its karat?

Yes, you can bring it for evaluation and explain what is unknown. The buyer needs to establish its material before making a meaningful offer; a photograph or color alone cannot confirm gold content.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

Bring a vintage Rolex in its current condition, together with service records, spare links and any earlier documentation. A careful evaluation should distinguish what is known about the watch from what still needs research.

In this guide

  • Preserve the watch before its first evaluation
  • Describe the history you actually know
  • Ask which components have changed
  • Understand what an examination does and does not establish
  • Compare offers for the same complete watch
  • Arrange a Downtown Los Angeles visit

Preserve the watch before its first evaluation

An older Rolex may have a long history of wear, servicing and replacement parts. Resist the urge to polish its case, refinish its dial or replace a worn bracelet simply to make it present better. First discuss how the watch will be evaluated in its existing condition.

Keep loose components and old paperwork together. Do not open the case or expose an unfamiliar watch to water. Rolex provides care and servicing guidance; the appropriate action still depends on the condition of your particular watch.

Describe the history you actually know

Record when and how you obtained the watch, what repairs you remember and which details come from family recollection rather than documents. An approximate purchase date is useful background, but it need not be the production date.

Bring receipts, warranty papers, service invoices, spare links and earlier photographs if available. Match records to the item being examined. A period box or an aged-looking dial alone does not establish the watch's age or originality.

Ask which components have changed

Discuss the case, dial, hands, bezel, bracelet, clasp and movement as separate components. An original part, a later manufacturer service part and an aftermarket part are different descriptions. Ask the evaluator to identify which conclusion is supported and which remains uncertain.

Research can be appropriate for an unusual reference or configuration. A careful buyer may need time or an additional specialist opinion. Speed and confidence by themselves are not evidence of accuracy.

Understand what an examination does and does not establish

Agree on any proposed opening or further work before it happens. If you need a written authentication opinion or insurance valuation, request that specific service and its scope rather than assuming a purchase offer supplies it.

Rolex Certified Pre-Owned is a defined brand programme available through participating Official Retailers. A general pre-owned buying evaluation should not be described as that programme or its guarantee. Our Rolex authentication guide explains why photographs and superficial checks are insufficient.

Compare offers for the same complete watch

State whether the offer includes the bracelet, spare links, box and records. Note assumptions about condition or further inspection and ask whether the figure is preliminary or final. There is no universal vintage premium or fixed increase for paperwork.

For an inherited timepiece, confirm that the people entitled to make the decision agree before arranging a sale. Our estate-jewelry service offers a starting point for discussing a collection.

Arrange a Downtown Los Angeles visit

Use the Rolex selling checklist to organize the watch and its accessories. Explain missing parts or a stopped movement when arranging the visit.

For an in-person purchase evaluation, contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, or call 310-663-1340. Payment for agreed purchases is available by cash, bank wire or business check; confirm the arrangements before accepting.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling a luxury watch in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Choose a diamond buyer who explains what is being evaluated, what the offer includes and when payment will be available. Compare offers for the same item and confirm the business location before arranging a visit.

In this guide

  • Start with the item you want to sell
  • Ask how the evaluation works
  • Bring records without treating them as a price guarantee
  • Compare the final terms for the same piece
  • Plan your downtown Los Angeles visit

Start with the item you want to sell

A useful search for a diamond buyer begins with a clear description: a loose natural diamond, an engagement ring, earrings or another finished piece. Note the shape, any known carat weight, the metal and the paperwork you have. If you do not know whether a stone is natural, say so when arranging the visit.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural cut and polished diamonds in any size or shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. Review our Los Angeles diamond-buying service before bringing an item for evaluation.

Ask how the evaluation works

Ask who will examine the item, what can be assessed while it is mounted and whether any further examination is proposed. Do not agree to stone removal, shipping or other handling without understanding the process, responsibility and any charges.

GIA describes diamond quality through cut, color, clarity and carat weight. A buyer should be able to explain which details are known and which remain estimates. A general claim of “high quality” gives you less to compare than a description tied to the actual stone.

Ask the buyerWhat the answer should clarify
What does this offer cover?The complete piece or specified stones and metal
Is further examination required?Any conditions that could change the amount
Are there fees or deductions?The amount you would actually receive
How long does the offer remain available?Whether you can compare it later on the same terms
When will payment be available?The method, timing and any verification steps

Bring records without treating them as a price guarantee

Bring an existing laboratory report, receipt or prior appraisal. A report helps describe a diamond; an appraisal states a value for a particular purpose. GIA explains that its grading work does not provide a monetary appraisal. Neither document requires a buyer to pay the amount on an insurance valuation.

You can look up an eligible GIA report through GIA Report Check. The record lookup is a preparation step; the presented diamond still needs to be matched to its documentation. Missing paperwork is a reason to ask what examination is needed, rather than to guess the grade.

Compare the final terms for the same piece

Request a written offer or a clear written summary you can keep. Compare the same item, including its setting and accent stones, with the same assumptions about further testing. A preliminary photograph estimate should not be compared as though it were a final in-person offer.

Use our diamond resale offer guide to record amounts and conditions side by side. If a buyer claims a particular credential, verify it with the organization named. Check recent customer feedback for specific experiences, but do not treat an online star rating as a promise about your transaction.

Plan your downtown Los Angeles visit

Our address is 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 310-663-1340 to describe your item and arrange the next step. For an accepted purchase, payment options include cash, bank wire and business check; confirm the preferred method and timing before finalizing the sale.

Should I choose the buyer advertising the highest price?

Compare the final amount offered for your actual item and the conditions attached to it. An advertised example may concern a different diamond, setting or transaction.

Do I need an insurance appraisal before contacting a buyer?

Ask what information is needed first. A sale evaluation and an insurance appraisal serve different purposes; avoid ordering a new document before establishing that you need it.

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Choose a buyer who identifies the pieces in your collection and explains the scope of the offer. Keep potentially significant jewelry separate from bulk metal calculations, and compare the final amount and conditions for the same items.

In this guide

  • Describe the collection before choosing a service
  • Ask how individual pieces are considered
  • Compare the type of transaction
  • Verify claims and keep the comparison specific
  • Bring your collection to downtown Los Angeles

Describe the collection before choosing a service

Estate jewelry can include contemporary as well as older pieces. GIA describes estate jewelry as previously owned jewelry; the term does not automatically establish age or rarity.

Make a short list of what you have: rings, necklaces, bracelets, brooches, watches and loose stones. Keep matching pieces together. If coins or scrap gold are part of the collection, identify them separately so you can ask which categories a prospective buyer evaluates.

Ask how individual pieces are considered

A mixed collection should not automatically become one undifferentiated weight. Ask whether the buyer considers the complete design, stones, condition and supported maker attribution before discussing metal alone. Preserve family records, receipts and any previous reports.

For an item that may require specialist research, ask what further work is proposed, whether it carries a charge and whether it affects the timing of an offer. A referral or additional examination is not by itself a sign of a poor buyer; unexplained terms are a reason to seek clarification.

Collection detailQuestion for the buyer
Signed or attributed jewelryWhat supports the maker identification?
Stone-set piecesHow are the stones and setting considered?
Broken or incomplete itemsAre matching parts and complete-piece potential included?
Several categoriesDoes the offer cover everything or selected items?

Compare the type of transaction

For a direct purchase, request the amount the buyer will pay and its conditions. For consignment or auction, request the written selling agreement, charges, payment schedule and treatment of unsold items. An estimated future selling price is not the same as an available purchase offer.

Use the jewelry selling options guide to compare those routes. Do not assume that a particular business offers every service; confirm the arrangement with the business itself.

Verify claims and keep the comparison specific

Ask about relevant experience and verify any named credential with the issuing organization. Read current feedback for the correct business and location. The FTC’s review guidance recommends considering multiple sources; a star average alone cannot establish how your sale will proceed.

Choose a coin buyer who can explain how your particular coins will be identified and evaluated. Modern bullion, potentially collectible issues and mixed collections raise different questions; ask about that fit before comparing purchase amounts.

In this guide

  • Describe the collection before choosing the visit
  • Ask how metal content will be established
  • Match collectible questions to the evaluator's knowledge
  • Check the transaction process as well as the amount
  • Bring questions you can compare across buyers

Describe the collection before choosing the visit

Tell the buyer whether you have familiar bullion coins, older or unidentified coins, or a mixture. Mention grading holders and original packaging. For a substantial lot, an approximate count helps the buyer plan time; you do not need a complete valuation before making contact.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold and silver coins, including large quantities, alongside gold jewelry and scrap. Ask about our Downtown Los Angeles gold-buying service if you want several types of items evaluated during the same visit.

Ask how metal content will be established

A useful explanation identifies the coin before assigning its metal content. The U.S. Mint's specifications show that its bullion programs use different metals, weights and fineness. A familiar color or denomination alone cannot establish composition.

Ask how the buyer handles an uncertain identity or inconsistent marking. Do not accept a calculation that assumes every gold-colored coin has the same purity. Keep suspected replicas separate and explain what you know about them.

Match collectible questions to the evaluator's knowledge

If a coin may have collector value, ask what characteristics the buyer will examine and whether an additional opinion would be useful. A bullion-only offer may answer a different question from an offer considering a specific collectible issue.

Neither an old date nor a grading holder guarantees a premium. Bring the complete information and ask how it affects the bid. Avoid cleaning coins or removing them from holders before the evaluation.

Check the transaction process as well as the amount

Ask when an estimate becomes a firm offer, what is included and how long it remains available. The World Gold Council's price data provides market context; it does not verify a particular buyer's offer.

For an in-person sale, confirm the location and visit time. For a mail-in route, read the receipt, inspection, acceptance, insurance and return terms before shipping. Our local versus online selling guide covers the process questions.

Bring questions you can compare across buyers

  • Which coins will you evaluate, and what information should I bring?
  • Will the offer identify the lot and any separately evaluated coins?
  • What happens if further identification is needed?
  • What are the payment method, timing and final amount?

Use the same collection when comparing coin offers. A confident sales pitch or a ranked list is less useful than a clear explanation of your actual coins.

Where can I arrange a Downtown LA coin evaluation?

Contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Call 310-663-1340, especially for a large gold or silver collection. Payment choices are cash, bank wire and business check; discuss your preference before the visit.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds does not buy laboratory-grown diamonds. We buy natural, cut and polished diamonds of any size and shape. This guide explains report wording so you can identify the paperwork you have before arranging a natural-diamond evaluation.

In this guide

  • Our diamond buying policy
  • Read the identification before the quality description
  • Understand the GIA assessment date
  • Check the report and the actual item
  • A quality assessment is not a purchase offer
  • Arrange a natural-diamond evaluation in Downtown LA

Our diamond buying policy

We welcome natural polished diamonds, loose or set in rings, necklaces, bracelets and other jewelry. Any size and any shape can be considered, including substantial individual diamonds and collections. We do not buy laboratory-grown diamonds, uncut crystals or rough diamond material.

If your report identifies a laboratory-grown diamond, it is outside our diamond-buying service. A laboratory name, a high quality assessment or the original purchase amount does not change that policy. See our large natural diamond buying guide for the items we buy.

Read the identification before the quality description

Look for the issuing laboratory, report number, date and the wording identifying the stone. Keep the original document with the correct item. Do not assume that a loose report found with inherited jewelry belongs to every diamond in the collection.

GIA explains that natural and laboratory-grown diamonds have essentially similar chemical and optical properties. Reliable separation can require specialist equipment or laboratory examination. A photograph, sparkle or a basic diamond tester is not enough to establish natural origin.

Understand the GIA assessment date

GIA launched its revised D-to-Z laboratory-grown diamond assessment on October 1, 2025. The official announcement describes Premium and Standard assessments, with no assessment for stones below the minimum Standard criteria.

Premium requires D color, VVS clarity or higher, Excellent polish and symmetry, and Excellent cut for round brilliants. Standard uses its own minimum criteria. Read those published criteria rather than assuming that the word Premium covers any color or clarity.

Older documents can use different terminology. Record the date and exact report type instead of converting an older grade into a new description yourself. A terminology change does not turn a laboratory-grown diamond into a natural one.

Check the report and the actual item

For GIA paperwork, use Report Check to compare the available record with your document. Then ask how the report number, measurements and identifying information are matched to the actual stone. An online record confirms report information; it does not inspect the item in your possession.

If documentation is missing or unclear, say so. Keep uncertain details marked as unknown. Before paying for new laboratory work, ask what identification is needed and what the service would establish.

A quality assessment is not a purchase offer

A grading or assessment document describes the examined stone. It does not name a buyer or guarantee a resale amount. GIA distinguishes its reports from monetary appraisals. An insurance replacement figure and the price originally paid also answer different questions.

If you own a laboratory-grown diamond, review the original retailer's written return or buyback terms and ask any prospective buyer whether it accepts that material before arranging a visit. Do not assume that a policy exists or that another business will buy the stone.

Arrange a natural-diamond evaluation in Downtown LA

For natural polished diamonds, call 310-663-1340 or contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Bring the complete item and existing records. Cash, bank wire and business check are available for agreed purchases.

Do you buy a laboratory-grown diamond with a GIA report?

No. We buy natural polished diamonds only. Having a GIA or other laboratory report does not change the material we accept.

Can I tell natural origin from a diamond photograph?

No. Tell us what the documentation says, and explain any uncertainty. Do not describe the stone as natural solely because of its appearance.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

Look for clear answers about who is examining your item, how it will be handled, what the offer includes and when payment will be available. Verify specific claims and keep a written record of the transaction you actually agree to.

In this guide

  • Ask questions about the service you need
  • Distinguish credentials from item documentation
  • Understand handling before agreeing to extra work
  • Compare written terms and relevant feedback
  • Bring those questions to your Los Angeles evaluation

Ask questions about the service you need

Describe the items before arranging a visit. A buyer who regularly handles scrap gold may use a different process for a signed bracelet, natural diamond ring or luxury watch. Ask who will examine your items and what information is needed to make an offer.

Look for explanations tied to your actual piece. If the buyer uses a term you do not understand, ask them to explain it. A clear discussion should leave you knowing what has been established, what remains uncertain and whether additional examination is proposed.

Distinguish credentials from item documentation

If someone claims a professional qualification, ask for its exact name and issuing organization so you can verify it. A laboratory report accompanying a diamond describes that examined stone; it does not certify the business holding the report.

GIA Report Check is a way to look up an eligible report record. The actual diamond still needs to be matched to the paperwork. Do not substitute a document lookup for questions about the item or the purchase process.

Understand handling before agreeing to extra work

Ask whether the evaluation occurs during the visit and whether any part needs to leave your possession for further work. If removal, shipping or outside examination is proposed, establish the reason, custody arrangements, timing and any charges first.

Keep an item list and photographs for a collection. If jewelry is left for examination, request documentation identifying what was received and the agreed purpose. A professional-looking room alone is not evidence of how custody or a particular transaction will be managed.

QuestionA useful answer identifies
What did you evaluate?The complete piece and relevant components
What remains uncertain?Estimates, limitations and proposed further examination
What amount would I receive?The final amount after stated deductions
What happens if I decline?Any pre-agreed service charges and return arrangements
How does payment work?The method and expected availability

Compare written terms and relevant feedback

Read reviews for the correct business and service. The FTC explains that reviews may be manipulated, so a rating should support further questions rather than replace them. Our jewelry buyer reviews guide shows how to turn feedback into a useful shortlist.

Compare final offers for the same item. Confirm the included setting, stones and any detached parts. If an amount changes after examination, ask what changed in the description or assumptions. Payment speed alone does not establish whether the amount or handling terms suit you.

Bring those questions to your Los Angeles evaluation

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. We buy gold jewelry and scrap gold and estate jewelry. Our diamond buying covers natural cut and polished diamonds of any size or shape; we do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds.

Contact us at 310-663-1340 to discuss your items. For an accepted purchase, ask about cash, bank wire or business check and confirm the payment timing.

Does a buyer holding a GIA report mean the buyer is certified by GIA?

No. Item documentation and a person’s qualifications are different things. Verify any specific credential separately.

Must I accept a first offer?

Decide after you understand the amount and terms. If you need time or want to compare, ask how long that offer remains available.

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling estate jewelry in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Bring the GIA report you already have and match it to the actual diamond being evaluated. Check the report type, number, shape, measurements and comments. The report describes the examined stone; it does not establish its current condition or a purchase amount.

In this guide

  • Start with the exact report type
  • Read the fields the document actually supplies
  • Use Report Check and match the item
  • Disclose what happened after the report date
  • Keep the report and purchase amount separate
  • Bring existing paperwork to Downtown Los Angeles

Start with the exact report type

Record the laboratory name, document title, report number and date. Use the wording on the actual document rather than relying on a seller's shorthand. Keep laboratory-grown identification separate from natural-diamond information.

GIA explains that it does not certify diamonds or businesses. “GIA-graded” or a reference to a GIA report describes the relevant service more accurately than a claim of GIA certification.

Read the fields the document actually supplies

GIA's sample natural-diamond reports are a useful reference. Its Diamond Grading Report includes quality information, clarity plotting and proportions. The overall cut grade described there applies to standard round brilliants in the D-to-Z color range.

Do not assume that every report format supplies the same fields. A missing overall cut grade on another shape is not a Poor grade. Read polish, symmetry, shape and cutting style as the separate descriptions they are.

Make a simple note of the reported weight, millimeter measurements, color, clarity and relevant comments. Our diamond grading chart helps decode the terminology without assigning a price to it.

Use Report Check and match the item

Look up the number through GIA Report Check and compare the available record with your document. Resolve discrepancies rather than assuming a familiar logo is enough.

The actual stone must still be matched to the information. Ask how the identification, measurements and any recorded inscription are checked. A successful online lookup is about a report record, not a remote examination of the diamond in front of you.

Disclose what happened after the report date

Bring records of repairs, damage or recutting that you know about. If the diamond has changed since the report was issued, ask which details remain relevant and whether another examination is appropriate.

For a mounted diamond, keep the ring intact and discuss any proposed removal first. The setting may limit what can be observed. Explain that limitation instead of converting an estimate into an exact grade.

Keep the report and purchase amount separate

GIA distinguishes grading reports from monetary appraisals. Neither its report nor an earlier insurance amount guarantees a particular offer.

Ask what the proposed purchase includes: just the diamond, the complete ring or additional pieces. Compare final amounts for the same items and conditions. No fixed percentage premium applies to every stone simply because a particular laboratory name appears on the document.

Bring existing paperwork to Downtown Los Angeles

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural polished diamonds of any size and shape, loose or in jewelry. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. If paperwork is missing, contact us with what you know before paying for replacement or new laboratory work.

Call 310-663-1340 or arrange an evaluation at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Our diamond-buying page explains the service. Cash, bank wire and business check are available for agreed purchases.

Bring unwanted rings, bracelets, broken jewelry, or Cuban chains for a local evaluation. Gold pieces with and without diamonds are welcome.

In this guide

  • Bring the pieces you want to sell
  • Organize the collection without guessing at its value
  • Include broken jewelry and unwanted gold
  • Heavy Cuban chains and diamond-set pieces
  • Gold coins and silver coins
  • Review the offer and choose your payment method
  • Plan your visit to 617 S. Hill Street

Bring the pieces you want to sell

Your collection may include wearable jewelry, broken pieces, or items that no longer fit your style. Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold rings, bracelets, necklaces, Cuban chains, and scrap gold, including pieces with or without diamonds.

Bring the actual items to our Downtown Los Angeles location at 617 S. Hill Street. Single pieces and substantial collections are welcome. If you have a large quantity, call ahead to discuss timing.

Organize the collection without guessing at its value

Keep matching items together and separate loose parts from unrelated pieces. If you have receipts, grading reports, maker information, or original packaging, bring them with the corresponding jewelry.

You do not need to know the exact karat, stone quality, or resale value of every piece before arranging an evaluation. Markings and documentation can provide context, but the buyer needs to review the jewelry itself.

Include broken jewelry and unwanted gold

A damaged bracelet, a broken chain, or a single earring can still be considered. Keep detached components with the item and mention any repairs you know about. Avoid unnecessary dismantling or aggressive cleaning before the visit.

Read our guide to selling scrap gold if much of your collection consists of broken or unwanted pieces.

Heavy Cuban chains and diamond-set pieces

We buy Cuban necklaces and bracelets both with diamonds and without diamonds. Discuss how the gold, construction, condition, and any stones are being considered in the purchase amount.

Total scale weight is not automatically the weight of pure gold. A gold estimate needs the item’s metal content, while diamonds and other components may need separate evaluation. The FTC guide to gold jewelry explains karat markings and how plated or gold-filled items differ. Our Cuban and 14K chain guide covers questions to bring to that conversation.

Gold coins and silver coins

You can also bring gold coins and silver coins for evaluation. Keep any coin packaging, grading holders, and documentation with the matching pieces. Let us know when arranging the visit if the collection includes a substantial number of coins.

For a collection-focused checklist, see preparing coins for a Downtown LA evaluation.

Review the offer and choose your payment method

Ask how the final offer accounts for your items, and compare the same group of pieces if you seek another purchase offer. Original retail prices and online estimates can be useful background, but they are different from an offer for the jewelry in front of the buyer.

Payment at Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is available by cash, bank wire, or business check. For a high-value transaction, discuss the method you prefer when scheduling the evaluation.

Plan your visit to 617 S. Hill Street

Our address is 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, in the Downtown Los Angeles Jewelry District. Call 310-663-1340 or contact us to arrange your visit and discuss the collection.

Can I bring jewelry without paperwork?

Yes. Bring the items you want evaluated and any documentation you do have. The jewelry itself is central to the purchase evaluation.

Is my collection too large to discuss?

Large quantities and high-value purchases are welcome. Call to describe what you have and discuss time for the evaluation and your preferred payment method.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

Gold buying in Downtown Los Angeles · 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

Before visiting a gold buyer in the Los Angeles Jewelry District, confirm the location, the types of items being evaluated and time for your collection. Keep an item list, compare offers for the same pieces, and discuss payment before agreeing to sell.

In this guide

  • Confirm the business and visit details
  • Pack the collection so you can follow the evaluation
  • Record markings without assuming they prove purity
  • Give diamond-set jewelry and coins separate attention
  • Compare the final amount on a consistent basis
  • Agree on payment arrangements before accepting

Confirm the business and visit details

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Use the contact page or call 310-663-1340 to arrange a visit. Confirm the time and any requested documents before traveling with valuable items.

A Jewelry District address helps you locate a business; it does not establish the quality of its offer. Evaluate the explanation and purchase terms for your jewelry. If you are seeing more than one buyer, allow time to review the same collection without rushing between appointments.

Pack the collection so you can follow the evaluation

Keep matching pieces together. Place detached links or a broken clasp with the bracelet they came from. Separate items you want to keep from those you are considering selling, and prepare a simple count or photograph for your records.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Describe a substantial lot when arranging the visit so the time and payment discussion fit the collection.

Record markings without assuming they prove purity

If you can read a marking, add it to your list. A 14K mark describes a different gold content from 18K, while gold plating and gold-filled construction need different interpretation. The FTC's gold-jewelry guidance explains these descriptions.

Leave unclear items marked as unknown rather than guessing. Ask how the buyer establishes the material and accounts for stones or non-gold components. A piece's overall scale weight is not automatically its pure-gold weight.

Give diamond-set jewelry and coins separate attention

A heavy Cuban chain, a diamond bracelet and a gold coin need different discussions. Keep reports and paperwork with the matching item. Before treating a complete or signed piece as scrap, ask whether its design, stones or condition affect the offer.

Do not remove stones or open coin holders to prepare for weighing. Use our scrap-gold checklist for broken jewelry and our coin collection guide for gold and silver coins.

Compare the final amount on a consistent basis

Ask which pieces, weights and purities the amount covers. If you remove items from a lot, request the revised amount. Record any conditions attached to an estimate and ask when it becomes a purchase offer.

A dated gold-price reference can help you understand the market input. It cannot tell you which buyer will make the best offer for a complete jewelry collection. Our gold-buyer comparison guide explains the questions to use.

Agree on payment arrangements before accepting

Payment at Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is available by cash, bank wire or business check. For a high-value transaction, discuss your preference ahead of the appointment and confirm the final amount and timing before accepting.

Do I need to sort every piece by karat first?

No. Organize what you can without testing or damaging it. Bring unmarked or mixed pieces for examination and explain what is uncertain.

Can I bring coins and jewelry together?

Yes. Mention both when arranging the visit and keep their paperwork separate. An inventory is especially useful when the collection contains many different items.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

Bring a diamond necklace as a complete piece, with its pendant, chain, matching components and existing reports. Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural polished diamonds of any size and shape, including substantial necklaces and multi-stone jewelry.

In this guide

  • Identify the necklace design and included parts
  • Separate individual and total diamond weight
  • Keep stone information matched to the jewelry
  • Point out condition and missing components
  • Compare offers for the same necklace
  • Arrange your Downtown LA necklace evaluation

Identify the necklace design and included parts

A solitaire pendant, a tennis necklace and a graduated riviere need different item descriptions. List the complete necklace, any detachable pendant, removable sections and matching jewelry you want considered. Keep pieces you plan to retain separate.

For a substantial necklace, bring its original accessories and documentation if available. A recognizable-looking design or branded box alone does not establish the maker of the jewelry inside it. Our fine-jewelry selling guide covers complete designs and records.

Separate individual and total diamond weight

GIA explains the quality factors considered for diamonds. A necklace's combined diamond weight should not be confused with the weight of its largest individual stone.

Ask whether the stated weight refers to one pendant diamond, several principal stones or every diamond in the necklace. Keep colored gemstones outside a diamond-only total. The carat-weight guide gives examples of these different descriptions.

Keep stone information matched to the jewelry

Bring existing grading reports and receipts. A report for the pendant's center stone does not automatically describe its surrounding diamonds or the chain. Note which document belongs to which item.

Sample GIA reports show the stone information to look for. If your necklace has no report, explain that when you contact the buyer. You do not need to invent grades to begin the conversation.

Point out condition and missing components

Describe a broken chain, replaced clasp, missing stone, repaired link or altered length you know about. Bring detached parts that belong to the piece. Ask whether the proposal considers the complete necklace's resale potential, its materials or both.

Do not assume that every defect causes only a small discount or that a repair will recover its cost. Discuss the actual piece before arranging polishing, stone removal or restoration. Keep fragile items supported in their own container for the visit.

Compare offers for the same necklace
