A diamond purchase evaluation supports a buyer’s offer. An insurance appraisal is a valuation prepared for a specified purpose and recipient. Before booking, explain which result you need and confirm the examination, documentation, fees and timing.

In this guide

  • Choose the result you actually need
  • Ask what the service includes
  • Understand qualifications without confusing labels
  • Prepare the item and its documents
  • Confirm evaluation and payment timing separately
  • Arrange a natural-diamond purchase evaluation

Choose the result you actually need

If you want to sell a diamond, ask for a purchase evaluation and an offer for the items you are presenting. If an insurer or another recipient requires a valuation report, tell the provider about that separate requirement before booking.

GIA's appraisal guidance explains that grading reports and monetary appraisals are different. A purchase offer is another distinct result: the amount a particular buyer proposes to pay under stated terms.

Ask what the service includes

The word appraisal is sometimes used loosely. Ask the provider to identify the actual deliverable, examination method and fee before agreeing. A free initial conversation does not automatically include a formal report or paid laboratory work.

Your needConfirm in advance
An offer to sellItems included, outstanding checks and the purchase amount
An insurance valuationThe recipient's requirements and the report's intended use
Stone identification or gradingThe laboratory service and information it establishes

If a report has already been prepared, bring it. Read its purpose and assumptions instead of assuming it can be used for every transaction.

Understand qualifications without confusing labels

Ask who will examine the item and which qualifications are relevant to the assignment. Gemological education and valuation training answer different questions.

GIA does not certify businesses, appraisers or gemstones. Ask for the exact credential rather than treating “GIA-certified” as proof of a service's scope. Our appraiser selection guide explains further questions.

Prepare the item and its documents

Bring the complete jewelry, existing grading reports and known repair or condition records. Describe loose stones or damaged settings. Ask before authorizing removal, repair or additional laboratory examination.

The 4Cs help organize quality information. A photo or a phone description cannot establish every relevant characteristic. A mounted piece may also limit what can be observed during the initial examination.

Confirm evaluation and payment timing separately

Tell the buyer if timing matters to you and describe the number of pieces. Ask whether any identification or other checks may be required before an offer is final. A large collection and a single well-documented stone may involve different work.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds offers payment by cash, bank wire or business check for agreed purchases. Confirm the method and arrangements before accepting. The time spent examining jewelry is a separate question from the completion or availability of a payment.

Arrange a natural-diamond purchase evaluation

We buy natural, cut and polished diamonds only, of any size and shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, rough or uncut diamonds. Visit our diamond-buying page for the service we provide.

Call 310-663-1340 or arrange your visit to 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Explain any formal appraisal requirement at the outset.

Does an evaluation require accepting an offer?

You decide whether to accept a purchase proposal. Clarify any separately agreed examination or report charges before commissioning that work.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

A natural diamond does not have one fixed price based on carat weight. To understand an offer, consider the actual stone, matching report, condition, included jewelry and current purchase terms. A retail listing or insurance value is not an offer to buy your item.

In this guide

  • Start by identifying the kind of price
  • Describe the diamond beyond its weight
  • Match the report to the stone being offered
  • Keep natural origin and current condition clear
  • Ask what is included in the final amount
  • Request an offer for your natural diamond in Downtown LA

Start by identifying the kind of price

Before comparing two amounts, write down what each represents. Is it an advertised retail asking price, a valuation prepared for a particular purpose, or a buyer's proposal for the diamond you own? Keep the date and item description beside the figure.

AmountQuestion to ask
Retail listingDoes it describe the same stone, setting and purchase terms?
Insurance appraisalWhat purpose and valuation date does the document state?
Preliminary estimateWhat assumptions or examinations remain?
Purchase offerWhat exact items, conditions and payment arrangements does it include?

GIA explains the difference between a diamond grading report and an appraisal. Its grading report does not supply a monetary value. A high replacement figure therefore should not be copied into the purchase-offer column.

Describe the diamond beyond its weight

GIA's quality factors describe carat weight, color, clarity and cut. Read those details together, alongside shape, measurements and any report comments. One carat describes weight; it does not identify one standard quality or price.

For a large stone, keep its individual weight separate from the total weight of diamonds in its setting. For an eternity band, necklace or tennis bracelet, ask which stones the stated total includes. Our carat-weight guide explains those distinctions.

Match the report to the stone being offered

Bring existing paperwork rather than recreating grades from memory. Use GIA Report Check for the available report record, and ask how the document is matched to your diamond. Keep any newer repair or condition information with it.

A missing report does not establish that a diamond is worthless. Ask which examination is appropriate before paying for new documentation. Conversely, a report alone does not show that a diamond has remained in the same condition since it was examined.

Keep natural origin and current condition clear

Tell the buyer about known chips, repairs, treatments or uncertainty about identification. GIA's identification guidance explains why natural origin cannot reliably be determined from ordinary appearance alone.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural, cut and polished diamonds only, of any size and shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. A quote describing another material is not a substitute for an offer for your natural diamond.

Ask what is included in the final amount

List the center diamond, mounting, side stones and any matching pieces. If you want to retain part of the jewelry, have the proposal revised before agreeing. Do not assume that an offer for a whole ring divides according to its retail component prices.

Record outstanding checks or charges, how long the offer is available, and the payment arrangement. Our diamond offer comparison guide provides a consistent checklist. Fixed resale percentages cannot account for every stone, purchase history and transaction.

Request an offer for your natural diamond in Downtown LA

Contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 310-663-1340. We are at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Bring the jewelry intact and share any reports you already have.

Large single diamonds, smaller natural stones and substantial collections are welcome. Cash, bank wire and business-check payment are available for agreed purchases. Confirm the final amount and arrangements before accepting.

Can a price-per-carat figure tell me my offer?

Only alongside the specific stone and transaction it describes. Multiplying your weight by a retail figure for a different diamond does not produce a buyer's offer.

Will waiting guarantee a higher price?

No. A future purchase price is uncertain. Compare a current offer with your own reasons for selling instead of relying on a promised return.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

Bring each loose natural diamond with its matching report and any known condition history. Keep stones and documents organized individually, explain uncertainties and state whether you need a purchase offer or a separate valuation report.

In this guide

  • Organize stones one at a time
  • Bring the records you already have
  • Prepare quality questions without assigning grades
  • Say what you need from the evaluation
  • Compare the offer against your item list
  • Contact the Downtown Los Angeles location

Organize stones one at a time

For several loose diamonds, make an item list and keep each stone in a separate suitable gem container. Match its paperwork to the list. This helps avoid confusing similar-looking stones or repeating a report's information for the wrong diamond.

Write down the known shape and report number. Distinguish a documented carat weight from an estimate. If you also have a ring or pendant you might sell, keep it intact instead of removing its stone to create another loose diamond.

Bring the records you already have

Useful records can include a grading report, receipt, prior appraisal and information about damage or recutting. For GIA paperwork, use Report Check to consult the available record.

Ask how the report is matched to the actual stone. If the report is missing or you are uncertain about a number, explain the gap. Do not pay for new documentation solely because you assume every buyer requires it.

Prepare quality questions without assigning grades

GIA's quality factors provide a useful vocabulary for carat, color, clarity and cut. Shape and millimeter measurements add further detail to the description.

The diamond grading chart guide explains the abbreviations and scales you may encounter on a report.

Ask which characteristics are confirmed by existing records and which need examination. Share known chips, abrasions or treatments. A diamond's weight alone does not establish its identity, quality or an offer.

If the report records fluorescence, ask how it affects this particular stone's appearance and offer. GIA explains that fluorescence can affect appearance or have no visible effect; its presence alone does not establish a fixed discount.

Our large natural diamond guide covers substantial stones as well as smaller diamonds of any shape. Keep a single stone's weight separate from totals for a collection.

Say what you need from the evaluation

A purchase proposal and a formal valuation report are different services. GIA explains why a grading report does not assign monetary value. An insurance or other formal appraisal also needs a stated purpose and scope.

If a third party needs a document, ask about its requirements first. Tell the provider what report is expected rather than assuming that a buyer's offer will meet that need. The evaluation-versus-appraisal guide explains the distinction.

Compare the offer against your item list

Check which stones are included and whether the amount is final or subject to additional work. For several items, ask for enough detail to understand the proposal before deciding to sell part or all of the collection.

Confirm any outstanding costs, the duration of the offer and payment arrangements. If you remove an item from the sale, request a revised amount. A quote for a different origin, grade or set of items cannot settle the comparison.

Contact the Downtown Los Angeles location

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural polished diamonds of any size and shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown diamonds or rough and uncut material. Tell us what the documentation says if origin is uncertain.

Call 310-663-1340 or contact us to arrange a visit to 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Our diamond-buying service offers cash, bank wire or business-check payment for agreed purchases.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys large, high-quality gemstones, including Ceylon blue sapphires, with or without certificates. Bring the complete jewelry and any existing records so the sapphire, natural diamonds and setting can be considered together.

In this guide

  • Start with our gemstone buying focus
  • Discuss quality, size and condition together
  • Bring a report if you have one
  • Keep sapphire and diamond acceptance distinct
  • Arrange your Los Angeles evaluation

Start with our gemstone buying focus

Our gemstone buying is limited to large, high-quality stones. We are interested in pieces such as Ceylon blue sapphires, green Colombian emeralds and Burmese rubies. A certificate or laboratory report is welcome but is not required to request an evaluation.

If you have a sapphire ring, pendant, earrings or another fine jewelry piece, describe the stone, its approximate dimensions if known and the setting. Explain what you know about its origin and what remains uncertain. Ceylon is the name traditionally used in the trade for Sri Lankan origin; a blue appearance alone does not establish that origin.

Discuss quality, size and condition together

GIA’s sapphire quality guide discusses color, clarity, cut and carat weight. A large stone should still be assessed for its actual quality and condition. Likewise, a desirable color description does not identify all the details needed for a purchase decision.

Bring the jewelry intact. Note chips, wear, repaired settings or replaced stones that you know about. If the sapphire is mounted, ask which details can be established and which are estimated. Do not remove it yourself just to prepare an inquiry.

Information to shareUseful context
Size or known weightThe actual measurement or record, with estimates labeled
Color and appearanceA description of the stone without assigning a grade from a photo
Claimed originWhether it comes from a report, receipt or family history
Treatment historyAny information already known or documented
Complete settingMetal, additional stones, condition and maker records

Bring a report if you have one

GIA’s colored-stone services distinguish identification reports from reports that also address geographic origin. Read the exact document and any treatment information, rather than assuming every certificate provides the same conclusions.

GIA’s sapphire buying guide explains that an origin opinion can be provided when possible. A buyer still needs to examine the actual item. If you have no certificate, contact us first; do not order a new report simply because you assume one is required to start.

Keep sapphire and diamond acceptance distinct

The large, high-quality requirement applies to our gemstone buying. Our separate diamond-buying service purchases natural cut and polished diamonds in any size or shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds.

For sapphire and diamond jewelry, ask what the offer includes and how the complete setting was considered. Existing records and the estate jewelry inventory guide can help organize a larger collection.

Arrange your Los Angeles evaluation

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Contact us at 310-663-1340 with your gemstone or jewelry details. Payment options for accepted purchases include cash, bank wire and business check; confirm the amount and timing before finalizing.

Can I bring a large, high-quality sapphire without a certificate?

Yes. Certificates are optional. Bring the stone or complete jewelry and any information you already have.

Do you buy every sapphire regardless of size or quality?

No. Our gemstone buying focuses only on large, high-quality stones. Describe your item so we can discuss an appropriate evaluation.

A 14K marking describes gold content; solid or hollow describes construction. Check both before valuing a ring. A stamp, weight comparison or magnet response alone cannot verify the entire piece.

In this guide

  • Read purity and construction as separate information
  • Inspect the ring without damaging it
  • Check whether the price is for metal or a complete ring
  • Bring the ring and its records for a sale

Read purity and construction as separate information

14K gold contains 14 parts gold in 24 parts of alloy. Fineness expresses gold content per thousand; 585 is a commonly used marking for 14K jewelry. The World Gold Council's purity guide explains these conventions.

The FTC describes solid gold as a gold item that is not hollow. Gold-filled and plated items have a gold layer over another material. Ask for an explicit description when a seller uses “solid gold” loosely to mean something different.

Inspect the ring without damaging it

Look at the inner band, visible seams, underside of the setting and signs of resizing. Note the markings and any worn areas, but do not scratch the ring on ceramic or apply chemicals to prove a claim. A missing stamp can leave uncertainty; it does not establish that the ring is plated.

A heavy ring may contain substantial metal, but weight alone does not identify that metal. Likewise, a nonmagnetic response does not prove gold. Have the actual ring evaluated and ask how the materials and different components were assessed.

Check whether the price is for metal or a complete ring

For a plain band, gold content and net metal weight are central to a metal estimate. For a signed ring or a ring with diamonds, the setting, maker information and stones may need separate consideration. Keep the item intact until that discussion.

Our 14K gold diamond-ring guide explains why a complete ring cannot always be valued from its scale weight. A purchase receipt documents an earlier transaction; it does not guarantee the current resale amount.

Bring the ring and its records for a sale

Keep detached parts, reports and repair records together. At Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds, you can discuss a single ring or a larger group of gold jewelry, scrap and chains through our gold-buying service.

Ask for the purchase amount for the actual ring and clarify how stones or non-gold parts were treated. Payment choices are cash, bank wire and business check. Call 310-663-1340 to plan your visit to 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014.

Does a 585 stamp guarantee that every part is 14K gold?

No. It is useful information for examination, but the item and any separate components still need assessment. Point out repairs or replaced parts that you know about.

We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

22K gold is nominally 22 parts gold out of 24, about 91.67%. A purchase evaluation still needs the actual material and net metal weight, plus consideration of the design, condition and any stones.

In this guide

  • Understand what 22K means
  • Keep the full piece separate from its gold content
  • Organize sets and inherited pieces carefully
  • Compare purchase offers without a fixed payout assumption

Understand what 22K means

Karat measures the gold proportion in an alloy. Dividing 22 by 24 gives about 91.67%, compared with 75% for 18K. The World Gold Council's karat and fineness guide provides the broader purity context. A 916 marking commonly describes approximately 91.6% fineness, but the marking still needs to be assessed against the piece.

Color is not a purity test. Nor does a high karat guarantee a particular level of resistance to wear: construction, thickness, alloy and use all matter. Do not squeeze a hollow bangle or bend a chain to test whether it is soft.

Keep the full piece separate from its gold content

A scale weighs stones, attachments and other components together with the gold alloy. Ask what weight is used in a metal estimate. The FTC's jewelry descriptions also distinguish karat-gold pieces from gold-filled and plated materials.

For a material-content example only, 12 grams of verified 22K alloy contains about 11 grams of gold: 12 × 22 ÷ 24. This assumes the full 12 grams is that alloy. It is not a market price or purchase offer, and it excludes any separate stones or components.

Organize sets and inherited pieces carefully

Keep matching necklaces, earrings and bangles together, with receipts or maker records where available. Note damage and previous repairs. Ask whether the complete set or a signed piece needs consideration beyond metal content before separating it into scrap.

For a large mixed lot, label the pieces you can identify and leave uncertain items for examination. Our gold-jewelry visit checklist covers preparation. You do not need to buy testing equipment or a new appraisal to start the conversation.

Compare purchase offers without a fixed payout assumption

Retail prices may include workmanship, distribution and brand premiums. Those are not automatically recovered when selling. Ask the buyer to explain the actual purchase amount, tested purity, weight and treatment of the whole item.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold jewelry and scrap in Downtown Los Angeles, including substantial quantities. Call 310-663-1340 to discuss your pieces and payment by cash, bank wire or business check.

Can I bring 22K jewelry without a receipt?

Yes. Bring existing records if you have them, and explain what you know about the jewelry. The purchase evaluation concerns the actual items.

Is 22K jewelry guaranteed to return its purchase price?

No. Gold content is only one part of a jewelry purchase. Current market conditions, the item and the buyer's offer determine what is available when you sell.

To estimate your gold, list each piece, its measured metal weight, verified purity and a dated gold-price reference in matching units. Keep unknown inputs visible and compare the result with an actual purchase offer; the estimate is not a guaranteed payout.

In this guide

  • Build a list before doing the calculation
  • Separate a marking from a verified input
  • Work through a clearly hypothetical example
  • Flag pieces that need more than a gold calculation
  • Use the worksheet to compare final offers

Build a list before doing the calculation

Use one line per item or clearly identified group. Start with a description you can match back to the jewelry: “broken yellow chain with detached clasp” is more useful than “miscellaneous gold.” Keep a photograph or count for your own records.

RecordWhat to note
ItemDescription, quantity and whether the piece is complete
MaterialVisible mark, tested purity and any uncertainty
WeightUnit used and whether stones or other components are included
DocumentsReports, maker records or repair history that match the item
OfferIncluded pieces, final amount, conditions and payment method

Separate a marking from a verified input

The World Gold Council explains karat and fineness: 18K is 75% gold, while 14K is approximately 58.3%. A stamp is information to investigate, not a substitute for assessing the piece. Write “marked 14K, not yet tested” when that is all you know.

Do not include gemstone weight as though it were gold alloy. Repairs, springs and other components can also change the applicable weight. Ask the buyer which measurement and purity were used before comparing calculations.

Work through a clearly hypothetical example

Suppose a plain piece contains 10 grams of verified 18K alloy, with no other components in that measurement. Its fine-gold content is 10 × 18 ÷ 24 = 7.5 grams. If a hypothetical pure-gold reference were $100 per gram, the reference metal value would be $750.

The $100 figure is an illustration, not today's gold price. The $750 is a calculated metal reference, not an offer from Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds. For a real calculation, use a dated reference such as the World Gold Council's gold-price data, checking currency and units.

Our guide to how gold is valued explains the calculation and purchase context in more depth.

Flag pieces that need more than a gold calculation

Keep diamond-set Cuban chains, signed jewelry and coins on separate lines. A metal estimate alone does not account for every stone, a complete jewelry piece or potential collectible characteristics. Bring existing records and ask how each factor was treated.

For a group of damaged jewelry, use our scrap-gold guide. Leave pieces intact until you have discussed the evaluation.

Use the worksheet to compare final offers

Ask whether each amount covers the same items and whether any conditions or charges remain. There is no universal payout percentage that establishes the correct result for every collection. Record the final amount you would receive and the payment arrangements.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold, scrap, Cuban chains with or without diamonds, and gold and silver coins. Large quantities are welcome at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Arrange an evaluation and discuss cash, bank wire or business-check payment.

Do I need to weigh everything before visiting?

No. A home measurement is optional and may include stones or use an unsuitable unit or scale. Bring the items and ask for the measurements used in the purchase evaluation.

A gold Rolex should be evaluated as a complete watch, including its exact reference, components, condition and accessories. Compare written purchase terms for the same package rather than applying a gold price to the entire watch weight.

In this guide

  • Ask the buyer to identify the complete watch
  • Keep metal content and watch value separate
  • Look for a clear account of condition
  • Bring documents without assigning a fixed premium
  • Compare like-for-like proposals
  • Discuss the sale in Downtown LA

Ask the buyer to identify the complete watch

Start with the model and reference if you know them, but do not guess a reference from a similar online photograph. Describe the dial, bezel, bracelet and material shown in your records. Bring the watch so its actual configuration can be examined.

The official Rolex Day-Date collection provides a manufacturer reference for that family. It is not an appraisal of an older watch or proof that a particular item matches the advertised configuration.

Keep metal content and watch value separate

A watch contains a movement, crystal and other components. Its entire measured weight is not the weight of pure gold. The case, bracelet and replacement components also need their own material descriptions.

The FTC explains gold terminology, including the difference between an alloy and a surface coating. If metal content is discussed, ask which components and verified fineness the calculation concerns. Our gold valuation guide explains the calculation without treating a luxury watch as one solid lump of gold.

Look for a clear account of condition

Ask about bracelet wear, missing links, case shape, dial condition, operation and known repairs. Disclose any aftermarket gem setting, replaced bezel or service work. A manufacturer service replacement and an aftermarket alteration should not be silently grouped together.

Request an evaluation before paying for cosmetic work. A repair expense does not guarantee an equal increase in a buying offer. Keep service estimates separate from the actual price proposed for the watch as presented.

Bring documents without assigning a fixed premium

Original purchase records, warranty papers, service invoices and spare links help describe what is included. Check that they belong to the watch. Missing paperwork does not prevent you from requesting an evaluation.

No universal percentage applies to a box, a warranty card or a complete package. Ask how the actual accessories were considered rather than adding a predetermined amount to an online asking price.

Compare like-for-like proposals

Record the buyer, evaluation date, included items, final amount and any conditions. Ask whether further inspection could change the figure and whether a fee applies if you decline. Verify individual qualifications or affiliations directly instead of relying on an unsourced ranking.

Our gold Rolex comparison guide helps distinguish configurations. The local Rolex buyer guide covers questions about an in-person transaction.

Discuss the sale in Downtown LA

For an in-person purchase evaluation, contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, or call 310-663-1340. Payment for agreed purchases is available by cash, bank wire or business check; confirm the arrangements before accepting.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling a luxury watch in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

When comparing 14K gold rings, look beyond the karat label. Compare construction, band thickness, stone descriptions, fit and written seller terms. For a future sale, keep the receipt and reports, but do not assume the retail price will be recovered.

In this guide

  • Compare the same kind of ring
  • Choose color with the finish and alloy in mind
  • Inspect fit, setting and stone information
  • Keep buying terms separate from resale expectations

Compare the same kind of ring

A plain band, a hollow fashion ring and a diamond-set ring can all be described as 14K. Their weights, construction and price components differ. Ask for a written material description and compare rings with similar size, width and stone specifications before drawing conclusions from price.

For the distinction between karat and construction, see our 14K solid-gold ring guide. The FTC's jewelry guidance explains material descriptions and recommends reviewing written seller policies.

Choose color with the finish and alloy in mind

Yellow, white and rose gold can each be made as 14K alloys. The World Gold Council describes how alloying affects gold color and notes the common rhodium finish on white gold. The same karat does not establish the same alloy formula or maintenance needs.

Ask about the actual finish and the work involved in maintaining it. If particular metals cause you skin problems, request the alloy information rather than relying on the color or karat as a guarantee.

Inspect fit, setting and stone information

Check whether the band is comfortable, whether neighboring rings rub, and what resizing is possible for the design. Ask how a resize could affect the setting or surface pattern. Thin sections and worn prongs deserve attention even when the gold purity is known.

For a ring with a diamond, ask whether it is natural or laboratory-grown, which report describes it, and whether the stated weight is for one stone or all stones combined. The setting's 14K label does not answer those questions.

Keep buying terms separate from resale expectations

Read the return, sizing and warranty terms for the exact purchase, including any customized work. Keep the receipt and matching stone reports. A buyback or trade-in offer, if available from a seller, should be understood on its written terms rather than assumed.

When you later sell, a buyer evaluates the ring you own under then-current conditions. A purchase offer need not match its retail cost or insurance replacement figure. Our metal-and-diamond value guide explains why both components matter.

Where can I have an unwanted 14K ring evaluated?

A diamond grading chart explains quality terms. Match its scale to the laboratory report, then compare the stone’s measurements, condition and identification. The chart does not establish a purchase price or an insurance value.

In this guide

  • Identify what the chart is showing
  • Read the D-to-Z color scale
  • Decode clarity abbreviations
  • Match the chart to the report type
  • Keep quality descriptions separate from money
  • Bring the chart questions to your evaluation

Identify what the chart is showing

Start with the heading and legend. A color scale, a diagram of clarity characteristics and a seller’s price grid answer different questions. Record the laboratory, report type and date before comparing their terminology.

FieldRead it asCheck separately
ColorThe grade on the stated color scaleWhether the report concerns a D-to-Z or fancy-color diamond
ClarityA grade describing clarity characteristicsThe actual stone, plotted features and report comments
CutA cut-quality grade where the report provides oneShape, cutting style, polish and symmetry
CaratThe stone’s weightMillimeter measurements and any total-weight wording

A useful comparison keeps the complete description together. Writing only “one carat, good quality” leaves out the details needed to understand the stone.

Read the D-to-Z color scale

The GIA color guide describes grading under controlled conditions against reference stones. The familiar groupings below are a reading aid; a screen image cannot reproduce those grading conditions.

GradesColor group
D–FColorless
G–JNear colorless
K–MFaint
N–RVery light
S–ZLight

Use the actual grade on the matching report. Do not assume that everyone sees the same difference between two grades or that a photograph establishes a grade. Fancy-color descriptions need their own context; they should not be forced into this chart.

Decode clarity abbreviations

GIA’s clarity scale has 11 grades and uses examination under 10× magnification. Characteristics are considered by their size, number, position, nature and relief, rather than by counting marks alone.

AbbreviationGrade name
FLFlawless
IFInternally Flawless
VVS1, VVS2Very, Very Slightly Included
VS1, VS2Very Slightly Included
SI1, SI2Slightly Included
I1, I2, I3Included

“Eye-clean” is not one of these grades. If a seller uses that phrase, ask what viewing conditions it describes and inspect the actual stone. A clarity abbreviation alone is not a promise that a feature will be invisible to you.

Match the chart to the report type

GIA’s sample natural-diamond reports show how quality information is recorded. The overall GIA cut grade applies to standard round brilliant diamonds in the D-to-Z color range; a missing overall cut grade on another shape does not mean that the stone received a poor grade.

Check laboratory-grown documents separately. GIA’s current Laboratory-Grown Diamond Quality Assessment uses Premium or Standard descriptions. Older documents and other report types may use different wording. Read the actual document instead of assuming that one grading chart fits every report.

Keep quality descriptions separate from money

A grade chart is not a quote. GIA explains that it does not provide monetary appraisals or participate in diamond pricing. A retail listing, an insurance replacement value and a buyer’s purchase offer therefore should not be treated as interchangeable amounts.

For a sale, ask what the offer includes: the center diamond, accent stones, setting and any associated jewelry. Bring the existing report and explain repairs or changes you know about. The carat-weight guide helps separate a single stone’s weight from the combined weight in a ring.

Bring the chart questions to your evaluation

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural polished diamonds of any size and shape at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. Review our diamond-buying service and contact us with the item and paperwork you have. Ask for an explanation of the final offer for your actual piece.

Can I grade my diamond from an online chart?

You can learn the terminology and prepare questions. The chart does not replace examination of the stone under the required grading conditions.

Does a report number guarantee the price?

No. A report supplies information about the examined stone. Confirm that it matches your item and ask the buyer to state a separate purchase amount.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Selling diamonds in Los Angeles · 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

  • GIA: sample natural diamond reports
  • GIA: laboratory-grown diamond services
  • GIA: appraisals and monetary value

Related guides

Start with an item-by-item inventory, preserve existing records and label unknown details honestly. An evaluator can then consider materials, stones, condition, workmanship and supported history before stating a value or purchase offer for a defined purpose.

In this guide

  • Create a simple inventory before assigning values
  • Keep materials and complete-piece features separate
  • Ask what supports stone and maker identification
  • Define the purpose of a requested value
  • Preserve the collection for evaluation

Create a simple inventory before assigning values

Give each piece a short identifier and photograph it from several angles. Keep matching earrings, chains and pendants associated with one another, and note any detached parts. Separate observations from assumptions: “blue stone” is more useful than an unsupported claim that it is sapphire.

Inventory fieldWhat to record
Item and identifierRing A, necklace B or another clear label
Visible marksLetters, numbers and symbols exactly as seen
ConditionMissing pieces, damage and known repairs
Associated recordsReceipts, reports, appraisals and maker information
Known historyDocumented facts, with family recollections labeled separately

Keep materials and complete-piece features separate

A collection may contain precious metals, plated items, costume jewelry and pieces whose materials are unknown. Do not assume that everything is gold because it came from the same jewelry box. Let examination establish which materials are present.

For gold jewelry, the relevant metal weight and purity must be distinguished from stones and other components. A complete piece also warrants consideration of its design and condition. GIA’s estate jewelry guide highlights examination for damage, missing stones and evidence of repairs.

Ask what supports stone and maker identification

Bring existing laboratory reports and ask which stones they describe. Natural origin and treatment status are separate details; an identification should not assume that every natural gemstone is untreated. Record what the examiner established and any limits on the assessment.

If a report describes a diamond, our diamond grading chart guide explains its color, clarity and cut terminology so you can prepare more specific evaluation questions.

A maker’s mark or period-style design can guide research, but it is not a substitute for authentication. Ask what supports the attribution and date. Avoid dismantling a possible antique or signed piece before its complete design has been considered; see the antique gold evaluation guide.

Define the purpose of a requested value

The Appraisal Foundation’s jewelry guide explains that a credible appraisal identifies the items, intended use, value definition and relevant date. Establish those requirements before commissioning a report.

A buyer’s current purchase amount answers a different practical question: what is offered for the stated items under the stated terms? Do not convert an old appraisal into that amount using a fixed percentage. Our inherited jewelry documentation guide helps you choose the right next step.

Preserve the collection for evaluation

Store pieces separately and avoid experimenting with cleaning on unfamiliar materials. GIA’s care guidance notes that gemstones and treatments can require different handling. Ask before paying for restoration intended only to improve a sale price.

For a purchase evaluation, contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 310-663-1340 or visit 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Our estate jewelry service can discuss the collection you have and the information needed for an offer.

Can I value an entire jewelry box by its total weight?

No. Different materials and individual pieces need identification. A combined scale weight does not establish the relevant precious-metal content or complete-piece value.

Should I discard items that look like costume jewelry?

Keep uncertain items identifiable until you know what they are. Appearance alone is not a reliable way to sort a collection by material or potential significance.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling estate jewelry in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Selling estate jewelry in Los Angeles · 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

  • GIA: estate jewelry examination
  • The Appraisal Foundation: gem and jewelry appraisal guide
  • GIA: caring for jewelry

  • Inherited Jewelry Valuation in Los Angeles: Documents & Next Steps

Read recent reviews for the correct business and the kind of sale you plan to make. Look for concrete details, compare sources and verify terms directly. A star rating or a large review count does not guarantee your offer or experience.

Match the review to the right business and service

Check the business name, location and type of transaction. A review of a jewelry repair or retail purchase may say little about selling a diamond or a mixed estate collection. Similar business names can also make it easy to read feedback about another location.

Record the date of the review and the service described. A useful shortlist should connect the feedback to what you need now: gold buying, a natural diamond evaluation, a luxury watch purchase or an estate jewelry offer.

Use ratings as a starting point for reading

The FTC’s online review guidance recommends checking multiple sources and considering recency and reviewer history. It also cautions that readers cannot reliably identify every fake review by appearance alone.

There is no magic threshold such as a particular star score or number of reviews that proves a buyer is trustworthy. A new business may have few reviews, while a long history of feedback may involve services unrelated to yours. Read the substance before drawing a conclusion.

Turn specific experiences into practical questions

A review mentionsAsk the buyer

A quick paymentWhat timing applies to my preferred payment method?
A collection purchaseWill my offer identify included items or selected pieces?

A reviewer’s outcome is not a promise about your transaction. A larger collection, an unfamiliar stone or a different payment method can require different steps. Ask about the process for your own items instead of assuming an identical timetable or price.

Read complaints and responses in context

Note the specific issue and whether the business response addresses it. Separate a disagreement about the amount offered from an allegation about custody, undisclosed charges or an unfulfilled agreement. Those concerns require different questions.

A repeated concern is a reason to investigate, not enough on its own to declare the business dishonest. Likewise, an enthusiastic comment about a high payout does not reveal the item’s full description. Use our buyer questions guide to verify the details directly.

Compare offers after doing the review research

Bring the same items and records to each evaluation. Ask for the final amount, included components, any deductions and the offer’s conditions. Keep that comparison separate from the online rating.

html:
A 24K chain is high-purity gold jewelry, but the actual fineness, link construction, clasp and condition still need examination. Keep a metal-content estimate separate from the price paid for design and workmanship.

In this guide

  • Read the fineness description carefully
  • Inspect the links and clasp as a connected piece
  • Separate the chain from a pendant in your inventory
  • Compare the actual offer, not a promised return

Read the fineness description carefully

24K describes essentially pure gold. In practical fineness descriptions, you may see figures such as 999 or 999.9 rather than a promise of absolute purity. The World Gold Council explains karat and fineness, including this distinction.

Photograph readable marks on your chain or record them with its paperwork. Ask how the actual chain and its components will be evaluated. Neither yellow color nor a stamp alone proves the composition of the complete necklace.

Inspect the links and clasp as a connected piece

Look for stretched links, flattening, previous repairs and an unreliable clasp. Different link styles use different construction, so identical appearance is not a universal quality test. A wide chain can be hollow or contain less metal than its size suggests.

The FTC notes that pure gold is soft. Handle the necklace carefully and avoid bending links to test it. Ask about the condition and construction before paying for polishing or a repair solely to prepare a sale.

Separate the chain from a pendant in your inventory

A pendant may have a different purity, maker or stone from the chain. Keep the set together but ask whether the components need separate evaluation. The same applies to a replacement clasp or a section repaired with different material.

For a necklace with diamonds, note that the total scale weight includes the stones. Our chain construction guide explains why weight and appearance need to be considered together, even though the nominal purity differs.

Compare the actual offer, not a promised return

The retail price of a chain can include design, labor and brand premiums. Those costs are not automatically recovered in a sale. Ask how the buyer considered net metal weight and whether the intact necklace has a separate resale opportunity.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold jewelry and chains in Downtown Los Angeles. Call 310-663-1340 to discuss your piece or a substantial collection. Payment is available by cash, bank wire or business check.

Should I sell a broken 24K chain only as scrap?

Ask for an evaluation first. Bring detached parts, explain known repairs and discuss whether the design or maker warrants consideration as a complete piece. Our scrap-gold guide covers broken-item preparation.

14K white gold is a gold alloy, often finished with rhodium. A worn finish and the amount of gold are different questions: evaluate the ring’s actual material, construction, condition and any diamonds before comparing purchase offers.

In this guide

  • Distinguish the alloy from the surface finish
  • Review worn areas and previous work
  • Keep diamond quality separate from the 14K label
  • Compare offers for the complete ring

Distinguish the alloy from the surface finish

White gold combines gold with other metals to produce a paler alloy. Many pieces also have a rhodium finish. The World Gold Council's color guide explains this combination. A bright white surface does not make the ring platinum, and surface wear alone does not establish that the underlying ring is fake.

Record the 14K or fineness marking and keep any material description from the original seller. Ask about the actual alloy if you need to avoid a particular metal; a color name is not an ingredient list.

Review worn areas and previous work

Look at the underside of the band, prongs and areas that rub against another ring. Note resizing, replacement sections or previous refinishing. These details help explain the current condition and any later repair estimate.

Before paying to replate a ring just to sell it, ask whether that work would affect the purchase offer enough to justify the cost. The FTC's jewelry guidance is useful for separating gold-alloy and plated-product descriptions.

Keep diamond quality separate from the 14K label

A 14K marking describes the metal, not the diamond. Bring any matching laboratory report and identify whether it describes the center stone or a collection of stones. GIA's diamond quality guide explains the separate roles of cut, color, clarity and carat weight.

No report establishes a fixed percentage of retail value for a sale. Use our white-gold diamond-ring guide for the combined metal-and-stone discussion.

Compare offers for the complete ring

Ask what metal weight was used and how the stones, condition and any maker information influenced the amount. Equal weights of equally pure white and yellow gold contain equal quantities of gold; complete jewelry offers can still differ.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds evaluates unwanted gold rings in Downtown Los Angeles. Arrange your visit with the ring and existing records. Discuss payment by cash, bank wire or business check before accepting an offer.

Does yellowing mean the ring has lost all its gold?

No. A change in surface appearance does not determine the gold content. Have the finish and underlying material examined rather than drawing a conclusion from color alone.

We buy large, high-quality gemstones, including green Colombian emeralds, and evaluate the complete gold ring. Certificates are welcome but not required. Bring existing records and keep the emerald and setting intact for examination.

In this guide

  • Describe the emerald and the complete ring
  • Consider quality and condition together
  • Use existing reports without making them a prerequisite
  • Protect the emerald while preparing the sale
  • Ask for an offer that covers the whole item

Describe the emerald and the complete ring

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys only large, high-quality gemstones. Green Colombian emeralds are among our focus areas, alongside Burmese rubies and Ceylon blue sapphires. If your emerald ring has no certificate, you can still contact us for an evaluation.

Share the known stone weight or dimensions, the ring’s metal description and any existing records. If the Colombian origin comes from a family account rather than a laboratory report, explain that distinction. Color alone cannot confirm where a gemstone formed.

Consider quality and condition together

GIA’s emerald quality guide discusses color, clarity, cut and carat weight, including the role of visible inclusions. A large emerald still needs a quality assessment; size by itself does not satisfy our selective gemstone buying focus.

Ask the evaluator to consider the stone’s appearance, condition and any known treatments. An inclusion seen in a photograph is not a complete identification, and an apparently clear stone should not be labeled laboratory-grown without examination.

DetailWhat to bring or ask
SizeKnown weight or measurements, with estimates labeled
OriginThe report, receipt or other source of the claim
TreatmentsExisting information about clarity enhancement or other work
Ring constructionGold marks, maker information and known repairs
ConditionChips, loose settings or replaced components to examine

Use existing reports without making them a prerequisite

GIA describes different colored-stone report services, including identification and reports that also address origin. Read what your actual report covers. A document does not automatically guarantee a particular purchase amount.

Certificates are welcome but not required here. Bring any records you already have and ask what further examination, if any, would be useful before commissioning additional work. Keep natural origin and treatment information as separate questions.

Protect the emerald while preparing the sale

GIA’s emerald care guide cautions against ultrasonic and steam cleaning because fractures and clarity-enhancement materials can be affected. A hardness number alone should not be treated as permission for rough handling or aggressive cleaning.

Bring the ring intact and disclose any damage you know about. Ask before polishing, repairing or removing the stone solely to prepare a sale. Preserve the complete design and records, especially if it may be an estate or signed piece.

Ask for an offer that covers the whole item

The finished ring’s scale weight includes the emerald and any other components. Ask how the gold setting and the gemstone are considered, and whether the offer includes the complete ring. The estate jewelry guide helps organize the information for an inherited piece.

For accompanying diamonds, our separate buying policy covers natural cut and polished diamonds of any size or shape, excluding laboratory-grown, uncut and rough diamonds.

Visit Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, or contact us at 310-663-1340 to describe your emerald ring and arrange the next step.

Is a certificate required to sell a large, high-quality emerald?

No. Bring the stone or jewelry and whatever information is available. A certificate is useful supporting documentation, not a prerequisite to requesting an evaluation.

Does a Colombian origin claim guarantee an offer?

No. The actual emerald’s quality, size, condition and identification must be considered. Explain the source of the origin claim so it can be assessed accurately.

Compare 14K chain weight, construction, condition, and any diamonds. Heavy Cuban chains and broken gold necklaces can both be brought for evaluation.

In this guide

  • What to check on a 14K gold chain
  • Cuban links: weight and construction matter
  • Gold chains with diamonds
  • Broken chains and damaged clasps
  • Estimating value before your visit
  • Selling several Cuban chains or bracelets together

What to check on a 14K gold chain

A 14K chain’s appearance tells only part of the story. Look for any purity markings, check the clasp and links, and note previous repairs. Bring the necklace itself for evaluation instead of relying on a photograph or the price of a similar chain online.

A receipt, original packaging, or maker information can add useful context. You can still bring the chain if those records are unavailable.

Cuban links: weight and construction matter

Cuban link chains and bracelets are often chosen for their substantial appearance. The width of the links, however, does not establish the amount of gold. Construction and actual weight must be considered together.

Solid and hollow construction can produce different weights in similarly sized pieces. The FTC guide to gold-jewelry descriptions explains the distinction between solid construction and karat purity. Ask how the buyer assessed the chain’s gold content, and keep stones or non-gold components separate from the weight used in a metal estimate.

Gold chains with diamonds

If your chain or bracelet contains diamonds, ask how both the gold and stones are evaluated. The overall weight of the piece includes everything on it. A simple gold calculator cannot determine the value of its diamonds. GIA describes diamond quality through cut, color, clarity and carat weight.

Bring any grading reports or original documentation you already have. Review the final offer for the complete piece and ask what it includes. For more on stone quality, read our guide to the 4 Cs of diamonds.

Broken chains and damaged clasps

A broken clasp or damaged link does not prevent you from bringing a gold chain for evaluation. Keep any detached parts with the necklace, and explain repairs or missing components that you know about.

Before paying for a repair solely to sell the chain, discuss the item’s current condition with the buyer. We also buy scrap gold and broken jewelry.

Estimating value before your visit

A chain’s original retail price can include design, labor, distribution, and other costs. A purchase offer for a used chain is a different figure. Start with the actual metal content and condition, then ask how the complete item is being considered.

Our 14K necklace value guide explains what information helps with an estimate. Use a dated metal-price reference and check the units rather than treating a calculator result as a guaranteed payout.

Selling several Cuban chains or bracelets together

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds welcomes substantial quantities, including multiple Cuban chains, gold bracelets, plain gold pieces, and diamond-set jewelry. Call to discuss the collection and arrange enough time to review the items.

Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check. Let us know your preferred method when arranging a large transaction. Our location is 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014.

Do you buy Cuban chains without diamonds?

Yes. We buy plain gold Cuban chains and bracelets as well as pieces set with diamonds.

Should I weigh my chain at home?

A home weight can help you describe the piece, but the purchase evaluation uses the actual item. Remember that the total weight may include stones and components other than gold.

Can I sell a necklace and other gold jewelry together?

Yes. Bring your chains, rings, bracelets, scrap gold, and coins together. Call ahead for a substantial quantity and keep any paperwork with the matching pieces.

A gold-colored watch may have a solid-gold alloy case, a surface coating or simply a gold-tone finish. Identify the actual materials, exact reference, movement and condition before comparing watches or asking for a selling offer.

In this guide

  • Read the material description carefully
  • Identify the movement and functions
  • Consider wear and complete construction
  • Use service records for the particular watch
  • Compare ownership cost and selling value separately
  • Bring your watch for a purchase evaluation

Read the material description carefully

Begin with the specification for the exact reference. A gold-colored dial or bracelet does not establish gold content. The case, bezel, bracelet and clasp may have different materials, and a replacement bracelet may differ from the original specification.

The FTC's precious-metal guide explains why descriptions such as karat gold and gold plated mean different things. Use marks as information to investigate, not a reason to skip examining the item.

Identify the movement and functions

Record whether the watch is quartz, manually wound or self-winding according to its documentation. Note the functions it actually has, such as a date, chronograph or calendar, and tell an evaluator if any function behaves differently than expected.

A stopped watch does not reveal the cause by itself. Do not assume a battery change or routine service will resolve every problem. Avoid opening the case or forcing controls on an unfamiliar watch.

Consider wear and complete construction

Examine the bracelet length and available extra links, clasp closure, visible case wear and any known replacement parts. A substantial bracelet and a watch on a leather strap are different packages even when the case designs look similar.

For gem-set models, note whether the setting was supplied by the maker or added later, if that history is documented. The look of diamonds alone cannot establish their origin or the originality of a bezel.

Use service records for the particular watch

Look up the maker's instructions for the exact model and discuss unknown condition with a qualified service provider. Rolex's care and service pages are a manufacturer starting point for Rolex owners; they are not a universal maintenance timetable for all watch brands.

Keep invoices describing what was done and which parts were replaced. Before paying for work solely to sell the watch, ask how its current condition would be considered in an offer.

Compare ownership cost and selling value separately

Retail prices, advertised pre-owned prices and a buyer's proposal answer different questions. Confirm whether a listed comparison includes taxes, a warranty, servicing or accessories. A watch that suits your taste does not come with a guaranteed resale return.

When selling, request consideration of the complete timepiece before any metal-only calculation. Our gold Rolex guide covers reference-level comparisons, while the women's gold watch guide focuses on fit and bracelet details.

Bring your watch for a purchase evaluation

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds discusses Rolex, Patek Philippe and other luxury watches through its Downtown Los Angeles watch-buying service. Bring available records and disclose missing components.

For an in-person purchase evaluation, contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, or call 310-663-1340. Payment for agreed purchases is available by cash, bank wire or business check; confirm the arrangements before accepting.

A 10K men’s ring may be a light hollow design or a substantial band. Nominal 10K alloy contains about 41.67% gold, but a purchase evaluation also needs its net metal weight, condition and any stones.

In this guide

  • Check the metal and construction together
  • Separate the band from its stones
  • Record wear, repairs and design details
  • Bring one ring or a larger collection
  • Review the final amount and payment terms

Check the metal and construction together

10K describes ten parts gold out of 24 parts of alloy. The World Gold Council’s purity guide puts that proportion at approximately 41.7%. It does not establish a ring’s weight or guarantee resistance to damage.

For a wide band or signet-style ring, inspect the underside as well as the face. A large profile may conceal hollow construction. Record a readable mark, but have the actual item assessed before treating it as proof. The FTC explains gold-jewelry descriptions, including karat and construction terminology.

Separate the band from its stones

The overall scale weight includes the complete ring; it is not automatically the weight of its gold alloy. Ask what metal weight and purity were used for the estimate. Our 10K gold value guide explains how those details enter a metal-content calculation.

If the ring contains stones, bring existing records and ask which stone each document describes. Keep the ring intact. Discuss what can be assessed while the stones are mounted and what remains uncertain, rather than removing them yourself.

Record wear, repairs and design details

AreaWhat to note
Band and undersideHollow areas, cracks, thinning or earlier resizing
Face and decorationEngraving, maker marks and worn details
Stone settingMissing stones, damaged prongs or known replacements
Matching recordsReceipts, reports and repair descriptions

A damaged plain band and a signed stone-set ring may require different evaluation questions. Ask whether the complete design was considered before treating the piece only as scrap. Avoid polishing away details or arranging repairs solely for resale before discussing the ring’s present condition.

Bring one ring or a larger collection

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold jewelry, scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, and gold and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Our scrap-gold preparation guide covers broken and mixed pieces.

We buy natural cut and polished diamonds in any size or shape, excluding laboratory-grown, uncut and rough diamonds. Other gemstone buying is limited to large, high-quality stones, including green Colombian emeralds, Burmese rubies and Ceylon blue sapphires. Certificates are optional.

Review the final amount and payment terms

List the items included in the offer and ask how metal, stones and condition were considered. Compare final purchase amounts for the same group of pieces. An advertised retail price for another ring is not an offer for yours.

Visit Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Call 310-663-1340 to arrange an evaluation. Payment is available by cash, bank wire or business check; confirm the amount and timing before completing the sale.

Does a larger signet ring always contain more gold?

No. Construction and net metal weight matter. Similar-looking rings can use different amounts of alloy.

Must a broken ring be repaired before an evaluation?

No. Bring it in its current condition, together with any detached parts and known repair history.

A 14K label describes gold content, not every aspect of a belly ring’s suitability. Ask about the alloy, post and decorative-end materials, dimensions and finish. A qualified piercer should assess fit and suitability for your piercing.

In this guide

  • Ask which components are actually gold
  • Separate material content from piercing suitability
  • Read gauge and length as different measurements
  • Understand gold value before considering a sale

Ask which components are actually gold

A decorative gold end may be attached to a post made from another material. Ask whether the price and 14K description refer to the complete assembly or only one component. Keep the manufacturer's description and matching receipt.

The FTC explains karat-gold, gold-filled and plated descriptions. A gold-colored surface does not establish a 14K gold component, and the weight of an assembled piece need not be entirely gold alloy.

Separate material content from piercing suitability

The Association of Professional Piercers' initial-jewelry guidance addresses material, dimensions, surface quality and construction. Its gold guidance includes requirements beyond karat alone, including alloy suitability. A “14K” label should not be treated as a universal guarantee against irritation.

Discuss your piercing and the exact item with a qualified piercer. Do not use a jewelry-value article to choose a healing schedule, replace professional fitting advice or decide that a worn or damaged piece is suitable for continued use.

Read gauge and length as different measurements

Gauge describes thickness; wearable length or diameter describes a different dimension. A listing that gives only one measurement may be insufficient to identify a matching replacement part. Ask the seller and piercer to verify the complete specification and closure compatibility.

Do not force mismatched ends and posts together or assume parts from different manufacturers will fit. Keep spare components labeled with their original description.

Understand gold value before considering a sale

For resale, identify which parts are gold, their tested purity and net weight. Stones and other materials need separate attention. A brand's retail price includes more than metal content, and a previous purchase price is not a promised payout.

If you have unwanted gold body jewelry, contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds to discuss whether the actual pieces can be evaluated. Describe all components and their condition. Do not assume every post or attachment is accepted as gold.

Our 14K value-per-gram guide explains how metal content is estimated once the gold parts and weight are established.

Does a heavier belly ring necessarily contain more gold?

No. Different posts, stones and decorative parts can change total weight. A meaningful comparison needs the same material basis, not the scale reading alone.

For an 18K ring, compare the design you will wear, its fit and construction, and the information supplied about any stones. If the ring is pre-owned, add repair history, condition and available records to the comparison.

In this guide

  • Start with how the ring fits your hand
  • Read the material and stone description together
  • Add condition checks for a pre-owned ring
  • Keep records for a later sale

Start with how the ring fits your hand

A broad band and a narrow solitaire can feel different even in the same nominal size. Try the design with any neighboring rings and check whether a raised setting catches or presses against them. Ask about sizing options before ordering or altering a ring.

18K means 75% gold. The World Gold Council's alloy guide explains how gold content and alloying relate to jewelry. Karat alone does not determine comfort, band thickness or the security of a setting.

Read the material and stone description together

Ask for the gold color, construction and exact stone description. A decorative cluster and a solitaire with the same total stone weight do not contain the same individual stones. Keep any report matched to the stone it describes.

The FTC advises checking jewelry descriptions and seller policies. Ask what the return and sizing terms cover, particularly for engraving or custom work. Do not assume every retailer provides the same terms.

Add condition checks for a pre-owned ring

Look for a thin shank, worn prongs, missing stones or evidence of previous sizing. Ask what repairs are known and whether further work is needed. GIA's estate-jewelry guidance offers context for assessing previously owned pieces.

Pre-owned does not automatically mean older, rare or less expensive. Compare the actual design, condition and documentation instead of assuming a standard discount. Our estate-jewelry valuation guide covers the additional evaluation questions.

Keep records for a later sale

Keep the receipt, original description and reports with the matching ring. Record significant repairs as they happen. These records provide context; they do not guarantee that a future buyer will pay the original price.

If you already own an unwanted ring, Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds can discuss a gold-jewelry evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles. Bring the complete piece before deciding whether it should be treated as metal, gemstone jewelry or a potentially collectible design.

Is an 18K ring always a better purchase than 14K?

No. It has a higher nominal gold proportion, but the right choice also depends on construction, fit, stones, condition and the price and terms of the actual ring.

Before buying a 14K yellow gold ring, confirm the material description, inspect its construction and fit, and read the seller’s terms. The gold color and karat label do not establish the exact alloy, stone quality or future resale price.

In this guide

  • Confirm the actual gold description
  • Ask about alloy and finish
  • Inspect the ring as something you will wear
  • Read the purchase terms before paying

Confirm the actual gold description

Ask whether the ring is karat-gold alloy throughout, whether any part is hollow, and what markings appear inside. The FTC's jewelry guide explains how karat and construction descriptions differ from gold-filled or plated products.

Nominal 14K is 14 parts gold out of 24; 585 is a commonly used fineness mark. The World Gold Council explains that convention. Treat the marking as part of the description to verify, rather than proof that every component matches.

Ask about alloy and finish

A yellow color does not disclose the full alloy composition. If you need to avoid a particular metal, request specific information from the seller. Do not rely on “yellow gold” or “hypoallergenic” without understanding what the seller means for that piece.

Compare polished, brushed and textured finishes in ordinary lighting. Ask how wear and later refinishing may affect the pattern, especially on an engraved or two-tone design.

Inspect the ring as something you will wear

  • Check the thickness and underside of the band.
  • Try the ring with any neighboring rings you intend to wear.
  • Ask whether and how the design can be resized.
  • Review stone descriptions and matching reports, if applicable.
  • Note worn prongs or previous repairs on a pre-owned piece.

A heavier ring is not automatically the better design. It may have a different profile, construction or stone content. Compare like-for-like details instead of using appearance alone.

Read the purchase terms before paying

Ask for the return window, any exclusions, sizing charges and warranty coverage in writing. Customization can have different terms. A future trade-in program, if offered, is separate from an unrestricted cash buyback.

Keep the receipt and description. If you later sell, an offer will concern the actual ring and then-current conditions. Our yellow-gold ring evaluation guide explains condition and resale questions.

In this guide

  • Start with the exact reference
  • Compare the parts that make up the watch
  • Account for condition without assuming repair is better

Start with the exact reference

A model family can include different sizes, movements, dials, bezels and bracelet configurations over time. Write down the reference from reliable records and ask how it matches the watch being examined.

The current Rolex Day-Date collection illustrates why material and configuration need specific descriptions. A current catalog is useful background; it cannot authenticate a watch or establish the originality of an older configuration.

Compare the parts that make up the watch

Use the same checklist for each example: case material, bezel, dial, bracelet or strap, clasp and included links. Separate factory configuration from later manufacturer service replacements and aftermarket changes where the history is known.

A nickname is not a complete reference. Similarly, a familiar bracelet style or gold-colored case does not establish the precise model or metal content.

Account for condition without assuming repair is better

Record visible wear, known damage, operation and service history. Ask whether case refinishing, bracelet work or dial changes can be identified. Describe uncertainty openly instead of presenting an assumed history as fact.

Before cleaning, polishing or servicing for a sale, obtain advice for that watch. Rolex's care and servicing guidance points owners toward appropriate support. Cosmetic improvement and preservation of a particular vintage example are not automatically the same objective.

Distinguish asking prices from actual proposals

An advertised retail watch may include a dealer warranty, service and return terms. A private owner's purchase offer is a different transaction. Compare the exact items, condition and sale terms before deciding two prices are meaningfully comparable.

Gold-market movement does not produce a fixed change in every Rolex offer. The complete watch's configuration and condition still need evaluation. Our gold Rolex buyer guide explains the questions to ask.

Gather the complete package

Bring matching warranty documents, receipts, service records, spare links and the box if you have them. Do not purchase substitute accessories just to make the package appear original. Explain which documents are missing.

For a Day-Date, use the Day-Date evaluation guide to organize its bracelet and configuration details. If you are ready to sell, the Rolex preparation checklist covers the visit.

A yellow-gold ring’s offer depends on what it contains and how the complete piece is assessed. Record its markings, wear, repairs and any stone or maker documents; color alone does not identify purity or establish resale value.

In this guide

  • Make a record of the ring before the visit
  • Look at wear and repairs, not just shine
  • Ask which parts of the ring contribute to the offer
  • Compare the same ring under the same terms

Make a record of the ring before the visit

Note visible markings inside the band and photograph the front, sides and underside. Keep a receipt or repair invoice if available. If the ring was inherited, distinguish documented information from a family recollection.

The FTC explains gold quality marks and plated-product descriptions. A yellow surface alone cannot determine the gold content. Unmarked pieces can be brought for assessment without guessing at a karat.

Look at wear and repairs, not just shine

A freshly polished surface may distract from a thin band or worn setting. Note bent or missing prongs, chipped stones, cracks and uneven sections. Explain any resizing or replacement parts you know about.

Do not polish aggressively or authorize repairs solely to make the ring look newer before selling. Ask whether an evaluation of its current condition is more useful. For a potentially older or signed piece, GIA's estate-jewelry guidance provides relevant background.

Ask which parts of the ring contribute to the offer

A plain band and a gemstone ring require different discussions. Net gold-alloy weight is not necessarily the scale weight of the whole ring. Ask how stones, non-gold components and any maker information were considered.

A complete piece may have a resale opportunity beyond metal content. That does not mean its complete resale estimate should be added to its full metal value. Our gold-valuation guide explains these distinctions.

Compare the same ring under the same terms

Identify the piece and accessories included in each offer. Clarify any conditions and the amount you would actually receive. There is no fixed percentage of retail or melt value that establishes the correct offer for every yellow-gold ring.

Does a scratch make a gold ring worthless?

No. Its gold content remains relevant, while damage can affect its suitability for resale as a complete ring. Point out the scratch and ask how the condition was treated.
