When comparing 10K rings, look at band thickness, construction and how the designs fit together. The 10K label describes nominal gold content, but it does not guarantee that a delicate band or stone setting will resist wear.

In this guide

  • Separate 10K alloy from gold-colored alternatives
  • Check a stack as a group of rings
  • Read the stone description beyond the sparkle
  • Keep expectations realistic when selling

Separate 10K alloy from gold-colored alternatives

10K gold is nominally ten parts gold out of 24, or about 41.67%. The World Gold Council's purity guide explains gold proportions. A 10K alloy ring is a different product from a plated ring over base metal, even if they look similar.

Ask for the complete material description. The FTC's gold-jewelry guidance explains terms such as gold-filled and gold plated. Read the description of the band and any stone separately.

Check a stack as a group of rings

Try the intended rings together. Look for contact between a neighboring band and a raised setting, and ask whether the combination could cause wear. A twisted or textured band may touch another ring differently from a smooth band.

Do not assume that a matching karat makes every combination suitable. Band shape, thickness, finish and setting height all deserve attention. Ask about sizing before buying an entire stack, especially if the combined width changes the fit.

Read the stone description beyond the sparkle

A solitaire and a cluster can have similar total stone weights while containing very different individual stones. Ask whether the stones are natural diamonds, laboratory-grown diamonds, simulants or another gemstone, and which documents support the description.

The 10K marking does not establish stone identity or quality. See our 10K diamond-ring guide for questions about the metal and stone together.

Keep expectations realistic when selling

A ring's original retail price includes more than its gold content. A buyer assesses the actual item, its condition and any stones under the current purchase terms. Keep reports and receipts, and avoid removing stones or cutting apart a stack before an evaluation.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold jewelry and scrap, including single pieces and large collections. Our Downtown LA visit checklist helps you organize what you want to sell. Payment choices are cash, bank wire and business check.

Is a thin 10K band automatically more durable than a thicker 14K band?

No. Karat alone cannot answer that comparison. The complete construction and condition matter, so inspect the actual designs and discuss how you intend to wear them.

Do not assign one gold purity to every Black Hills Gold ring. The band, colored leaves and other components may use different materials. Read the specific maker or product description and have the complete ring evaluated.

In this guide

  • Identify the parts before assigning a karat
  • Read markings with the construction in mind
  • Preserve leaf details and known history
  • Ask whether the offer considers the complete ring

Identify the parts before assigning a karat

Black Hills Gold designs often feature grape leaves, clusters and vines with contrasting gold colors. The name is not a universal metal recipe. For a concrete example, this Zales product description identifies a 10K gold ring with 12K green and rose-gold leaves.

That example explains why the whole ring should not automatically be valued as 18K. Your ring may have a different specification. Keep its maker information, original description and receipt if available, and note which components each description covers.

Read markings with the construction in mind

Photograph clear markings on the inner band and record any maker's symbol. A worn or missing mark leaves a question to investigate; it does not prove a fake. Likewise, a heavy ring does not prove a particular alloy.

The FTC explains gold and silver quality descriptions. Ask an evaluator to distinguish the ring's components rather than assuming a gold-colored ornament establishes the material of the band.

Preserve leaf details and known history

Look for missing leaf tips, flattened engraving, repairs and worn settings. Point out any replaced section. Avoid aggressive polishing or removing decorative parts before an evaluation; the complete design may be relevant to the offer.

If it is inherited, distinguish a documented maker or date from a family description. Our estate-jewelry valuation guide explains how to organize that information.

Ask whether the offer considers the complete ring

A metal estimate must reflect the actual materials and their applicable weights. A complete-jewelry offer may also consider condition, design, stones and maker information. Do not assume a brand adds a premium, or that it must be ignored.

Are all three colors the same karat?

Not necessarily. The specification of the actual piece and its examination matter. Ask how each metal component is being considered in the purchase offer.

18K gold contains 75% gold, commonly expressed by a 750 fineness mark. To estimate its gold content, apply that fraction to the verified net alloy weight; stones, repairs, condition and complete-jewelry resale still need separate consideration.

In this guide

  • Understand the 18K and 750 descriptions
  • Calculate using the weight of the alloy
  • Inspect condition before spending on restoration
  • Discuss stones and maker information

Understand the 18K and 750 descriptions

18 divided by 24 is 0.75, so 18K describes an alloy with 75% gold. Fineness expresses that proportion per thousand as 750. The World Gold Council's purity guide explains both ways of describing gold content.

A visible mark is useful, but the ring still needs examination. A repaired section or different setting component may deserve closer attention. Yellow, white and rose 18K alloys share the nominal gold proportion without necessarily sharing the same other metals or finish.

Calculate using the weight of the alloy

For an example of metal quantity only, 8 grams of verified 18K alloy contains 6 grams of gold: 8 × 0.75. This assumes the eight grams excludes stones and any components that are not that alloy.

A ring weighing eight grams overall may not meet that assumption. Ask how the buyer accounts for stones and other materials. Our gold-valuation guide explains the next step from metal quantity to a dated reference and purchase offer.

Inspect condition before spending on restoration

Record worn prongs, a thinning band, cracks and previous sizing. Keep detached parts and repair records with the ring. Ask whether a complete piece has resale potential before authorizing polishing, stone removal or repairs.

The FTC's jewelry guidance distinguishes material descriptions and advises checking seller terms. Neither karat nor a shiny surface establishes the ring's overall condition or guarantees suitability for every wearer.

Discuss stones and maker information

Bring matching diamond reports, receipts and original packaging if available. A signed ring or an unusual older setting may need a different discussion from a plain band being evaluated for metal. Do not add a complete-ring estimate to its full gold value, which could count the same material twice.

Is an 18K ring always worth more than a 14K ring?

Only the gold proportion is necessarily higher. The total amount of material, stones, maker, condition and purchase terms can make the complete-ring comparison different.

A 14K diamond ring needs two connected assessments: the gold setting and the diamond or diamonds. The karat mark describes the metal, while stone identity, quality and reports inform the diamond assessment. Compare the final offer for the complete ring.

In this guide

  • Identify the setting without counting stone weight as gold
  • Describe each diamond, not just a total weight
  • Match existing reports to the ring
  • Inspect the complete setting and its condition
  • Compare the final purchase amount

Identify the setting without counting stone weight as gold

A 14K alloy contains 14 parts gold out of 24. The FTC explains karat markings and the distinction between gold-alloy and plated products. The ring's total weight includes its stones, so it is not automatically the weight to use in a gold calculation.

Point out repairs, changed prongs or a replaced band. Ask how the metal and non-gold components were assessed. Leave the ring intact until you have discussed whether any additional examination is necessary.

Describe each diamond, not just a total weight

GIA's diamond-quality guide explains carat weight, color, clarity and cut. A single center stone and a group of small accent stones totaling the same carat weight are different comparisons. Shape, dimensions and condition also help describe the stone being evaluated.

Ask whether the stone is natural or laboratory-grown and what supports that identification. Do not assign a quality or origin from the appearance of the gold setting. For more detail, read our 4Cs guide.

Match existing reports to the ring

Bring any laboratory report, receipt and repair record you already have. Clarify which stone the report describes and whether the ring has changed since the document was issued. A document about one diamond does not automatically describe every accent stone.

A grading report and a monetary appraisal serve different purposes. GIA explains that it does not assign monetary values. An insurance replacement figure is also different from a buyer's purchase amount. Ask before paying for a new report solely to prepare a sale.

Inspect the complete setting and its condition

Note loose or missing stones, chipped edges, worn prongs, cracks and previous resizing. A ring's construction and current condition matter alongside the metal's karat. Avoid a blanket assumption that every 14K setting is stronger or more secure than every 18K design.

For a signed or inherited ring, bring maker information and known history. Ask whether the intact jewelry deserves consideration beyond separate material estimates.

Compare the final purchase amount

Ask which stones and accessories are included and whether any conditions remain. Do not add the full estimated value of an intact ring to the full value of its component materials. Compare offers on a consistent basis for the same item.

Yes. Bring the ring and any records you do have. The evaluation can identify what information is available and what, if anything, needs further examination.

Choose a promise ring for its personal meaning and a design that suits the wearer. Confirm whether it is gold alloy, plated or vermeil, read any stone description and check sizing terms. Its meaning and its possible resale amount are separate questions.

In this guide

  • Decide on the design before treating it as an asset
  • Read the complete metal description
  • Keep stone information and receipts together
  • If you later decide to sell

Decide on the design before treating it as an asset

A plain band, an engraved ring and a small stone setting can each serve as a promise ring. The right choice depends on the wearer, the intended meaning and your budget. A higher karat or purchase price does not make the promise more meaningful.

If you are buying a gift, consider fit and whether engraving or a custom design changes the return terms. Ask for the seller's actual policy before paying, instead of assuming a universal return or resizing period.

Read the complete metal description

Karat-gold alloy, gold-filled, gold plated and vermeil are different descriptions. The FTC's jewelry guide explains that vermeil is a gold-plated product with a sterling-silver base. A gold surface is not the same as a ring made from that gold alloy throughout.

Ask about the band construction and actual alloy, along with the finish. The gold color alone does not identify all the metals used. For an alloy ring, our 14K ring design guide gives further comparison questions.

Keep stone information and receipts together

If the ring has a stone, request its exact description. Natural diamond, laboratory-grown diamond, cubic zirconia and colored gemstone describe different materials. Keep any report matched to the stone it covers.

An appraisal, where obtained for a specific purpose, is not a guarantee of resale. GIA's appraisal guidance explains the difference between gem information and monetary valuation. Keep the purchase receipt and important repair records for future reference.

If you later decide to sell

A buyer considers the actual material, weight, condition, stones and possible resale of the complete ring. Neither the original retail cost nor the sentimental meaning determines the amount offered. Market conditions and individual offers can change.

For an unwanted gold ring, contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds to arrange a Downtown Los Angeles evaluation. Bring the complete ring and existing records, and explain any changes or repairs.

Does engraving need to be removed before selling?

Ask about the ring in its current condition before paying to remove an engraving. Its effect on an offer depends on the piece and how the buyer intends to evaluate it.

A 10K ring is nominally 10 parts gold out of 24, approximately 41.67%. Its gold content depends on the net weight of that alloy, while stones, construction, condition and a complete-ring resale opportunity can also affect an offer.

In this guide

  • Read the karat as a proportion
  • Check construction as well as purity
  • Include stones and condition in the conversation
  • Compare a real purchase amount

Read the karat as a proportion

10K does not mean ten grams of gold, and it does not identify every metal in the alloy. The World Gold Council's purity guide lists the approximate proportion and the 417 fineness convention. Have the actual material assessed before treating a visible mark as a verified input.

For an example of quantity only, six grams of verified 10K alloy contains about 2.5 grams of gold: 6 × 10 ÷ 24. That assumes the weight excludes stones or other components. It is not a purchase amount.

Check construction as well as purity

A wide hollow ring and a compact solid band can have quite different weights. The FTC distinguishes solid construction from karat and plated-product descriptions. Ask what the label means for the particular ring.

A karat alone does not guarantee wear resistance or secure prongs. Examine band thickness, worn sections and the actual setting. Read our substantial 10K ring guide for wide bands and signet-style designs.

Include stones and condition in the conversation

Bring matching reports and explain loose stones, repairs or missing parts. A simple gold calculation cannot determine a diamond's quality or the resale potential of a signed ring.

Keep the piece intact until you have discussed the evaluation. For a delicate or stacked design, our 10K bands and settings guide covers how construction and contact affect the inspection.

Compare a real purchase amount

A retail tag includes more than the gold content. A current offer concerns the actual ring, its materials and the purchase terms. There is no universal fraction of the original price that every 10K ring will recover.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold rings and scrap in Downtown Los Angeles. Arrange your evaluation and discuss cash, bank wire or business-check payment. Single pieces and large collections are welcome.

Can an unmarked ring still be gold?

Yes. An absent or worn mark leaves a question for examination rather than proving a particular material. Bring the piece and describe what you know.

To sell gold in Los Angeles, first identify the types of items you have and choose a buyer suited to them. Compare final offers for the same pieces, with tested purity, weight and payment terms explained. Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold, scrap, Cuban chains and gold or silver coins in Downtown LA.

In this guide

  • Start with the items you actually want to sell
  • Choose an evaluation that fits the collection
  • Understand the material calculation
  • Keep complete-jewelry value in the discussion
  • Compare the selling process as well as the price
  • Compare final offer with final offer
  • Prepare the visit and payment arrangements

Start with the items you actually want to sell

A broken chain, diamond bracelet, signed ring and collectible coin should not all be treated as the same material on a scale. Sort what you can identify and leave uncertain pieces for examination. Keep any items you intend to retain separate from those you may sell.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold jewelry, scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins and silver coins at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Single pieces and substantial quantities are welcome. Our gold-buying service explains the main buying categories.

Choose an evaluation that fits the collection

What you haveWhat to discuss
Broken or unwanted goldTested purity, net metal weight and detached parts
Cuban chains or braceletsSolid or hollow construction, clasp components and any diamonds
Gold or silver coinsExact issue, metal content, condition and collectible characteristics
Diamond or designer jewelryStone information, maker documentation and the complete piece
Luxury watchesReference, components, condition and service history

Use our scrap-gold preparation guide, Cuban and 14K chain guide, or coin collection checklist for the relevant items. Gold coins and silver coins should be identified individually or in clearly matched groups; face value is not a purchase valuation.

Understand the material calculation

Karat describes a proportion of gold in an alloy. Nominal 10K is about 41.67% gold, 14K about 58.33%, 18K 75% and 22K about 91.67%. The World Gold Council explains purity and fineness. Higher purity means more gold only when the applicable alloy weights are equal.

A scale reading for a complete piece may also include diamonds, other stones, springs or other materials. Ask which weight and tested fraction are used. A stamp helps identify a question to investigate; it does not establish the composition on its own. The FTC's jewelry guide explains common metal descriptions.

Check the currency, unit and date of a gold-price reference. That market input is not itself a bid for your jewelry. Our valuation checklist helps separate known inputs from assumptions.

Keep complete-jewelry value in the discussion

Damage does not remove the gold already present in a chain. It can, however, change a piece's suitability for resale as jewelry. Ask whether stones, design, condition or maker information deserve consideration before calling everything scrap.

Bring reports for a significant diamond and matching paperwork for a signed piece. Our guides to Cartier jewelry, Tiffany jewelry and inherited collections explain the additional questions. A watch also needs its own evaluation; see the Rolex selling guide.

Consider the complete piece and its components without counting the same value twice. An intact jewelry resale estimate already includes the material in that jewelry; it is not automatically an amount to add to the full metal and stone values.

Compare the selling process as well as the price

A local evaluation allows a direct conversation about the actual items. A mail-in buyer needs to receive them before completing a physical examination, so shipping, insurance, return arrangements and timing matter. Read those terms before sending valuables. Our local versus online buyer guide covers that decision.

Ask whether a proposal is an outright purchase, trade-in, consignment or loan. Those arrangements should not be compared as though they all provide the same unconditional purchase payment. A business category alone does not establish which offer is strongest for your particular collection.

Compare final offer with final offer

Suppose one buyer gives a high estimate from a photograph while another examines the jewelry and gives a purchase amount. Those figures are based on different information. Ask what assumptions the estimate used and what could change after inspection.

  • Which items and accessories are included?
  • What purity, weight and units were used?
  • How were stones and complete-jewelry resale considered?
  • Are any charges, conditions or further checks outstanding?
  • What is the final amount, and how long is it available?
  • What are the payment method and timing?

No single payout percentage applies to every piece. Compare the net amounts offered on a consistent basis and ask for an explanation if the included items or terms change.

Prepare the visit and payment arrangements

Bring the actual items, detached parts and any matching receipts, reports, boxes or repair records. Avoid aggressive cleaning or dismantling. Confirm any requested identification and documents when arranging the visit.

For large quantities of scrap, heavy chains or gold and silver coins, call 310-663-1340 with an approximate description of the collection. Payment is available by cash, bank wire or business check. Discuss your preference and timing before accepting an offer.

Contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds to arrange your visit to 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014.

Can I sell only part of a collection?

Identify the pieces you want to sell and ask for a revised offer for that group. An amount quoted for an entire lot does not automatically apply to a smaller selection.

Do I need the original receipt for ordinary gold jewelry?

Bring it if available, but the material must still be evaluated. Ask what identification or ownership documents are needed for the transaction, and keep useful reports with the matching pieces.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

Gold buying in Downtown Los Angeles · 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

  • FTC: gold-jewelry quality descriptions
  • World Gold Council: gold purity and fineness
  • World Gold Council: dated gold-price reference data

Start with the items you own and the type of transaction you want. Ask prospective buyers whether they evaluate that category, then compare final offers for the same complete pieces, including deductions, conditions and payment terms.

In this guide

  • Match the evaluation to the jewelry
  • Identify the proposed selling arrangement
  • Compare final offers for the same items
  • Verify the business and prepare your records
  • Discuss your items with Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds

Match the evaluation to the jewelry

A broken gold chain, a natural diamond ring and a signed bracelet need different questions. Describe the actual item before choosing a buyer, and ask whether that category is part of the business’s purchasing service.

For a collection, keep potentially significant pieces identifiable. GIA’s estate jewelry guidance emphasizes examination of condition and repairs. A complete piece should be considered before reducing it to a combined weight.

ItemUseful evaluation question
Gold jewelry or scrapWhat purity and relevant metal weight are being used?
Natural diamond jewelryHow are the stone, setting and condition considered?
Large, high-quality gemstone jewelryWhat can be established about the stone and any claimed origin?
Designer or estate jewelryWhat supports the attribution and complete-piece assessment?
Luxury watchesHow are reference, condition, components and records considered?

Identify the proposed selling arrangement

Ask whether a business offers an outright purchase, a trade-in credit, consignment or an auction arrangement. At a pawn business, clarify whether the amount concerns a loan or a purchase. Those figures should not be treated as interchangeable.

For a direct purchase, request the final amount you would receive. For a future-sale arrangement, obtain the agreement and ask about charges, custody, payment timing and unsold items. For a remote buyer, agree on the evaluation and return arrangements before sending jewelry.

Compare final offers for the same items

A photograph or telephone estimate may depend on unverified assumptions. Ask what has been physically examined, whether further testing is required and what could change the proposed amount. Compare final offers after the scope and conditions are clear.

Record included stones, setting and any detached parts. If the offer covers a whole ring, do not add a separate metal estimate to it as though the setting were excluded. Our diamond resale offer guide provides more detail for stone-set jewelry.

Verify the business and prepare your records

Check the exact location and service before visiting. Read relevant feedback, while remembering the FTC’s advice to consider reviews in context. Ask directly about any qualification or service claim that matters to your decision.

Bring existing receipts, reports, maker information and repair history. Certificates are useful records, but their absence does not automatically prevent an evaluation. Keep unfamiliar or damaged pieces intact and ask before commissioning repairs solely to prepare a sale.

Discuss your items with Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds

We buy gold jewelry, scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets, with or without diamonds, plus gold and silver coins in large quantities. Our diamond buying covers natural cut and polished diamonds in any size or shape; we do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds.

Our gemstone buying is limited to large, high-quality stones, including green Colombian emeralds, Burmese rubies and Ceylon blue sapphires. Certificates are welcome but not required. Describe the stone and what you know about its origin when arranging an evaluation.

Visit 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, or contact us at 310-663-1340. Payment options for accepted purchases include cash, bank wire and business check; confirm the amount and timing before completing the sale.

Does every jewelry store buy pre-owned jewelry?

Ask directly. A store may focus on retail, repairs or trade-ins rather than purchasing the kind of item you want to sell.

Is the largest preliminary quote necessarily the best offer?

No. Compare the final amounts for the same inspected items, with all conditions and deductions stated.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling estate jewelry in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

Start with an evaluation of the actual diamond and complete piece, then decide whether the offer meets your needs. Do not reject a natural cut and polished diamond solely because it is small, has visible characteristics or lacks a report.

In this guide

  • Begin with your reason for considering a sale
  • Do not impose an invented minimum size or grade
  • Gather information without guessing the result
  • Compare a real offer with your priorities
  • Arrange an evaluation in downtown Los Angeles

Begin with your reason for considering a sale

You may have jewelry you no longer wear, a loose diamond or several pieces from a collection. Decide which items you are comfortable considering for sale and which you want to keep. Separate that decision from an estimate of what a buyer might offer.

For inherited pieces, make sure any family or ownership questions are settled before committing to a transaction. You can organize records and learn about evaluation without promising to sell the entire collection.

Do not impose an invented minimum size or grade

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural cut and polished diamonds in any size or shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. A small natural stone or a diamond without paperwork can still be discussed with our Los Angeles diamond-buying service.

GIA’s quality factors describe cut, color, clarity and carat weight. These details help an evaluator understand the item; they should not be turned into a generic rule that only a particular clarity or carat range is worth bringing in.

Gather information without guessing the result

Bring existing reports, receipts and previous appraisals. Note the diamond’s setting and any known repairs, chips or replacement stones. If you have several items, keep records matched to the correct piece.

A fluorescence description is also information to assess in context. GIA explains that fluorescence can affect appearance or have little visible effect; it is not by itself a reason to discard a diamond or assume a fixed discount.

What you knowWhat to ask
No report is availableWhat examination is needed before an offer?
The stone is mountedWhich details can be established and which are estimated?
There is damage or a past repairHow does it affect this complete piece?
An old appraisal shows a valueWhat purpose and assumptions did that figure use?

Compare a real offer with your priorities

GIA’s appraisal guidance distinguishes monetary valuation from laboratory grading. An insurance amount or the original purchase price should not be converted into an expected offer using a universal resale percentage.

Ask what the purchase amount includes, whether it is final and what payment terms apply. If comparing buyers, use the diamond offer comparison guide to keep the same item and conditions together. Then consider whether the amount, timing and decision to part with the piece work for you.

Arrange an evaluation in downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items to Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Contact us at 310-663-1340 to describe what you have. Payment options for accepted purchases include cash, bank wire and business check; confirm the method and availability before completing a sale.

Is a diamond too small to ask about?

Our natural cut and polished diamond buying covers any size or shape. Describe the stone or complete jewelry piece and ask what evaluation is needed.

Should I pay for a new report before contacting a buyer?

Bring existing information first and discuss what is missing. A new report is not automatically necessary for every item or every sale.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Selling diamonds in Los Angeles · 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

  • GIA: appraisal purpose

“White diamond” is often informal wording for a diamond in the D-to-Z range. Fancy white describes a different appearance outside that scale. Ask for the actual report terminology rather than assuming that white, clear and colorless mean the same thing.

In this guide

  • Clarify what the seller means by white
  • Read color separately from clarity
  • Check the report type and the physical item
  • Compare appearance and transaction terms
  • Discuss a natural diamond evaluation locally

Clarify what the seller means by white

A description such as “white diamond ring” may be useful for browsing jewelry, but it is not a complete color grade. Ask whether the wording refers informally to a diamond on the D-to-Z scale or to a diamond described as Fancy white.

GIA’s explanation of white diamonds distinguishes those usages. D-to-Z diamonds range from colorless through light tints. Fancy white diamonds have a white appearance associated with light scattering and are not graded as colorless on that same scale.

Read color separately from clarity

The GIA color guide describes controlled comparison against reference stones. D, E and F make up the colorless group. A photograph on a white background cannot establish one of those grades.

Clarity is a different characteristic. Calling a stone “clear” does not supply either its formal clarity grade or its color grade. Likewise, a hazy-looking photograph cannot prove that the diamond is Fancy white; the actual stone and the relevant examination are needed.

WordingUseful follow-up
White diamondIs this informal color wording or a report description?
ColorlessWhat is the actual color grade and laboratory?
Fancy whiteWhat report identifies the stone and its color?
Clear or eye-cleanWhat formal information and viewing conditions support the description?

Check the report type and the physical item

GIA’s colored-diamond guide explains why identification and color-origin information matter for colored diamonds. Keep natural origin, color description and any treatment information as separate questions. A color name alone does not answer all three.

Bring or request the existing report and ask which stone it describes. For earrings, a necklace or a ring with several diamonds, establish whether documentation covers one stone or multiple stones. Our diamond grading chart guide helps you read the fields without turning them into a price schedule.

Compare appearance and transaction terms

When buying, view the actual piece in more than one lighting condition when possible. Ask about its complete description, total price and return terms. Separate personal preference for an appearance from the laboratory information needed to describe it accurately.

When selling, an evaluation should concern your stone, its condition and its setting. Avoid using a generic price for a “one-carat white diamond” as a promise about your ring. The resale offer guide explains how to compare actual amounts and included components.

Discuss a natural diamond evaluation locally

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural cut and polished diamonds in any size or shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. If origin or color terminology is uncertain, explain that when you contact us.

Our address is 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Bring your complete piece and any paperwork so the evaluation starts with the actual item.

Does white mean the diamond is D color?

No. Informal white wording does not specify an exact grade. Read the color description on the matching report.

Is Fancy white the same as a poorly photographed colorless diamond?

No. A photograph cannot establish that distinction. Have the stone examined and read the appropriate report information.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Selling diamonds in Los Angeles · 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

Bring the pieces you may sell, matching documents and detached parts to your first gold evaluation. Ask the buyer to explain the tested material, weight, treatment of stones and final offer. You can then decide which items to sell and discuss the payment arrangements.

In this guide

  • Before you visit: describe the collection
  • Bring each piece as it is
  • Ask what the test and scale readings mean
  • Discuss stones and the complete piece
  • Review the offer before deciding
  • Agree on payment and keep the record

Before you visit: describe the collection

A brief description helps the buyer understand what needs examination. Mention whether you have broken jewelry, heavy Cuban chains, diamond bracelets, gold coins, silver coins or a mixed inherited collection. For a large quantity, give an approximate count or weight if known; a home estimate does not need to be exact.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Call 310-663-1340 to arrange the visit and confirm any requested identification or ownership documents. Our jewelry preparation checklist covers packing and records.

Bring each piece as it is

Keep chains, clasps, broken links and detached components together. Bring any matching grading reports, receipts, designer paperwork or repair history. Separate pieces you intend to keep so they are not included in a group purchase proposal.

Avoid polishing coins, removing stones or taking apart a potentially collectible piece. If something has sentimental importance, mention that before examination. Use the coin collection checklist for boxed coins and grouped bullion.

Ask what the test and scale readings mean

The World Gold Council explains karat as the proportion of gold in an alloy. A 14K mark is a useful starting clue, but the actual material still needs assessment. White, yellow and rose colors do not establish purity.

Ask which weight belongs to the gold alloy and which components are excluded. A complete bracelet's weight may include stones or non-gold parts. For mixed items, ask how different purities are separated. The FTC's metal-label guide helps distinguish gold alloy from plated and filled products.

Discuss stones and the complete piece

For a diamond Cuban chain, signed ring or estate jewel, ask what deserves consideration beyond gold content. Describe any repairs or replaced parts you know about. A laboratory report can help describe a stone, but the buyer still needs to evaluate the actual item.

An estimate for the complete piece already includes its materials. It should not simply be added to a full separate valuation of those same materials. Our gold valuation guide explains the distinction between material estimates and purchase offers.

Review the offer before deciding

  • Which exact items does the amount cover?
  • Is it a final purchase offer or an estimate awaiting further checks?
  • What purity, net weight and price reference were used?
  • Are any charges or conditions outstanding?
  • How would selling only part of the collection change the amount?

Write down the amount and included pieces when comparing buyers. Our Los Angeles selling-options guide explains how to compare different purchase arrangements. A higher preliminary phone quote is not yet a higher final offer.

Agree on payment and keep the record

html:
White gold is a gold alloy made with other metals to produce a pale color. Many pieces also have a rhodium surface finish. The finish and the gold content are different questions: a purchase evaluation considers the actual alloy, net weight, stones and complete piece.

In this guide

  • The white color does not identify the material
  • Karat describes the gold proportion
  • Rhodium wear and damage are different questions
  • Separate gold content from the jewelry offer
  • Bring the stone information and matching documents
  • Arrange a white-gold evaluation

The white color does not identify the material

A pale ring might be white gold, platinum, silver or a plated base metal. Appearance alone cannot reliably distinguish them. Check available marks and paperwork, then have the actual piece examined.

The World Gold Council describes white-gold alloys and rhodium finishes. The added metals vary by alloy. A color or karat description does not disclose every ingredient or establish suitability for someone with a metal sensitivity; ask the maker for the composition.

Karat describes the gold proportion

Nominal 14K is 14 parts gold out of 24, approximately 58.33%; 18K is 75%. The remaining alloy can differ even between two pieces with the same karat. Pure gold is naturally yellow, so a white surface is not evidence of pure 24K gold.

For equal net weights of verified alloy, a higher gold fraction means more gold. It does not mean every light 18K ring contains more gold than every heavy 10K ring. See our 14K per-gram explanation for a worked calculation that separates alloy weight from fine-gold weight.

Rhodium wear and damage are different questions

A bright surface can change as its finish wears. That observation alone cannot tell you whether prongs are sound, a band is thinning or the underlying metal is what a stamp suggests. Have structural concerns examined separately.

Before paying for replating solely to sell a ring, discuss whether it would affect an actual purchase offer. A fresh finish does not increase the amount of gold in the alloy, and its cost may not be recovered. Bring the ring in its existing condition and disclose known repairs.

Separate gold content from the jewelry offer

Two verified alloys with the same net weight and gold fraction contain the same quantity of gold, regardless of white or yellow color. Their complete-jewelry offers may differ because of stones, design, maker, condition or saleability.

A pure-gold market quote multiplied by the whole ring's weight skips both the alloy fraction and any stones or other materials. Read the FTC's jewelry descriptions when distinguishing an alloy from a gold-plated or filled item.

Bring the stone information and matching documents

Keep a report with the diamond it describes, and bring receipts or maker documentation if available. A report describes the stone; it does not turn a metal estimate into a guaranteed purchase amount. Our white-gold diamond ring guide covers the setting and stone together.

For an uncertain white-metal piece, our platinum and white-gold comparison explains the separate material questions. Ask what documentation is needed for a sale even when the original receipt is missing.

Arrange a white-gold evaluation

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold jewelry, broken pieces and substantial collections in Downtown Los Angeles. Arrange an evaluation at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, and discuss payment by cash, bank wire or business check.

A published gold price is a reference for fine gold under specified market terms. To use it for jewelry, check its date, currency and unit, then account for verified alloy purity and net metal weight. The resulting metal estimate is still different from an item-specific purchase offer.

In this guide

  • Start with the source and timestamp
  • Use the same currency and weight unit
  • Apply purity to the right weight
  • Keep other sources of value visible
  • Compare offers with matching assumptions
  • Get an item-specific offer in Downtown LA

Start with the source and timestamp

An article's publication year does not make a quoted price current. Check the observation date and whether a display represents a live quote, a benchmark observation or a historical series. The World Gold Council's gold-price data provides a dated reference with its own methodology and units.

This guide explains how to read those inputs. It does not claim to measure Los Angeles jewelry sales or supply a live buying rate for Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds. A local purchase amount requires examination of your items.

Use the same currency and weight unit

A price per troy ounce cannot be multiplied directly by a jewelry weight measured in grams. Likewise, a dollar quote and a quote in another currency cannot be compared without a matching conversion and timestamp. Record the units next to every number before calculating.

If two buyers describe rates differently, ask them to express the final amount for the same actual collection. A higher number per unit does not establish a higher offer when the unit or included material differs.

Apply purity to the right weight

The World Gold Council's fineness guide explains gold proportions. Nominal 14K is 14/24, about 58.33%, while a 585 mark denotes a fineness convention of 58.5%. Use the verified input appropriate to the piece and explain any approximation.

For a simple quantity example, 20 grams of verified 18K alloy contains 15 grams of gold. The calculation assumes the 20 grams excludes stones and other non-alloy components. Multiplying that fine-gold quantity by a compatible market reference produces a theoretical metal amount, not a buyer's commitment.

Our 14K gold-price guide shows the same distinction for 14K jewelry. Avoid applying the purity factor twice if a rate has already been expressed per gram of that alloy.

Keep other sources of value visible

A signed bracelet, diamond Cuban chain or collectible coin needs questions beyond the bulk gold calculation. Condition and identifying documents can matter to an intact item's resale potential. Coins also require the correct issue and stated metal content.

Ask whether the proposal covers the complete piece, its materials or separate components. Our valuation guide explains how to avoid counting the same material twice, and the coin collection checklist helps keep coin groups identifiable.

Compare offers with matching assumptions

  • Use the same pieces and accessories in each evaluation.
  • Record the tested purity, applicable weight and units.
  • Distinguish an estimate from a final purchase amount.
  • Ask about any charges, remaining checks and offer validity.
  • Confirm payment method and timing.

A market change between two evaluations can explain part of an offer change; altered weight assumptions or item selection can also matter. Ask for the explanation instead of attributing every difference to the gold market.

Get an item-specific offer in Downtown LA

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys scrap, Cuban chains and bracelets, gold jewelry, and gold or silver coins in single pieces or large quantities. Arrange your evaluation at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Payment is available by cash, bank wire or business check; discuss your preferred method before accepting.

Compare the final purchase amounts offered for the same items and under the same conditions. Record the tested purity, applicable weight, treatment of stones, remaining charges and payment terms. A preliminary quote or advertised percentage alone is not enough to rank an offer.

In this guide

  • Make one list of the pieces being compared
  • Record the inputs behind each amount
  • Check a mixed-karat collection without blending assumptions
  • Resolve differences before calling one offer better
  • Keep estimates and purchase offers separate
  • Request an evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Make one list of the pieces being compared

Photograph or describe each ring, chain, bracelet and coin group so you know what a total includes. Separate items you plan to keep. If an offer is for a complete lot, ask for a revised amount before assuming it also applies when you remove a piece.

Keep a diamond bracelet or signed jewel identifiable instead of mixing it into ordinary scrap. Our gold-selling options guide explains the evaluation questions for different collections.

Record the inputs behind each amount

  • Buyer and date of the evaluation.
  • Items, stones and accessories included.
  • Verified purity and net alloy weight, with units.
  • Price reference and whether it is for pure gold or a specific alloy.
  • Final amount after any stated charges.
  • Remaining checks, offer validity and payment arrangements.

The World Gold Council's dated gold-price data is a reference for checking a market input. It is not a substitute for an item-specific offer, and a price from one date should not be presented as another day's rate.

Check a mixed-karat collection without blending assumptions

For an illustrative quantity example, 15 grams of verified 14K alloy contains nominally 8.75 grams of gold; eight grams of verified 18K alloy contains six grams. Together that is 14.75 grams of contained gold, assuming the alloy weights exclude stones and other components.

The World Gold Council explains the purity proportions. Keep each group separate in your notes. Do not apply the highest karat to the whole collection or apply an alloy fraction again to a rate that already accounts for it.

Resolve differences before calling one offer better

If the weights differ, ask whether both buyers included the same pieces and used the same unit. If purity differs, ask about the test and whether a clasp, repair or plated area affected the reading. If one offer includes a diamond and another excludes it, the totals are not directly comparable yet.

A difference does not establish dishonesty by itself. Buyers may have different resale plans, costs or information. The useful next step is an explanation of the included items and final amount. See how testing and weight inform an offer.

Keep estimates and purchase offers separate

A photograph may help describe a piece without confirming its purity, weight or components. Mark a phone or online estimate as preliminary until the buyer explains what remains to be checked. Also distinguish an outright purchase from a loan, trade-in or consignment arrangement.

Before accepting, confirm the payment method, timing and sale terms, and keep the transaction record. No fixed percentage or business category can guarantee the strongest outcome for every item.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold, scrap, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, and gold or silver coins in large quantities. Arrange a visit to 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Cash, bank wire and business-check payment are available.

A gold evaluation combines identification, suitable material tests and weight measurements with an assessment of the complete item. Ask which components were measured or estimated, how purity was established, and what further checks are needed before the purchase offer is final.

In this guide

  • Inspect the piece before choosing a test
  • Understand what the method can show
  • Distinguish the scale reading from net alloy weight
  • Apply purity to the applicable alloy
  • Evaluate what should remain jewelry
  • Bring your questions to the evaluation

Inspect the piece before choosing a test

Marks, joins, repairs, plating and mixed components give the evaluator clues about what needs examination. A bracelet body and clasp may not be identical material. An unmarked piece can still warrant testing, while a visible karat mark is not conclusive proof.

Tell the buyer about replaced parts or previous work and bring matching records. Keep an intact piece together until the proposed examination has been explained.

Understand what the method can show

GIA's comparison of gold-testing methods documents limitations as well as useful applications. The right interpretation depends on the method, sample and item; the name of a machine is not itself a guarantee of an exact result.

Surface composition can also be misleading. In a GIA case study of gold-plated gold, plating complicated XRF readings of the underlying alloy. Ask how mixed materials or surface layers are addressed when they are relevant.

Before a procedure that could mark, scratch or alter jewelry, discuss what is proposed. Do not assume every testing method is non-destructive or that one reading resolves every question.

Distinguish the scale reading from net alloy weight

The whole-item reading can include stones, springs, steel components or other materials. With a mounted stone, its weight may be estimated unless a matching report or direct measurement supplies better information. Ask which quantities were measured and which remain estimates.

Removing stones is not automatically necessary or appropriate for every initial evaluation. Discuss the consequences and any further work before agreeing to dismantling. For a heavy chain or bracelet, our Cuban bracelet guide covers construction and diamond-set pieces.

Apply purity to the applicable alloy

If a ring contains five grams of verified 14K alloy after other components are excluded, nominal contained gold is 5 × 14 ÷ 24, or about 2.92 grams. The World Gold Council explains karat and fineness. A five-gram total ring weight is not automatically five grams of that alloy.

A compatible fine-gold market reference can then inform a material estimate. It does not establish a final jewelry purchase amount. Our valuation guide develops that distinction.

Evaluate what should remain jewelry

Damage does not erase the gold in an item, but condition can affect an intact piece's resale potential. Maker information, diamonds, design and collectible characteristics may deserve separate consideration before everything is treated as scrap.

Ask for an explanation of the complete offer without counting the same material twice. Use our offer-comparison checklist to record the inputs and any outstanding checks.

Bring your questions to the evaluation

An outright sale exchanges ownership of the jewelry for an agreed purchase amount. A pawn loan uses the item as collateral and has repayment and redemption terms. First identify which transaction is offered, then compare the relevant amounts and conditions.

In this guide

  • Start with what you want to happen to the jewelry
  • A loan amount and a sale price answer different questions
  • Compare purchase offers on equal terms
  • Choose expertise relevant to the items
  • Leave room to understand the agreement
  • Request a gold purchase evaluation in Downtown LA

Start with what you want to happen to the jewelry

If you intend to part with an item, ask for an outright purchase offer. If you want to borrow against it and potentially reclaim it, ask about the pawn agreement. A shop may offer both, so its name alone does not identify the transaction.

The CFPB's description of pawn credit distinguishes lending against retained property from an ordinary purchase. Read the actual agreement for the repayment and redemption conditions that apply to the proposed loan.

A loan amount and a sale price answer different questions

The money advanced under a loan is not an unconditional purchase price. To assess a loan, ask for the full cost, due dates, redemption requirements and what happens if you do not repay. Consider whether the arrangement fits your ability and intention to reclaim the piece.

For an outright sale, ask for the final amount, the items included, payment arrangements and any remaining checks. Do not assume you can undo a completed sale; clarify the terms before accepting.

Compare purchase offers on equal terms

When both proposals are outright purchases, use the same pieces and accessories. Ask how purity, applicable weight, stones and complete-jewelry resale were considered. A business category does not establish which buyer will offer more for your collection.

A dated gold-price reference can help explain the metal input. It does not supply a universal percentage that every pawn shop or specialist pays. Our offer worksheet helps record the actual numbers.

Choose expertise relevant to the items

A broken gold chain, diamond bracelet, signed estate jewel and collectible coin need different questions. Ask whether the proposed evaluation covers those characteristics and what documentation would help. Neither a storefront's appearance nor a list of equipment is sufficient evidence of expertise or a good offer.

Keep distinctive pieces intact while discussing the evaluation. For gold mixed with diamonds or other specialty items, use the gold-selling options guide to find the right preparation checklist.

Leave room to understand the agreement

Ask for unclear terms to be explained and keep a copy of the transaction record. If an amount changes, establish whether the included items, verified information or conditions changed. Speed alone cannot tell you whether a proposal suits your needs.

When comparing a mail-in purchase, also review shipping, insurance and return terms. See our local versus online guide for those additional steps.

A useful diamond resale comparison uses final offers for the same physical item, with the same included components and clearly stated conditions. A retail listing, insurance value or online estimate is not a guaranteed amount a buyer will pay.

In this guide

  • Compare the type of price before the amount
  • Identify the exact natural diamond and complete piece
  • Use one comparison sheet for every offer
  • Ask for an explanation when offers differ
  • Request an offer in downtown Los Angeles

Compare the type of price before the amount

An online retail listing is an asking price for a described item. An insurance appraisal may address replacement value. A buyer’s offer is a proposed purchase amount for the item presented, under that buyer’s terms. Comparing these figures without their purpose can create an expectation that the documents do not support.

GIA’s appraisal guidance separates laboratory grading from monetary valuation. A grading report is useful evidence about quality, but it does not contain a resale price or require a buyer to pay an insurance figure. Keep the original paperwork and ask what each number represents.

Identify the exact natural diamond and complete piece

Record the shape, stated carat weight and available report details. GIA identifies cut, color, clarity and carat weight as the four quality factors. One matching characteristic does not make two diamonds equivalent; compare the complete descriptions rather than only the carat number.

For a ring, necklace or earrings, describe the setting and additional stones too. Note condition, repairs and any maker attribution supported by records. If the offer concerns a mounted stone, ask which details were established and which remain estimates. Do not remove a stone yourself to obtain a quote.

Use GIA’s sample reports and our 4 Cs guide to prepare questions about the information you already have. Avoid ordering new paperwork until you have discussed what further information is actually needed.

Use one comparison sheet for every offer

Ask each buyer to describe the item covered and write down the final amount you would receive. Include the date and the period for which the offer is available. If an amount is conditional, record the condition beside it so it cannot be mistaken for a firm offer.

RecordWhy it matters
Exact item and included componentsOne offer may cover a loose stone while another includes the setting
Final amount after stated deductionsThe headline number may not equal the amount received
Further testing or other conditionsA provisional estimate may change after examination
Offer date and expirationAn older amount may no longer be available
Payment method and availabilityDifferent methods may involve different completion steps

Ask for an explanation when offers differ

Start with scope: did both buyers evaluate the same complete piece? Then ask whether they used different assumptions about identity, condition, quality or additional examination. A buyer may offer a combined amount rather than a separate price for every component; clarify how the setting and accent stones were considered.

Do not add a separate metal estimate to an offer that already includes the jewelry. Likewise, a photograph-based estimate should not be treated as equivalent to a final amount after physical inspection. Our diamond buyer checklist gives you questions to use when selecting whom to visit.

Request an offer in downtown Los Angeles

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural cut and polished diamonds in any size or shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. See our diamond-buying service and contact us at 310-663-1340 with a description of your item.

We are at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Payment options for an accepted purchase include cash, bank wire and business check. Discuss the method and expected availability before agreeing to the sale.

Can a one-carat price chart tell me my resale offer?

No. Weight alone leaves out other quality information, condition and the details of the transaction. An offer requires an assessment of the item being sold.

Is the largest quoted number always the best offer?

Check that it covers the same item, includes all deductions and is available on acceptable terms. Compare the final amount and conditions together.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

If you decide to sell fewer pieces, request a new total for that selection. A buyer's offer for a complete lot should not be divided into assumed individual prices without discussion.

Resolve outstanding checks and conditions

Ask whether the amount is final, what further inspection is required, how long the proposal remains available and whether any stated charges affect the amount received. A market-price reference helps explain an input; it does not lock an offer indefinitely.

Keep the agreed items and record together

Before handing over the collection, review the final amount, included items and payment details. Keep the transaction record. If an inherited collection includes pieces with sentimental importance, set those aside in advance rather than deciding while a group sale is being finalized.

html:
10K gold is nominally 10/24 gold, about 41.67%. A fine-gold price per gram multiplied by that fraction gives a theoretical metal reference per gram of 10K alloy. A pawn-shop purchase offer or loan amount is a different figure and has its own terms.

In this guide

  • Convert the price before applying purity
  • Work through a clearly hypothetical example
  • Ask whether the quote already includes the karat adjustment
  • Separate a pawn loan from an outright sale
  • Keep diamonds and intact-jewelry value in view
  • Get your 10K pieces evaluated in Downtown LA

Convert the price before applying purity

Check the currency, date and unit of a gold-price reference. If the quote is per troy ounce, convert to grams before using a jewelry weight in grams. NIST's mass conversions give approximately 31.1035 grams per troy ounce.

For 10K alloy, multiply a fine-gold rate per gram by 10/24. The World Gold Council lists karat and fineness proportions, including the 417 convention associated with 10K. The actual piece still needs material verification.

Work through a clearly hypothetical example

Suppose the net weight is ten grams of verified 10K alloy, with stones and non-alloy components excluded. Nominal contained gold is 10 × 10 ÷ 24, or approximately 4.1667 grams.

If fine gold were hypothetically $100 per gram, that contained gold would have a theoretical reference amount of about $416.67. This is an illustration, not today's price or a purchase offer. A whole-item scale reading that includes other materials would need further adjustment before using this calculation.

Ask whether the quote already includes the karat adjustment

A buyer may express a proposed rate per gram of verified 10K alloy. That is different from a fine-gold market rate. Applying the 10/24 factor again to an already adjusted 10K rate would reduce it twice.

Ask for the final amount for your exact pieces, then record the applicable weight and units. Our offer-comparison worksheet helps keep the assumptions clear.

Separate a pawn loan from an outright sale

A pawn loan uses property as collateral and involves repayment and redemption conditions, as reflected in the CFPB's description of pawn credit. An outright purchase exchanges the item for the agreed sale amount.

Compare purchase offer with purchase offer. For a loan, examine the full cost, due dates and conditions for reclaiming your item. See our sale-versus-loan guide before treating the two amounts as equivalent.

Keep diamonds and intact-jewelry value in view

A 10K ring may include a diamond, while a chain may have a separate pendant or non-gold components. Have those identified instead of assuming the whole weight is 10K or that every stone adds the same amount.

A broken clasp does not erase the gold already in a chain. It can affect suitability for resale as jewelry. The scrap-gold guide explains what to keep together for examination.

Get your 10K pieces evaluated in Downtown LA

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys 10K jewelry and scrap, including heavy chains and large collections. Arrange a visit to 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Discuss cash, bank wire or business-check payment before accepting the offer.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds evaluates Rolex watches for purchase in Downtown Los Angeles. Bring the actual watch and available records, review the proposed amount and confirm payment arrangements before deciding to sell.

In this guide

  • Tell us about the watch before visiting
  • Bring the watch and its available records
  • Ask what the evaluation establishes
  • Review an offer for your actual package
  • Agree on payment and handover
  • Visit the Downtown Los Angeles location

Tell us about the watch before visiting

Share the model or reference if you know it, its general condition and whether you have the box, papers or spare links. If the watch has stopped or been altered, mention that when arranging the visit.

A description or photograph can help start the conversation, but it does not establish a final purchase amount. Inspection of the actual timepiece is necessary to assess details that may be missing from photographs.

Bring the watch and its available records

Keep warranty papers, service invoices, receipts and accessories together. Match them to the watch where possible. You can request an evaluation if papers or the original box are missing.

Avoid polishing, opening or immersing an unfamiliar watch before the visit. For manufacturer information, use Rolex's care and service guidance. Our step-by-step Rolex selling guide provides a preparation checklist.

Ask what the evaluation establishes

Discuss the reference, material, case and bracelet condition, known service work and any aftermarket components. Ask what further inspection may be needed and approve proposed work before it occurs.

Do not confuse a buying evaluation with a separate formal appraisal or a brand-backed guarantee. Rolex Certified Pre-Owned has its own participating Official Retailers and programme requirements. A reference to that programme here does not imply this business is part of it.

Review an offer for your actual package

Confirm which watch, bracelet, links and accessories the offer includes. Ask whether the amount is final or subject to a stated condition and whether any charges apply. Keep the terms in a form you can review.

No universal percentage of the original retail price fits every Rolex. Similar-looking watches can have different references, condition and alterations. Our selling-options guide helps compare the process offered by different buyers.

Agree on payment and handover

Payment for agreed purchases is available by cash, bank wire or business check. Discuss your preference and confirm the amount, timing and handover arrangements before accepting. A general article cannot promise a completion time for every evaluation or payment method.

Keep the transaction record and an item description. You can consider the proposal before deciding; requesting an evaluation is not itself an agreement to sell.

Visit the Downtown Los Angeles location

For an in-person purchase evaluation, contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, or call 310-663-1340. Payment for agreed purchases is available by cash, bank wire or business check; confirm the arrangements before accepting.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling a luxury watch in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Estimate 14K gold content using net alloy weight × 14/24, then multiply by the pure-gold price per gram. The result is a metal-content estimate, not a purchase offer.

In this guide

  • Calculate the gold content before comparing prices
  • Convert a troy-ounce reference into grams
  • Worked example: a 25-gram 14K bracelet
  • Understand the difference between a reference and an offer
  • Compare 14K gold offers on the same basis
  • Arrange a 14K gold evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Calculate the gold content before comparing prices

To estimate the metal value of 14K gold, multiply the pure-gold price per gram by 14 ÷ 24, or approximately 0.5833. Then multiply by the net weight of the 14K alloy. This estimates contained gold value; a purchase offer also depends on the actual item and the buyer's terms.

14K means 14 parts gold in a 24-part alloy. A 585 fineness mark indicates 58.5% gold and is commonly associated with 14K jewelry. The World Gold Council's explanation of karat and fineness describes the small distinction between nominal 14K and 585. Use the purity established during the evaluation when comparing a real offer. Our guide to 14K marks, color and construction explains what these descriptions tell you.

A marking is a starting clue: stamps can wear, repairs can introduce other metals, and separate components may have different purities. Ask how purity will be checked and whether a proposed test could mark the piece. GIA’s 1992 study of gold-testing methods provides historical background on touchstone, electronic and X-ray fluorescence (XRF) testing and their limitations.

Convert a troy-ounce reference into grams

If a gold-price reference is quoted in dollars per troy ounce, first divide it by 31.1034768 to obtain dollars per gram of pure gold. A troy ounce is different from an ordinary household ounce. The NIST mass reference provides the conversion.

Estimated contained gold value = net alloy weight in grams × tested gold fraction × pure-gold price per gram.

The World Gold Council's gold-price data offers market references. Check the currency, unit, date, and whether a displayed value is an average or benchmark. It is not a binding offer for your jewelry, and this article does not display a live buying rate.

Worked example: a 25-gram 14K bracelet

Assume a plain bracelet contains 25 grams of 14K alloy after accounting for any non-gold components. Its estimated pure-gold content is 25 × 14 ÷ 24 = approximately 14.58 grams. Multiply that amount by the current reference price per gram of pure gold to obtain a metal-content estimate.

These are calculated metal quantities, not promised payouts. A bracelet's total weight may also include diamonds, non-gold springs, or other materials. A household scale and a visible stamp can help you prepare questions, but they do not establish a tested net gold weight.

Understand the difference between a reference and an offer

A metal-only purchase offer can reflect testing, processing, refining, resale costs, and the buyer's margin. Jewelry with a desirable maker, significant stones, or collectible features may instead deserve evaluation as a complete piece. Do not add an intact jewelry resale estimate to its full metal value; that could count the same material twice. To distinguish a retail receipt or replacement appraisal from a current offer, read what to expect for gold jewelry.

For heavy Cuban chains and bracelets, ask about construction as well as weight. Hollow links and solid links can look similar while containing different amounts of metal. If diamonds are present, ask how the stones affect both the weight calculation and the offer. See our 14K chain guide for these item-specific checks.

Compare 14K gold offers on the same basis

Keep the same pieces together when requesting comparisons. Ask each buyer to state the tested purity, weight unit, weight used, whether stones are included, any charges, and the final payment. If one quote uses grams and another uses pennyweights, ask for matching units before comparing rates. Use the gold-offer comparison worksheet to record the same details for each buyer.

An estimate given before examination may change if the item differs from the description. Compare final amounts for the actual jewelry, not only an advertised per-gram figure. Our gold-valuation guide covers the broader factors behind an offer.

Arrange a 14K gold evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys 14K jewelry, scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Single pieces, large quantities, and high-value transactions are welcome.

Keep matching pieces and existing reports together. The Downtown LA gold-evaluation checklist covers what to bring. Call 310-663-1340 to discuss a substantial lot and your preferred payment method. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check. Visit our gold-buying page for the full buying scope.

Are equal weights of 14K white, yellow and rose gold worth the same?

At the same tested gold fraction, they contain the same amount of gold. A complete piece's offer may still differ because of its stones, maker, condition, or resale demand. Read more about white gold's alloy and finish.

Should I remove stones before weighing my jewelry?

No. Have the intact jewelry evaluated first and ask how non-gold weight is accounted for. Removing stones can damage the setting and make an evaluation of the complete piece more difficult.

Can this formula tell me the best day to sell?

No. It explains metal content using a stated price reference; it does not predict markets. Decide using an actual offer, the items you own, and your circumstances.

White and yellow gold with the same verified gold fraction and net alloy weight contain the same amount of gold. Their appearance, alloy ingredients and surface finish can differ, while the complete piece may also be valued for stones, maker, design and condition.

In this guide

  • Compare equal quantities of the same purity
  • Look at the finish as well as the underlying alloy
  • Choose appearance by the actual piece
  • Ask about composition and construction
  • Compare complete-jewelry offers separately from gold content
  • Bring either color for a gold evaluation

Compare equal quantities of the same purity

Color does not set the karat. A white 14K ring and a yellow 18K ring have different nominal gold fractions; two verified 14K alloys share the same nominal fraction but may have different weights. Keep both inputs visible before comparing their gold content.

The World Gold Council explains how alloy composition affects color. The other metals vary, so two pieces with the same karat need not have the same complete alloy recipe.

Look at the finish as well as the underlying alloy

Many white-gold pieces have a bright rhodium surface. Wear can change that appearance without changing the stated gold proportion of the underlying alloy. Yellow-gold pieces also need inspection for wear, repairs and structural condition.

There is no universal replating schedule or maintenance cost for every ring. Ask the maker or jeweler about the specific finish and your pattern of wear. Our white-gold guide explains the alloy-versus-surface distinction.

Choose appearance by the actual piece

Compare the jewelry in ordinary lighting and alongside pieces you wear. A bright polished surface, a matte finish and a diamond setting can change the overall appearance as much as the broad color name. Personal preference is more useful than a rule assigning one metal to a particular skin tone.

If you plan to wear rings together, ask about their fit and contact points. Color alone cannot tell you whether adjoining settings will rub or whether prongs are secure.

Ask about composition and construction

Karat does not certify that an alloy is free of a particular metal. If composition matters to you, request information about the actual item instead of assuming that a higher karat or a white or yellow color provides an answer.

Likewise, do not infer sturdiness from color. Band thickness, hollow or solid construction, worn sections and the setting all deserve inspection. The FTC distinguishes construction and metal-quality descriptions.

Compare complete-jewelry offers separately from gold content

A diamond, recognized maker, unusual design or condition difference can affect an intact item's resale potential. There is no fixed color premium that can establish the offer for two different pieces, and retail price differences do not automatically carry over to resale.

For chains, the 14K necklace value guide covers weight and construction. For an offer on a mixed collection, use the buyer-comparison checklist to record the actual items and terms.
