One metric carat is 0.2 grams, or 200 milligrams, and contains 100 points. Carat weight describes mass rather than visible size. Confirm whether a number refers to one stone, all diamonds in the jewelry, or an estimate for a mounted stone.

In this guide

  • Convert carats, points and grams
  • Distinguish the center stone from total carat weight
  • Use millimeter measurements for visible size
  • Ask whether the weight was measured or estimated
  • Keep weight separate from a purchase amount
  • Organize the weights before a Downtown LA visit

Convert carats, points and grams

GIA defines a metric carat as 200 milligrams. One hundred points equal one carat, so a “75-point diamond” weighs 0.75 ct. The following are unit conversions, not price estimates.

CaratsPointsGrams
0.25 ct250.05 g
0.50 ct500.10 g
0.75 ct750.15 g
1.00 ct1000.20 g
2.00 ct2000.40 g
5.00 ct5001.00 g

To convert carats to grams, multiply by 0.2. To convert points to carats, divide by 100. Keep the unit beside the number when comparing documents; “0.75” without a unit is incomplete information.

Distinguish the center stone from total carat weight

GIA explains total carat weight as the combined weight of the diamonds in a piece. A listing for a one-carat-total-weight ring does not necessarily describe a one-carat center diamond.

For example, a ring with a 0.70 ct center diamond and 0.30 ct of smaller diamonds has 1.00 ct total diamond weight. The center remains 0.70 ct. This arithmetic does not make the ring equivalent to a solitaire containing one 1.00 ct diamond.

Ask for the center-stone weight and the combined side-stone weight separately. If the item includes colored gemstones, ask exactly which stones the stated total includes.

Use millimeter measurements for visible size

Weight and face-up dimensions are different measurements. Two stones can weigh the same while having different lengths, widths or depths. Compare the millimeter measurements on their reports rather than relying on a generic carat-to-diameter picture.

A stone’s proportions also matter. Greater depth can add weight without providing the face-up dimensions you expect. View the actual jewelry alongside its measurements; neither the weight nor a zoomed product photograph tells the whole story.

For rounds, the round brilliant comparison guide connects measurements with the other report fields.

Ask whether the weight was measured or estimated

A loose diamond can be weighed independently. A mounted piece presents a different question because the setting and other stones are also present. Ask whether its stated diamond weight comes from an existing report, a prior record or a current estimate.

GIA’s appraisal guidance identifies estimated mounted-stone weight as an example of an assumption that should be disclosed. Record that limitation instead of repeating an estimate as an exact measurement.

Bring the jewelry intact. Before authorizing stone removal, discuss why it is needed, the condition of the setting and who would perform the work. A kitchen scale reading for an entire ring is not the center diamond’s carat weight.

Keep weight separate from a purchase amount

A price per carat is meaningful only alongside the actual stone description and the transaction it refers to. Do not multiply a retail listing for a different stone by your diamond’s weight and treat the result as a purchase offer.

Compare the other diamond quality factors, report information, condition and any jewelry included in the sale. A larger weight does not create a guaranteed price multiple, future appreciation or a deadline to sell.

Organize the weights before a Downtown LA visit

Make a short list of the items and attach copies of the matching documents. Separate a confirmed loose-stone weight from a total-weight description or an estimate. This makes it easier to discuss several rings, loose stones or a larger collection without mixing their records.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural polished diamonds and diamond jewelry at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Any size and shape are welcome; we do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. Contact us with what you have and ask about an evaluation and payment arrangements.

Are carat and karat the same?

No. Carat is a gemstone weight unit. Karat describes the gold proportion of a gold alloy. Keep the stone weight and the metal description separate on your item list.

Can I discuss selling a diamond without its report?

Yes. Describe the item and any missing paperwork when arranging the evaluation. Ask which information can be established from the actual piece and whether additional documentation would be useful before paying for it.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Selling diamonds in Los Angeles · 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

Champagne is a trade description used for brown-toned diamonds, not one exact GIA grade. Read the actual color wording, diamond origin and any treatment information on the relevant report before comparing stones or requesting an offer.

In this guide

  • Translate the color name into report information
  • Separate three questions about origin and color
  • Compare the actual appearance you prefer
  • Ask for an item-specific price or offer
  • Arrange a natural diamond evaluation in Los Angeles

Translate the color name into report information

Champagne, cognac and chocolate are descriptions you may encounter while browsing brown diamonds. GIA’s brown-diamond guide discusses these trade names and the grading context. The word champagne does not specify a single GIA color grade.

Read the actual report instead of assigning every warm brown diamond to K–Z. GIA’s fancy-color guide includes brown among fancy diamond colors. The appropriate description depends on the stone; a marketing name cannot replace that distinction.

Separate three questions about origin and color

Ask whether the stone is a natural diamond, how its color is described and whether the color is natural or treated. These are separate questions. “Natural diamond” by itself does not supply every detail about its color history.

GIA’s colored-diamond buying guide explains the role of identification and color-origin information. Read the scope and comments on the available report. If a seller uses a proprietary color scale, request an explanation and keep it distinct from a laboratory grade.

Description to recordQuestion it answers
Diamond identificationWhat is the stone and what is its origin?
Reported color wordingHow did the laboratory describe its color?
Color-origin or treatment informationWhat is known about the source of that appearance?
Weight and dimensionsHow heavy is the stone and what are its measurements?
Report type and commentsWhat was examined and what information is provided?

Compare the actual appearance you prefer

View the diamond under more than one lighting condition when possible. Look at how the color appears across the face of the stone and in the proposed setting. Compare examples side by side instead of assuming that similarly named diamonds have the same hue or appearance.

A photograph, lighting setup and surrounding metal can affect what you see. Keep your visual preference separate from formal identification and grading. Our white diamond terminology guide offers another example of why an informal color name needs context.

Ask for an item-specific price or offer

A champagne label does not establish a fixed discount from a colorless diamond or a predictable resale percentage. Compare the actual descriptions, condition, included setting and terms. Do not treat a retail asking price as an offer to purchase your jewelry.

If selling, bring existing reports and explain any known alterations or damage. Ask what further examination is needed before paying for new documentation. The diamond resale comparison guide helps you record firm amounts and conditions for the same complete piece.

Arrange a natural diamond evaluation in Los Angeles

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural cut and polished diamonds in any size or shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. Contact us with the item and paperwork you have.

Our address is 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Ask how the final offer accounts for the identified stone and complete jewelry piece.

Does champagne mean K–Z on every report?

No. It is not a single laboratory grade. Read the specific color description and report type for the stone.

Does a natural diamond automatically have untreated color?

No. Diamond origin and color origin are separate information. Ask what the relevant examination and report establish.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Evaluate a women’s gold watch by the exact reference and materials, then check bracelet fit, included links, condition and records. A gold color or familiar brand name alone does not establish gold content or a selling amount.

In this guide

  • Describe the watch without assumptions about size
  • Check case and bracelet materials separately
  • Keep bracelet fit and missing pieces visible
  • Gather service and family records
  • Request evaluation before cosmetic work
  • Discuss an individual selling proposal

Describe the watch without assumptions about size

Begin with the reference and case dimensions in its documentation. Smaller dress watches, larger contemporary models and bracelet watches have different proportions; a gender label is not a specification.

Note whether the watch has its original bracelet, a later replacement or a leather strap. Include the clasp and any detached links when requesting an evaluation.

Check case and bracelet materials separately

A gold-tone finish, gold plating and a gold alloy are different descriptions. The back, bezel and bracelet may also differ from the case. The FTC's guide to precious-metal descriptions helps interpret these terms.

Do not assume an inherited watch is entirely gold because its visible surfaces are yellow. Marks and old receipts can guide an examination, but a buying evaluation still concerns the actual item. Our gold watch materials guide covers the distinctions.

Keep bracelet fit and missing pieces visible

Record whether the bracelet closes securely and whether you have additional links. For a fitted or integrated bracelet, missing components can be particularly relevant to the complete package.

Do not stretch a bracelet, force a clasp or improvise a repair. Keep any detached parts with the watch and explain what happened. A polished appearance should not hide a functional issue.

Gather service and family records

Bring service invoices, purchase documents, warranty papers and the box if available. For an inherited watch, distinguish remembered family history from documented dates or maker information.

A stopped movement needs diagnosis rather than an assumed battery change. Use the manufacturer's support for the specific watch; Rolex's care and service pages are one such source. Avoid water cleaning or opening an unfamiliar older watch.

Request evaluation before cosmetic work

If the purpose is selling, ask about the watch in its current condition before commissioning polishing, stone replacement or refinishing. Those expenses do not guarantee an equivalent increase in a purchase offer.

For a collection, identify which watches and jewelry you want evaluated together and which you plan to keep. The estate-jewelry page provides a way to discuss inherited pieces.

Discuss an individual selling proposal

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds considers luxury watches through its Downtown Los Angeles watch-buying service. An individual evaluation replaces assumptions about brand-wide resale percentages.

Contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, or call 310-663-1340 to arrange an evaluation. Cash, bank wire and business check are available for agreed purchases; confirm the payment arrangements before accepting.

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling a luxury watch in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

First identify the purpose. A grading report describes diamond quality, an appraisal addresses value for a stated use, and a purchase offer states what a buyer will pay. Ask for the service that answers your actual question.

In this guide

  • Define what you need the document to do
  • Understand what a laboratory report contains
  • Ask practical questions before an appraisal appointment
  • Prepare the stone and the records safely
  • Request a purchase evaluation if your purpose is selling

Define what you need the document to do

“Appraise my diamond” can mean several different requests. You might need documentation for insurance, information about an inherited stone or a price for selling it. Explain that purpose before booking an appointment so you do not pay for a document that fails to answer your question.

If an insurer, estate representative or another recipient has requested an appraisal, obtain their requirements first. Ask the prospective appraiser whether the assignment is within their experience and whether the proposed report meets those requirements. Do not assume that a buyer’s offer can stand in for a formal appraisal.

ServiceMain question it answersAsk for
Identification or gradingWhat is the stone, and how is its quality described?The examination scope and resulting report
Purpose-specific appraisalWhat value applies to the stated assignment?The intended use, value basis and report requirements
Purchase evaluationWhat would this buyer pay for this item?A purchase amount and its terms

Understand what a laboratory report contains

GIA’s sample diamond reports illustrate the quality information available for different report services. Read the report type and comments as well as the main grades. For help with the abbreviations, use our diamond grading chart guide.

A report is not a cash offer or an insurance replacement amount. GIA’s appraisal guidance explains that GIA does not assign monetary value and that an appraisal must be understood in the context of its purpose. This distinction matters when someone compares an old insurance figure with a current offer to buy.

Ask practical questions before an appraisal appointment

Request the fee basis, expected schedule and a description of the finished document. Ask about relevant qualifications, how they can be verified and whether any additional laboratory work may be recommended. Agree on any extra work and charges before it begins.

Explain whether the diamond is loose or mounted. Ask how the appraiser will identify the item, record its condition and describe any limits on examination. If you are considering both appraisal and sale, ask about any buying interest or other conflict so the roles are clear.

Prepare the stone and the records safely

Keep loose stones separated in suitable individual containers; do not carry several together loose in a pocket or bag. Bring existing grading reports, receipts, previous appraisals and any documentation of repairs, treatment or recutting. Keep the paperwork associated with the correct stone.

If you have a GIA report number, look up the report record before the appointment. Note any discrepancy for the examiner. A matching database record does not by itself identify the physical stone you are holding. Ask how to prepare a fragile or damaged item before attempting cleaning or removing it from jewelry.

Request a purchase evaluation if your purpose is selling

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural cut and polished diamonds in any size or shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. Our diamond-buying service concerns an offer to purchase; ask separately about any formal appraisal document you require.

Visit us at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, or contact us at 310-663-1340 to describe what you have. Bring existing records and ask what else is needed before purchasing a new report.

Does a loose diamond need a new appraisal every time it is sold?

Establish what the buyer needs to examine and document first. A newly commissioned appraisal is not automatically the right first step for every sale.

Why can an appraisal and a purchase offer differ?

They can answer different questions and use different assumptions. Ask what each amount represents, when it was determined and exactly which item or components it covers.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

html:
The 4 Cs are cut, color, clarity and carat weight. Read them together, then examine the actual diamond and its paperwork. They help describe quality, but they do not by themselves establish appearance, provenance or a resale offer.

In this guide

  • Start with four different questions
  • Look at cut through the actual diamond
  • Use the color grade without making assumptions about visibility
  • Ask what the clarity grade means for this stone
  • Separate carat weight from the size you see
  • Compare the paperwork and the transaction
  • Prepare a diamond evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Start with four different questions

Use GIA’s four quality factors to organize the discussion: how the diamond was cut, its color description, its clarity characteristics and how much it weighs. There is no single combined 4Cs score that gives every diamond a fixed price.

  • Cut: how the cutting and proportions contribute to appearance.
  • Color: the reported color grade or description.
  • Clarity: the internal and surface characteristics considered in grading.
  • Carat: the weight of the diamond.

Write down these fields for each stone you are considering. Leave unknown information marked as unknown instead of filling the gap with a sales phrase such as “premium quality.”

Look at cut through the actual diamond

Shape and cutting style describe what kind of stone you are viewing. Cut quality concerns how it is fashioned. Two round diamonds with similar weights may still show different patterns of brightness and contrast.

Compare stones in the same lighting and viewing position, then ask to see them under another ordinary lighting condition. Record what you prefer rather than assuming that one sales label guarantees the appearance you want. For a round brilliant, our cut-comparison guide explains which report fields to compare.

Use the color grade without making assumptions about visibility

GIA describes color grading under controlled lighting. Your impression when viewing a mounted ring is a separate observation. Ask to compare the actual items instead of accepting a promise that a particular range of grades always looks identical.

If a warmer appearance appeals to you, say so. If you want a less visible tint, compare that preference against the complete piece and its price. A universal recommendation to buy one color grade cannot account for every person, stone or setting.

Ask what the clarity grade means for this stone

Clarity is more than the number of visible dots on a diagram. GIA considers several characteristics under magnification. Ask which features are present in the diamond you are viewing and whether any deserve closer attention.

Do not treat “eye-clean” as a laboratory grade or assume that every SI1 or VS2 diamond will look the same to you. View the actual stone and ask the seller to point out the feature being discussed. Keep appearance, the written grade and any condition concern as separate notes.

Separate carat weight from the size you see

Carat measures weight. For visible size, compare the reported millimeter dimensions as well. A ring’s total diamond weight is also different from the weight of its center stone. The carat-weight guide includes examples of both terms.

When comparing two rings, ask for the center-stone weight, the side-stone total and the metal description separately. This avoids comparing a multi-stone total with a single-stone listing.

Compare the paperwork and the transaction

A sample GIA natural-diamond report shows the information to look for. Check the report type, identification and measurements; ask how the document is matched to the item. The report’s scope matters, and a general grading report does not answer every sourcing or ownership question.

For a purchase, also read the return conditions and complete item description. For a sale, ask for an offer for the exact item being presented, including its setting and any accent stones. A retail asking price or earlier insurance value is not the same as an offer to buy it today.

Bring your item intact, with existing reports, receipts and repair records. You do not need to assign grades yourself before contacting Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds. Explain any missing paperwork and ask what the evaluation can establish.

We buy natural polished diamonds of any size and shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. Visit 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Arrange the visit and discuss payment by cash, bank wire or business check before accepting a purchase offer.

Which C should I prioritize?

Start with your purpose and what you observe in the actual item. For buying, compare your preferences against complete descriptions and prices. For selling, ask the buyer to explain the factors affecting the offer rather than choosing one grade in isolation.

Do excellent grades guarantee a profitable resale?

No. Quality descriptions do not establish a future buyer, price or return. Keep the report information separate from the terms of any actual transaction.

When selling gold and diamonds together, ask whether the offer covers the complete jewelry, its metal and stones, or selected items only. Keep the pieces intact and compare final amounts for the same collection to avoid omitting or double counting components.

In this guide

  • Start with the complete piece
  • Ask how metal and diamonds were considered
  • Keep a clear record for a larger collection
  • Know our diamond and gemstone buying policies
  • Discuss the purchase and payment

Start with the complete piece

A diamond-set Cuban chain contains more information than its total weight. Its gold alloy, construction, clasp, condition and diamonds all need consideration. The same applies to rings, bracelets, earrings and mixed collections containing both intact and broken jewelry.

Bring the pieces together with a simple list. Identify the items you want to sell and anything you want to retain. Keep paired earrings, matching components and any maker records together. Do not remove stones or cut apart chains in preparation for an offer.

Ask how metal and diamonds were considered

The FTC’s precious-metal jewelry guide explains gold content and coating descriptions. Ask which materials were identified and what weight was used for the gold estimate. A scale reading for an entire diamond bracelet is not automatically its net gold weight.

GIA’s diamond quality factors explain why carat weight is only one part of evaluating a diamond. Ask what is known about the stones, which details remain estimates while mounted and how their condition affects the assessment.

A buyer may present one amount for the complete piece. Clarify that the diamonds are included before comparing it with another offer split into metal and stone components. Adding a separate diamond estimate to an already complete offer would count them twice.

Keep a clear record for a larger collection

GroupDetails to record
Cuban chains and braceletsIntact or broken, stone-set or plain, known markings
Rings and other jewelryMetal, maker information, complete pairs and missing parts
Loose natural diamondsIndividual stones and matching reports, if available
Gold and silver coinsSeparate inventory, holders and identifying records

Request the final amount for the same listed items from each buyer. If one offer excludes a ring or returns some stones, make that difference visible in your notes. Our gold bracelet and Cuban-link guide helps prepare heavier jewelry.

Know our diamond and gemstone buying policies

Our diamond-buying service buys natural cut and polished diamonds in any size or shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. Bring existing reports if you have them; describe anything you do not know.

Other gemstone buying is limited to large, high-quality stones, including green Colombian emeralds, Burmese rubies and Ceylon blue sapphires. Certificates are welcome but not required. Mention those stones separately when arranging an evaluation.

Discuss the purchase and payment

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold jewelry, scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, plus gold and silver coins in large quantities. Visit 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Contact us at 310-663-1340 to arrange your evaluation.

Payment options include cash, bank wire and business check. Confirm the agreed items, final amount and payment timing before completing the sale. Keep a copy of the transaction record.

Does broken jewelry need to be repaired before an evaluation?

No. Bring it as it is and discuss the existing condition before spending money on repairs.

Should every small diamond have its own report?

Do not order reports simply to begin an inquiry. Bring existing documents and ask what examination is appropriate for the actual jewelry.

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Confirm whether one carat describes a single diamond or the combined diamonds in a piece. Bring the existing report and complete jewelry, then request a purchase offer that identifies exactly what is included.

In this guide

  • Confirm what the one-carat description covers
  • Bring the full report information
  • Request an offer for the actual item
  • Clarify missing information before commissioning work
  • Sell natural diamonds in downtown Los Angeles

Confirm what the one-carat description covers

GIA defines one metric carat as 200 milligrams. A one-carat center diamond and jewelry containing several diamonds totaling one carat are different descriptions. Establish which you have before using a price comparison.

GIA’s carat-weight report guide explains the distinction between individual and combined weights. For example, a pair of earrings described as one carat total does not state that each earring contains a one-carat diamond. Read the original wording and ask for clarification where needed.

Bring the full report information

Record the laboratory and report number, stated weight, measurements, shape, color, clarity and any comments. GIA’s sample reports show how fields differ by report service. Match the documentation to the stone being presented rather than relying on a report found with other jewelry.

Two diamonds with the same weight may have different dimensions, appearance and quality descriptions. Use our carat-weight guide to separate measurements from weight. If the stone remains mounted, ask what the evaluator can establish and what must be estimated.

Bring or recordWhat it clarifies
The complete pieceWhether the setting and additional stones are part of the sale
Existing laboratory reportThe recorded information for the examined diamond
Purchase and repair recordsKnown descriptions, replacements or alterations
Current condition notesChips, missing parts or other concerns to examine

Request an offer for the actual item

Ask the buyer to state what the amount covers. If the offer includes a ring setting, do not add a second metal estimate as though the setting were excluded. If there are accent stones, establish whether they are included too.

A retail listing for another one-carat diamond does not determine the purchase amount for yours. There is no single resale price attached to the weight. Compare firm offers under the same conditions using our diamond resale offer guide.

Clarify missing information before commissioning work

If you have no report, explain what you know about the stone and ask what examination is needed. A new report, repair or removal from a setting may involve time and cost. Discuss the reason for any proposed work and agree on the scope before it begins.

Use the diamond buyer checklist to ask about handling, final amount and payment availability. Keep a written record of the offer so you can consider it without relying on memory.

Sell natural diamonds in downtown Los Angeles

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural cut and polished diamonds in any size or shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. Visit 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, or contact us at 310-663-1340 with your item’s details.

Must a diamond weigh at least one carat to be evaluated?

No. Our natural cut and polished diamond buying covers any size or shape. This guide addresses the specific questions raised by one-carat descriptions.

Does one carat total mean a one-carat center diamond?

No. Total weight combines the diamonds described. Ask for the center diamond’s individual weight when that is the information you need.

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

html:
Gold valuation starts with tested purity, net metal weight, and a dated price reference. Stones, condition, and resale potential can also affect an offer.

In this guide

  • What Determines the Value of Gold?
  • What Does Gold Karat Mean?
  • How Do You Identify the Karat of Gold Jewelry?
  • Why Does Gold Weight Matter?
  • What Is a Troy Ounce?
  • What Is the Gold Spot Price?
  • Why Isn’t My 14K Jewelry Worth the Full Gold Spot Price?
  • How Is the Gold Content of Jewelry Estimated?
  • How Do Gold Buyers Test Gold?
  • Does the Condition of Gold Jewelry Affect Its Value?
  • Can Broken Gold Still Be Valuable?
  • Are Diamonds and Gemstones Included in Gold Value?
  • Can Designer Jewelry Be Worth More Than Its Gold Content?
  • How Much Is My Gold Worth Today?
  • How Can I Estimate My Gold’s Value Before Selling?
  • How Can I Get a Better Offer for My Gold?
  • Do Pawn Shops Value Gold Differently?
  • Frequently Asked Questions About Gold Value
  • Get Your Gold Evaluated in Los Angeles

If you’re thinking about selling gold in Los Angeles, one of the first questions you may have is: How is gold valued?

The value of gold jewelry is generally influenced by several factors, including its gold purity, weight, current gold market price, and the type of item being evaluated. Some jewelry may also have additional value because of its brand, craftsmanship, gemstones, condition, or collectibility.

Understanding these factors before you sell can make it easier to evaluate an offer and ask the right questions.

At Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds, we believe sellers should understand how their valuables are evaluated before deciding whether to sell.

What Determines the Value of Gold?

When evaluating gold, buyers typically consider several important factors.

These include:

  • Gold purity or karat
  • Weight
  • Current gold market price
  • Whether the item is solid gold, plated, or another type of material
  • Refining or resale considerations
  • Condition and design
  • Brand or collectible value
  • Diamonds or other gemstones

For ordinary gold jewelry being purchased primarily for its precious metal content, purity, weight, and the prevailing gold price are especially important.

What Does Gold Karat Mean?

Gold karat describes how much pure gold is contained in an alloy.

Pure gold is 24 karat. Jewelry is often made by combining gold with other metals to improve durability or achieve different colors and characteristics.

The FTC explains that an 18K item consists of 18 parts gold and six parts other metal, while a 14K item consists of 14 parts gold and ten parts other metal.

How Pure Is 24K Gold?

24K represents essentially pure gold.

Because pure gold is relatively soft, jewelry is frequently made using lower

karat alloys rather than 24K gold.

How Pure Is 22K Gold?

22K gold contains approximately 91.7% gold.

It is commonly seen in certain types of jewelry and gold coins.

How Pure Is 18K Gold?

18K gold contains 75% gold.

The remaining 25% consists of other metals used in the alloy.

How Pure Is 14K Gold?

14K gold contains approximately 58.3% gold.

It is one of the commonly encountered gold purities in jewelry.

How Pure Is 10K Gold?

10K gold contains approximately 41.7% gold.

Because the gold percentage is lower than in 14K or 18K jewelry, two items of identical weight can have substantially different gold content.

How Do You Identify the Karat of Gold Jewelry?

Many pieces of jewelry contain a quality mark indicating their gold content.

You may see markings such as:

  • 10K
  • 14K
  • 18K
  • 22K
  • 24K
  • 417
  • 585
  • 750
  • 916

For example, 585 generally corresponds to approximately 58.5% gold, while 750 corresponds to 75% gold.

However, a stamp alone should not always be treated as conclusive proof of an item’s composition.

A professional evaluation may include testing to confirm the actual precious metal content.

The FTC provides consumer guidance about gold quality marks and how they communicate the amount of gold in jewelry.

Why Does Gold Weight Matter?

Once the purity of an item is established, its weight becomes another major part of determining its underlying gold content.

In simple terms, an item containing more actual gold generally has a higher underlying metal value than an otherwise comparable item containing less gold.

However, sellers should understand what exactly is being weighed.

A piece of jewelry may contain:

  • Gold
  • Diamonds
  • Gemstones
  • Clasps
  • Springs
  • Other metals
  • Non metal components

These components can affect how the total weight relates to the actual amount of gold.

What Is a Troy Ounce?

Gold markets commonly quote precious metals using troy ounces, rather than the ordinary avoirdupois ounces Americans commonly use for everyday goods.

One troy ounce is approximately 31.103 grams, according to NIST.

This distinction is important because a standard ounce and a troy ounce are not the same measurement.

You may also encounter gold buyers using grams or pennyweights.

When receiving an evaluation, ask which unit of measurement is being used.

What Is the Gold Spot Price?

The spot price of gold is a market reference for gold.

Gold prices fluctuate as markets change, so the price you see today may differ from the price on another day.

The World Gold Council provides gold spot price information and notes that the gold market also uses benchmarks such as the LBMA Gold Price.

This market price is an important starting point for understanding gold value—but it does not automatically equal the amount a buyer will pay for your jewelry.

Why Isn’t My 14K Jewelry Worth the Full Gold Spot Price?

This is one of the most important concepts for gold sellers to understand.

The quoted gold price generally refers to gold at a specified market standard. Your jewelry may contain considerably less than 100% gold.

For example, 14K jewelry contains roughly 14 parts gold out of 24.

So if you have a 14K bracelet weighing 20 grams, you should not simply multiply all 20 grams by the market price of pure gold per gram and assume that is what a buyer should pay.

The actual gold content first needs to be considered.

The buyer may then account for additional factors involved in purchasing, processing, refining, or reselling the item.

How Is the Gold Content of Jewelry Estimated?

A simplified way of understanding the underlying gold content is:

Net alloy weight × gold purity = approximate pure-gold weight

For example, imagine the gold alloy in a piece weighs 20 grams after accounting for stones and non-gold components, and tests as 18K.

18K gold is 75% gold.

A simplified calculation would therefore be:

20 grams × 75% = approximately 15 grams of gold content

That does not mean the item’s purchase offer will equal the market value of exactly 15 grams of pure gold.

Instead, it helps explain the relationship between the item’s total weight, purity, and underlying precious-metal content.

How Do Gold Buyers Test Gold?

Gold buyers may use different methods depending on the item being evaluated.

Visual Inspection and Hallmarks

An evaluator may first inspect the item for markings indicating karat or fineness.

These markings provide useful information but may still need verification.

Electronic or X-Ray Testing

Some professional buyers use electronic equipment or X-ray fluorescence technology to help analyze metal composition.

GIA research compares gold-testing methods and their limitations. Different methods have different applications and limitations, which is why an experienced evaluator may use more than one piece of information when determining an item’s composition.

Acid Testing

Acid testing is another traditional method used to help assess gold purity.

The appropriate testing method depends on the type and condition of the item.

If you’re selling gold, you can ask the buyer how your gold was tested and how the purity was determined.

Does the Condition of Gold Jewelry Affect Its Value?

It depends on how the item is being valued.

If a broken chain is being purchased primarily for its precious-metal content, the fact that the chain is broken may matter less than its purity and gold weight.

But some jewelry may have additional resale value when it is:

  • Made by a desirable designer
  • Antique or vintage
  • In excellent condition
  • Rare
  • Collectible
  • Set with valuable gemstones

That is why potentially important jewelry shouldn’t automatically be treated as scrap.

Can Broken Gold Still Be Valuable?

Yes.

A broken gold necklace, damaged bracelet, bent ring, single earring, or other unwanted piece can still contain valuable gold.

Its precious-metal content does not disappear simply because the jewelry can no longer be worn.

If you have broken or unwanted jewelry, having it evaluated can help you understand whether it has precious-metal or additional resale value.

Are Diamonds and Gemstones Included in Gold Value?

Diamonds and gemstones should be considered separately from the gold content when they may have meaningful value.

A piece of jewelry might therefore have several potential components of value:

Consider metal content, stones, and the resale value of the complete piece without counting the same value twice.

Not every stone necessarily has significant secondary-market value, but valuable diamonds or gemstones should not automatically be ignored.

If your jewelry contains diamonds or significant gemstones, ask whether they are being evaluated separately from the gold.

Can Designer Jewelry Be Worth More Than Its Gold Content?

Yes.

Some designer, vintage, antique, collectible, or luxury jewelry can potentially be worth more as a complete piece than simply as precious metal.

Before selling potentially valuable branded jewelry, consider whether the piece has characteristics such as:

  • Recognizable designer markings
  • Original documentation
  • Serial numbers
  • Original boxes
  • Certificates
  • Historical or collectible significance

A knowledgeable evaluator should consider whether an item deserves evaluation beyond its melt or precious-metal value.

How Much Is My Gold Worth Today?

There is no single accurate answer without knowing what you have.

Determining your gold’s potential value requires information such as:

  • Weight
  • Karat or purity
  • Current gold market price
  • Whether the item contains gemstones
  • Brand or maker
  • Condition
  • Potential resale or collectible value

Because the gold market changes, avoid relying on an old article containing a fixed dollar amount for what gold is supposedly “worth today.”

For current market information, the World Gold Council gold-price data provides a useful reference.

How Can I Estimate My Gold’s Value Before Selling?

You can start by looking for the karat mark on your jewelry and getting an approximate weight.

Then check a reputable source for the current gold market price.

However, treat any home calculation as an estimate, not a guaranteed purchase offer.

Professional testing may determine that the item’s actual composition or weight differs from what you expected.

Additionally, jewelry with diamonds, gemstones, designer provenance, or collectible value may require a different type of evaluation.

How Can I Get a Better Offer for My Gold?

The goal shouldn’t simply be finding the buyer making the biggest advertising claim.

Instead, look for a buyer who provides a transparent evaluation.

Before selling:

  • Know what type of gold you have
  • Ask how purity was determined
  • Ask to understand the weight
  • Check the current gold market
  • Ask whether gemstones have separate value
  • Ask whether designer or collectible value was considered
  • Understand the offer before accepting it

If you’re comparing different ways to sell, read our guide Where to Sell Gold in Los Angeles: How to Get the Best Price for Your Gold.

Do Pawn Shops Value Gold Differently?

Different buyers can have different business models, operating costs, resale opportunities, and purchasing criteria.

That means offers for the same item may vary.

If you’re considering a pawn shop, see our guide How Much Do Pawn Shops Pay for Gold? What Los Angeles Sellers Should Know for a more detailed explanation.

Frequently Asked Questions About Gold Value

Is 18K gold worth more than 14K gold?

Per equal unit of weight, 18K gold contains more pure gold than 14K gold. However, the total value of a specific piece also depends on its weight and potentially its design, gemstones, brand, condition, and resale value.

Is 14K gold real gold?

Yes. 14K gold is a gold alloy containing 14 parts gold out of 24 total parts. The FTC’s consumer guidance explains how karat markings indicate the proportion of gold in jewelry.

Is broken gold worth less?

If an item is being valued primarily for its precious-metal content, being broken does not eliminate the value of the gold it contains. A wearable or collectible piece, however, may have additional value based on condition.

Do gold prices change every day?

Gold prices fluctuate with market activity. For that reason, the reference price used when evaluating gold can change over time. The World Gold Council maintains gold spot-price data and related market information.

Should I sell gold based only on its weight?

No. Weight is only one part of the evaluation. Purity is crucial, and some jewelry can also have value from diamonds, gemstones, brand, craftsmanship, rarity, or collectibility.

How do I know whether a gold offer is fair?

Ask the buyer to explain the item’s tested purity, weight, market-price reference, and any other factors used in calculating the offer. Understanding those components makes comparing evaluations easier.

Get Your Gold Evaluated in Los Angeles

Understanding how gold is valued can help you make a more informed decision before selling.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds evaluates gold jewelry and other valuables for customers in Los Angeles.

If you have gold jewelry, broken gold, coins, bullion, estate jewelry, diamonds, or other valuables, bring the items in for an evaluation and ask questions about how their value is determined.

There should be no mystery about the basic factors affecting your gold’s value.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

Sources and further reading

  • FTC: gold-jewelry quality marks
  • World Gold Council: gold purity, karat and fineness
  • World Gold Council: gold-price data
  • NIST: mass units
  • GIA: methods for determining gold content

Per equal unit of weight, 18K gold contains more pure gold than 14K gold. However, the total value of a specific piece also depends on its weight and potentially its design, gemstones, brand, condition, and resale value. Is 14K gold real gold? Yes. 14K gold is a gold alloy containing 14 parts gold out of 24 total parts. The FTC’s consumer guidance explains how karat markings indicate the proportion of gold in jewelry. Before buying a 14K yellow gold ring, confirm the material description, inspect its construction and fit, and read the seller’s terms. The gold color and karat label do not establish the exact alloy, stone quality or future resale price.

In this guide

  • Confirm the actual gold description
  • Ask about alloy and finish
  • Inspect the ring as something you will wear
  • Read the purchase terms before paying

Confirm the actual gold description

Ask whether the ring is karat-gold alloy throughout, whether any part is hollow, and what markings appear inside. The FTC's jewelry guide explains how karat and construction descriptions differ from gold-filled or plated products.

Nominal 14K is 14 parts gold out of 24; 585 is a commonly used fineness mark. The World Gold Council explains that convention. Treat the marking as part of the description to verify, rather than proof that every component matches.

Ask about alloy and finish

A yellow color does not disclose the full alloy composition. If you need to avoid a particular metal, request specific information from the seller. Do not rely on “yellow gold” or “hypoallergenic” without understanding what the seller means for that piece.

Compare polished, brushed and textured finishes in ordinary lighting. Ask how wear and later refinishing may affect the pattern, especially on an engraved or two-tone design.

Inspect the ring as something you will wear

  • Check the thickness and underside of the band.
  • Try the ring with any neighboring rings you intend to wear.
  • Ask whether and how the design can be resized.
  • Review stone descriptions and matching reports, if applicable.
  • Note worn prongs or previous repairs on a pre-owned piece.

A heavier ring is not automatically the better design. It may have a different profile, construction or stone content. Compare like-for-like details instead of using appearance alone.

Read the purchase terms before paying

Ask for the return window, any exclusions, sizing charges and warranty coverage in writing. Customization can have different terms. A future trade-in program, if offered, is separate from an unrestricted cash buyback.

Keep the receipt and description. If you later sell, an offer will concern the actual ring and then-current conditions. Our yellow-gold ring evaluation guide explains condition and resale questions.

There is no fixed percentage that all pawn shops pay for gold. A meaningful comparison starts with tested purity, net metal weight, the dated price reference and the final purchase amount, including any separately considered jewelry or diamond value.

In this guide

  • Identify the kind of number you received
  • Understand weight, purity and price units
  • Ask what was measured and what was estimated
  • Consider more than the gold calculation
  • Request an evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Identify the kind of number you received

A gold purchase offer is the amount a buyer proposes to pay for your items. A metal-content estimate describes a quantity of gold using a chosen reference price. A retail price describes a different transaction again. None of these figures should be silently substituted for another.

Also separate selling from borrowing. The CFPB describes pawn loans as borrowing against an item held as collateral. If you want an outright sale, ask the shop for that offer specifically.

Understand weight, purity and price units

The World Gold Council’s jewelry guide explains that 18K gold contains 75% gold, while 14K is approximately 58.3%. The relevant calculation uses the weight of the gold alloy being assessed, excluding stones and other non-gold parts.

For a hypothetical example, 12 grams of verified 18K gold alloy contains 9 grams of pure gold: 12 × 0.75 = 9. Multiplying those 9 grams by a dated pure-gold reference per gram produces a reference metal-content value. It does not produce a promised purchase offer.

If the reference is quoted per troy ounce, convert it to the same weight unit before multiplying. Do not mix a pure-gold price with a price already adjusted for 18K purity, or apply the purity reduction twice.

Ask what was measured and what was estimated

DetailWhy it matters
Gross item weightMay include stones or non-gold components
Net metal weightThe weight actually used for the alloy calculation
Tested purityMixed-karat pieces need separate treatment
Price reference and dateShows the basis of the estimate
Final purchase amountStates what you receive for the agreed items

A claim such as “we pay a high percentage” is incomplete unless you know the reference amount, items included and deductions. Ask for an explanation in plain language. Our gold-testing and valuation guide covers the examination behind those numbers.

Consider more than the gold calculation

A diamond-set bracelet, signed necklace or collectible coin should not automatically be treated as an anonymous lump of alloy. Ask whether the buyer evaluated the complete item and how that affected the offer. Do not add a separate stone estimate to a whole-piece offer if that offer already includes the stones.

For a local comparison, use the Los Angeles gold-offer checklist. Compare the same collection and request clear payment terms.

Request an evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys scrap gold, gold jewelry, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins and silver coins, including large quantities. Our address is 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Call 310-663-1340 to discuss your items. Payment is available by cash, bank wire or business check, with the amount and timing agreed for the purchase.

Can I get an accurate offer from weight alone?

No. Purity, non-gold components, the actual items and the buyer’s purchase terms also matter.

Is there a standard pawn-shop payout percentage?

No single percentage applies to every shop or item. Request a final purchase offer and its basis.

Compare round brilliant diamonds using the complete reports and the actual stones. Read the cut grade together with measurements, polish, symmetry, color and clarity, then ask about condition and the terms of any purchase offer.

In this guide

  • Confirm shape, cutting style and report scope
  • Understand what the cut grade considers
  • Compare the same fields on both reports
  • View the diamonds under comparable conditions
  • Evaluate a sale without assuming a shape premium
  • Arrange a round-diamond evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Confirm shape, cutting style and report scope

Read the report’s shape and cutting-style description before comparing grades. “Round” describes an outline; an older round stone may use a different cutting arrangement from a modern round brilliant. Do not assign a grade from the name alone.

GIA’s cut-grade guide explains the system for standard round brilliant diamonds in the D-to-Z color range. Its grades run from Excellent through Very Good, Good and Fair to Poor. That scope should not be applied automatically to every diamond shape or report type.

For another shape, ask which quality information the report does supply rather than treating the absence of the same overall cut grade as a defect.

Understand what the cut grade considers

GIA’s system considers brightness, fire, scintillation, weight ratio, durability, polish and symmetry. Its published cut-grading research explains why appearance, design and craftsmanship belong in the assessment.

Brightness refers to white-light return; fire describes colored flashes; scintillation concerns sparkle and the pattern of light and dark areas. Treat these as aspects to observe together rather than expecting one photograph to show all of them.

Polish and symmetry are also reported separately. As GIA explains, a diamond can have an Excellent overall cut grade with Very Good polish or symmetry. Read each field instead of assuming that one grade makes all of the others identical.

Compare the same fields on both reports

Set the reports beside each other and record the following details. GIA’s sample natural-diamond reports provide a useful reference for the layout and terminology.

FieldComparison question
Report and itemDo the report number, description and presented stone match?
Carat and measurementsHow do weight, diameter measurements and depth differ?
CutIs an overall cut grade provided, and what is it?
Polish and symmetryWhat does each separate finish grade say?
Color and clarityAre the same quality descriptions being compared?
Comments and conditionWhich report notes or later changes need explanation?

Keep report observations separate from what you learn during the current examination. Ask about a chip, abrasion, recutting or repair rather than assuming an older document answers a present-day condition question.

View the diamonds under comparable conditions

Ask to view both stones under the same lighting, at the same distance, and then under another ordinary light source. Move them gently through similar angles. This lets you compare your own impressions of brightness, contrast and appearance more consistently.

A photograph can be useful for discussion, but exposure, magnification and reflections affect what it shows. Use the picture to identify questions, and use the report and actual examination to address them. Do not infer an exact cut grade from sparkle alone.

For a mounted stone, consider how the setting affects what is visible. Compare the complete jewelry as well as the diamond rather than overlooking a loose setting or missing accent stone.

Evaluate a sale without assuming a shape premium

The round brilliant label does not establish a guaranteed resale percentage, buyer or holding-period return. Ask for a purchase offer for your actual stone and specify whether the setting and other jewelry are included.

If you have an inherited round diamond, bring the history and paperwork you possess. Ask about its cutting style before authorizing polishing, repairs or recutting. The weight guide and grading-chart reference can help organize the report details.

Arrange a round-diamond evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Bring the diamond or complete jewelry, existing reports and any repair records. Contact us to discuss the item and timing.

We buy natural polished diamonds of any size and shape, including round brilliants. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. Payment choices are cash, bank wire and business check. Confirm the offer, included items and payment arrangements for the transaction you choose.

Does Excellent cut mean two diamonds look identical?

No. Compare the full report information and the actual stones. A shared grade is a starting point for comparison, not a guarantee of identical appearance.

Should I sell now because my diamond is round brilliant?

Shape alone is not a reason to predict a future price. Base the decision on your circumstances and a current offer for the actual item, rather than a promised investment return.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Selling diamonds in Los Angeles · 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

When choosing a 14K white gold engagement ring, compare the actual setting, alloy, finish and diamond together. Karat describes gold content; it does not guarantee a particular level of durability, stone security or maintenance.

In this guide

  • Know what 14K white gold tells you
  • Examine the setting as a structure
  • View the diamond in the complete ring
  • Plan care around the actual jewelry
  • If you are selling an existing ring

Know what 14K white gold tells you

According to the World Gold Council’s jewelry guide, 14K gold is approximately 58.3% gold combined with other metals. White gold is an alloy, often finished with rhodium. Two rings with the same karat can still differ in alloy recipe, construction and surface finish.

Ask the seller to identify the setting material and finish in writing. If you have a known metal sensitivity, ask about the actual alloy rather than treating the words “white gold” as an assurance of suitability. For a broader material comparison, read our platinum and white gold guide.

Examine the setting as a structure

Look at the ring from above, from the side and beneath the center stone. Discuss prong condition, the thickness of the band, how high the stone sits and how the ring fits beside a wedding band. A low profile, halo or narrow band changes the design questions; a single karat number does not answer them.

CheckAsk before choosing
Stone mountingHow is this particular stone supported and inspected?
Band and fitIs the size comfortable, and is future resizing practical?
Side stonesWhat care does this setting require?
FinishIs it rhodium plated, and what service is recommended?
Written specificationsAre metal, diamond details and service terms recorded?

Do not infer that every 14K setting is stronger than every 18K setting. The actual alloy, design, manufacture, wear and repairs all deserve attention. A worn prong needs examination regardless of the ring’s original specifications.

View the diamond in the complete ring

GIA explains how setting metal affects diamond color appearance through reflected surroundings. View the ring in more than one ordinary lighting condition. A bright display light or photograph may not show how the piece looks on your hand.

Keep appearance separate from documented diamond grades. Compare the diamond’s 4Cs, dimensions and report details alongside your visual preferences. Ask whether a quoted carat weight refers to the center stone or all the diamonds combined.

Plan care around the actual jewelry

There is no universal replating deadline for every wearer. Ask about the finish and have wear assessed when necessary. GIA’s jewelry-care guidance discusses cleaning, chemicals and storage; the appropriate approach depends on the materials and condition.

Keep purchase and service records. Before choosing a ring, clarify any resizing, inspection, repair and return terms directly with its seller. An attractive retail presentation does not establish its future resale amount.

If you are selling an existing ring

Use our diamond-selling decision guide to prepare your piece. Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Call 310-663-1340 to discuss an evaluation. We buy natural cut and polished diamonds in any size or shape; payment options are cash, bank wire or business check.

Does a 14K mark tell me the ring never needs repairs?

No. It describes gold content, not the ongoing condition of prongs, joints or other components.

Will rhodium plating change a diamond’s recorded grade?

No. The setting can influence the stone’s appearance, but a surface finish is not a new diamond grading result.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

18K gold contains 75% gold, commonly expressed by a 750 fineness mark. To estimate its gold content, apply that fraction to the verified net alloy weight; stones, repairs, condition and complete-jewelry resale still need separate consideration.

In this guide

  • Understand the 18K and 750 descriptions

In this guide

  • Identify the parts before assigning a karat

Identify the parts before assigning a karat

Black Hills Gold designs often feature grape leaves, clusters and vines with contrasting gold colors. The name is not a universal metal recipe. For a concrete example, this Zales product description identifies a 10K gold ring with 12K green and rose-gold leaves.

That example explains why the whole ring should not automatically be valued as 18K. Your ring may have a different specification. Keep its maker information, original description and receipt if available, and note which components each description covers.

Read markings with the construction in mind

Photograph clear markings on the inner band and record any maker's symbol. A worn or missing mark leaves a question to investigate; it does not prove a fake. Likewise, a heavy ring does not prove a particular alloy.

The FTC explains gold and silver quality descriptions. Ask an evaluator to distinguish the ring's components rather than assuming a gold-colored ornament establishes the material of the band.

Preserve leaf details and known history

Look for missing leaf tips, flattened engraving, repairs and worn settings. Point out any replaced section. Avoid aggressive polishing or removing decorative parts before an evaluation; the complete design may be relevant to the offer.

If it is inherited, distinguish a documented maker or date from a family description. Our estate-jewelry valuation guide explains how to organize that information.

Ask whether the offer considers the complete ring

A metal estimate must reflect the actual materials and their applicable weights. A complete-jewelry offer may also consider condition, design, stones and maker information. Do not assume a brand adds a premium, or that it must be ignored.

Not necessarily. The specification of the actual piece and its examination matter. Ask how each metal component is being considered in the purchase offer.

What counts as scrap gold?

Scrap gold is a useful description for gold items being considered primarily for their metal content. It can include broken chains, a damaged bracelet, a single earring, an unwanted ring, or a mixture of small jewelry pieces. An item does not need to be wearable to be brought for an evaluation.

At Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds, we buy scrap gold alongside complete jewelry, heavy Cuban chains and bracelets, and gold and silver coins. Bring what you actually have; the evaluation can account for the differences between individual pieces.

Separate gold purity from the weight of the whole item

The weight of a necklace or ring is not necessarily the weight of its gold. Karat describes the proportion of gold in a gold alloy, while a scale measures everything placed on it. Stones, clasps, inserts, and other components may need separate consideration.

Group pieces by their markings if that is easy, but do not guess at unmarked items or damage them with a home test. A buyer needs to evaluate the actual material. Our guide to gold valuation explains the relationship between weight, purity, and an offer.

Broken does not always mean metal value only

A broken item may still have diamonds, a maker’s signature, unusual construction, or paperwork worth discussing. Before treating a complete piece as scrap, ask how the jewelry itself and any stones are being considered.

Bring detached parts and any loose stones with the matching item if you have them. Keep each group together so you can explain what belongs to what. Avoid unnecessary dismantling or polishing before the evaluation.

Selling a Cuban chain with or without diamonds

Heavy Cuban link necklaces and bracelets can represent a substantial collection of gold. Construction matters: two chains that look similar can have different weights or different internal construction. Diamond-set pieces also need a discussion of their stones.

We buy Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds. Ask how the gold and any diamonds contribute to the offer, and review the total amount for the pieces you are selling. See our 14K gold chain guide for more preparation questions.

Preparing a large quantity of scrap gold

For a substantial group of items, call ahead to arrange enough time for a review. Describe the types of pieces, the approximate quantity, and whether diamonds or coins are included. You do not need to know the exact value before making that call.

A simple list or photographs can help you keep track of the collection, but the purchase evaluation still requires the actual items. Bring any records you already have and keep similar pieces together where practical.

Compare the final offer and payment arrangements

Compare purchase amounts for the same group of items. Ask what the offer includes, how the gold was assessed, and how other components were treated. An online estimate or an advertised percentage does not establish the amount you will receive for your particular collection.

Payment at Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is available by cash, bank wire, or business check. For a large transaction, discuss the method you prefer when arranging your evaluation.

Visit Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Contact us to arrange your visit, or call 310-663-1340 to discuss your scrap gold, chains, jewelry, or coins.

Can I bring mixed or unmarked gold pieces?

Yes. Bring the actual pieces for evaluation. Markings can be useful, but you do not need to assign a karat to an unmarked item yourself.

Do you buy small pieces as well as large collections?

Yes. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Call ahead when bringing a substantial collection so you can discuss timing and payment.

html:
A 14K necklace or Cuban chain is evaluated using its gold content, weight, and construction. Diamond-set chains may require separate consideration of the stones.

In this guide

  • Start with the necklace’s weight and purity
  • An example of gold content, not a live quote
  • Cuban chains, hollow links, and complete jewelry
  • What if the necklace has diamonds?
  • Does a broken necklace still have value?
  • Compare offers for your actual necklace

Start with the necklace’s weight and purity

A 14K necklace contains gold alloyed with other metals. The World Gold Council explains the nominal 14/24 purity and common fineness markings. To understand a metal-value estimate, you need its gold content and the weight attributable to that material. A chain’s length or width alone does not provide those figures.

Look for any markings near the clasp, but have the actual piece evaluated before relying on a karat assumption. Read how gold is valued for a fuller explanation of the process.

An example of gold content, not a live quote

For an illustrative calculation, 10 grams of 14K gold contains about 5.83 grams of pure gold. If pure gold were hypothetically $100 per gram, the gold content in that example would be about $583.

This calculation is an example only. It is not today’s gold price and it is not a purchase offer. It assumes the weight is gold alloy and excludes adjustments for stones, other components, and the evaluation of the actual necklace.

Cuban chains, hollow links, and complete jewelry

Two necklaces with similar dimensions can have different weights. Cuban link chains, delicate necklaces, and hollow designs need to be evaluated as the pieces they are. Ask how the buyer accounts for construction and condition.

A maker’s signature, unusual design, or accompanying documentation may also merit discussion. Do not assume that the complete piece must be valued solely as scrap. Bring any paperwork you already have without delaying a call if it is missing.

What if the necklace has diamonds?

A diamond-set necklace needs consideration of its stones as well as its gold. Total scale weight includes both. Ask how the buyer assessed the diamonds and whether the purchase amount covers the complete piece.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys gold necklaces and Cuban chains with or without diamonds. If you have grading reports or original documentation, bring them with the matching items. Our diamond-buying page explains how to arrange a stone evaluation.

Does a broken necklace still have value?

Broken links, damaged clasps, and detached sections can still be brought for evaluation. Keep the pieces together and describe any known repairs. You do not need to make the necklace wearable before asking about a purchase.

If you also have single earrings, damaged bracelets, or other unwanted gold, bring them with the chain. See our scrap gold guide for preparation advice.

Compare offers for your actual necklace

Compare the same item or group of items when reviewing offers. Ask for the basis of the amount and check whether stones and other components were included. An advertised rate or the retail listing of another necklace cannot establish your final payout.

For a local evaluation, contact Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014. Single pieces, heavy chains, and large collections are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

Can I get a final offer from a necklace calculator?

A calculator provides an estimate based on the inputs you enter. The final purchase offer requires evaluation of the actual necklace and agreement on the terms.

Can I sell several necklaces at once?

Yes. We welcome multiple necklaces, Cuban chains, bracelets, and other gold pieces. Call ahead for a substantial collection so you can discuss timing and payment.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

We buy scrap gold, Cuban chains and bracelets with or without diamonds, gold coins, and silver coins. Single pieces and large quantities are welcome. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check.

Gold buying in Downtown Los Angeles · 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

Keep antique gold jewelry intact and gather records before seeking an offer. Ask the evaluator to consider the complete design, condition, stones and supported maker attribution, then compare final purchase terms for the same piece.

In this guide

  • Establish what antique means for your piece
  • Preserve details before testing or repair
  • Ask about more than gold weight
  • Compare the selling route and net result
  • Arrange an antique jewelry evaluation in Los Angeles

Establish what antique means for your piece

GIA’s antique and vintage jewelry guide describes antique jewelry as more than 100 years old and estate jewelry as pre-owned. A period-inspired design can resemble an older style without having been made in that period.

Record what you know about the item’s history and what remains uncertain. A family story, a maker’s mark and a dated receipt are different forms of evidence. Ask what supports a proposed date or attribution rather than assuming appearance alone establishes either.

Preserve details before testing or repair

Photograph the front, reverse, clasp or shank and any visible marks. Keep matching pieces and detached components together. Do not dismantle a ring, cut a chain or polish away decoration before discussing the complete item.

GIA’s care guidance explains why cleaning methods need to account for different materials and treatments. For an unfamiliar antique, ask before using chemicals or cleaning equipment. A home acid test or magnet observation is not a substitute for a suitable professional examination.

Ask about more than gold weight

Evaluation detailWhat to discuss
Gold and other materialsIdentified purity and the relevant component weights
WorkmanshipEngraving, settings, construction and repairs
StonesIdentification, condition and existing records
Maker or periodEvidence supporting the attribution
Complete conditionMissing parts, alterations and the item as it stands

A kitchen-scale reading of a finished piece includes its stones and other components. It cannot establish pure-gold content by itself. Nor does age guarantee a premium over a newer piece. Ask how the evaluator considered the actual jewelry and what uncertainties remain.

Compare the selling route and net result

A buyer’s direct purchase amount can be compared with other final purchase offers. A consignment or auction estimate concerns a possible future sale and needs its own written terms. Ask about fees, custody, payment timing and what happens if the item does not sell.

If further specialist research is proposed, clarify the purpose, cost and handling before agreeing. Our jewelry selling options guide helps you compare the arrangements, while the estate inventory guide helps organize the supporting records.

Arrange an antique jewelry evaluation in Los Angeles

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds evaluates estate and antique jewelry and buys gold jewelry and scrap gold. For diamonds, we buy natural cut and polished stones in any size or shape, excluding laboratory-grown, uncut and rough diamonds.

Our gemstone buying focuses only on large, high-quality stones, including green Colombian emeralds, Burmese rubies and Ceylon blue sapphires. A certificate is welcome but not required. Share whatever identification or origin information you already have.

Visit 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, or contact us at 310-663-1340. Confirm the exact items, purchase amount and payment terms before finalizing a sale.

Does missing a hallmark mean antique jewelry is worthless?

No. A missing or worn mark leaves a question for examination. Materials, condition and the complete piece still need evaluation.

Should I sell an antique as scrap immediately if it is damaged?

Have the complete piece considered first. Keep detached parts and records so you can understand the available offer before choosing how to sell.

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling estate jewelry in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Selling estate jewelry in Los Angeles · 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

A diamond-set watch raises three separate questions: whether the watch is authentic, what the stones are, and whether the setting was supplied by the manufacturer or added later. Appearance alone cannot answer all three.

In this guide

  • Identify the watch and the stones separately
  • Ask whether the gem setting is original
  • Read diamond descriptions in context
  • Assess the complete timepiece
  • Preserve the watch before evaluation
  • Discuss a natural-diamond watch in Downtown LA

Identify the watch and the stones separately

A familiar dial logo does not authenticate a complete watch, and bright sparkle does not establish natural diamond origin. An altered watch can contain genuine components while still differing from its original configuration.

GIA explains why natural and laboratory-grown diamond identification requires appropriate examination. Do not rely on color flashes, touch or a simple at-home visual test to decide what is set in a bezel or bracelet.

Ask whether the gem setting is original

Bring records identifying the original reference and any later work. Distinguish manufacturer-set stones, later manufacturer service components and independent aftermarket alterations where the evidence allows.

A custom diamond bezel is not automatically the same product as a factory gem-set reference. Ask how the alteration affects the complete-watch assessment. Our Rolex authentication guide explains why individual observations should not become a blanket conclusion.

Read diamond descriptions in context

The GIA diamond quality factors provide a vocabulary for discussing stones. For a watch with many small stones, distinguish a total stated weight from the weight of one diamond and ask which details were measured, documented or estimated.

Mountings may limit examination. A report concerning one stone should not be presented as identifying every stone in the watch. Keep treatment or origin information attached to the item it actually describes.

Assess the complete timepiece

Include the movement, case, dial, bezel, bracelet and clasp in the evaluation. Disclose loose stones, repairs, missing links and any known change in operation.

Adding diamonds does not guarantee an increase in resale value. A buyer's offer depends on the complete configuration and condition, rather than simply adding a retail stone bill to another watch's advertised price.

Preserve the watch before evaluation

Do not remove stones, open the case or immerse an unfamiliar watch. Ask for advice about a loose setting before handling it further. Rolex's care and servicing information is a manufacturer resource for Rolex owners; instructions for another reference should not be assumed to fit yours.

Discuss a natural-diamond watch in Downtown LA

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds buys natural, cut and polished diamonds of any size or shape. We do not buy laboratory-grown, uncut or rough diamonds. Describe any aftermarket setting when arranging a luxury-watch evaluation.
